abstract: Recognizing patterns with temporal context is important for such tasks as speech recognition, motion detection and signature verification. We propose an architecture in which time serves as its own representation, and temporal context is encoded in the state of the nodes. We contrast this with the approach of replicating portions of the architecture to represent time. As one example of these ideas, we demonstrate an architecture with capacitive inputs serving as temporal feature detectors in an otherwise standard back propagation model. Experiments involving motion detection and word discrimination serve to illustrate novel features of the system. Finally, we discuss possible extensions of the architecture.

paragraphs: A temporal pattern depends on how a signal unfolds, so its meaning cannot always be read from a single instant. This paper proposes a neural architecture in which the changing state of the nodes carries information about earlier input. Time is represented through the network’s ongoing dynamics, allowing present responses to depend on temporal context.

The authors contrast this approach with making additional copies of network components to represent different times. Their concrete example adds capacitive inputs to an otherwise standard back-propagation model. These inputs act as temporal feature detectors: they let the network respond to features of a signal’s evolution rather than only to its current value.

Experiments on motion detection and word discrimination illustrate features of the architecture. Both tasks make temporal context relevant, connecting the design to recognizable processing problems. The contribution is a way to incorporate time into the behavior of network components while retaining a familiar learning framework. The paper also discusses possible extensions of that architecture.
summary.tldr: The paper represents temporal context through changing neural states and demonstrates capacitive temporal feature detectors within a back-propagation network.

title: A Dynamical Approach to Temporal Pattern Processing

paragraphs: This study evaluates neural networks that identify five commercial aircraft from radar backscatter measurements. It examines two network types: a multilayer perceptron and a frequency-sensitive competitive learning network. Their classification performance is compared with nearest-neighbor and maximum-likelihood methods, placing the neural approaches alongside established alternatives on the same problem.

The results indicate that the neural classifiers are relatively insensitive to changes in network topology and to noise levels in the training data. For this task, changing the network's arrangement or training-data noise does not strongly change performance. This is useful information about the behavior of the classifiers, separate from how accurately they classify aircraft overall.

The traditional methods outperform the simple neural classifiers studied. The authors nevertheless see potential for improved neural-network performance. The distinction matters: the observed result favors the traditional algorithms, while the case for better neural methods remains prospective. The paper therefore offers both a direct comparative finding and evidence about which changes the tested networks tolerate relatively well.
summary.tldr: Traditional classifiers outperform the tested neural networks on aircraft radar identification, although the networks show relative insensitivity to topology and training noise.

abstract: A high speed implementation of the CMAC neural network was designed using dedicated CMOS logic. This technology was then used to implement two general purpose CMAC associative memory boards for the VME bus. Each board implements up to 8 independent CMAC networks with a total of one million adjustable weights. Each CMAC network can be configured to have from 1 to 512 integer inputs and from 1 to 8 integer outputs. Response times for typical CMAC networks are well below 1 millisecond, making the networks sufficiently fast for most robot control problems, and many pattern recognition and signal processing problems.

paragraphs: The paper describes a dedicated hardware implementation of a CMAC neural network using CMOS logic. The authors use this technology to build two general-purpose associative-memory boards for the VME bus. The contribution centers on making configurable neural computation available as a hardware component with response times suitable for time-sensitive applications.

Each board supports up to eight independent CMAC networks and contains a total of one million adjustable weights. Individual networks can be configured with between one and 512 integer inputs and between one and eight integer outputs. These options allow the same board design to accommodate different input sizes and output requirements rather than a single fixed network configuration.

Typical networks respond in well under one millisecond. The authors identify this speed as sufficient for most robot-control problems and many pattern-recognition and signal-processing problems. The significance is the combination of capacity, configurability, and short response time: the hardware is designed to make learned mappings usable where a system must react promptly.
summary.tldr: Dedicated CMOS boards support configurable CMAC networks with a million adjustable weights per board and typical response times below one millisecond.

title: Design and Implementation of a High Speed CMAC Neural Network Using Programmable CMOS Logic Cell Arrays

abstract: A second-order architecture is presented here for translation, rotation and scale invariant processing of 2-D images mapped to n input units. This new architecture has a complexity of O( n) weights as opposed to the O( n 3 ) weights usually required for a third-order, rotation invariant architecture. The reduction in complexity is due to the use of discrete frequency infor(cid:173) mation. Simulations show favorable comparisons to other neural network architectures.
originalAbstract: A second-order architecture is presented here for translation, rotation and scale invariant processing of 2-D images mapped to n input units. This new architecture has a complexity of O( n) weights as opposed to the O( n 3 ) weights usually required for a third-order, rotation invariant architecture. The reduction in complexity is due to the use of discrete frequency infor(cid:173) mation. Simulations show favorable comparisons to other neural network architectures.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a neural architecture for processing two-dimensional images while remaining insensitive to translation, rotation, and changes of scale. These invariances mean that moving, turning, or resizing an image should preserve the relevant processing result. The architectural challenge is to provide those properties without requiring an excessively large number of connection weights.

The proposed network is second-order and uses discrete frequency information. For an image represented by n input units, its weight count grows linearly with n. The abstract contrasts this with the cubic weight growth usually required by a third-order architecture that provides rotation invariance. The use of frequency information is identified as the reason for this reduction.

This difference matters as the input representation grows: linear weight growth makes expansion substantially less demanding than cubic growth. Simulations also compare the proposed design favorably with other neural architectures. The central contribution combines an invariance-oriented representation with a more economical network structure, showing that the way image information is represented can strongly affect the cost of building invariance into a model.
summary.tldr: Using discrete frequency information, a second-order image network achieves translation, rotation, and scale invariance with linearly growing weight count.

title: A Second-Order Translation, Rotation and Scale Invariant Neural Network

paragraphs: This paper asks how training data should guide the choice among neural classifiers of different complexities. Searching a large family of candidate networks can be difficult, so the authors investigate whether theoretical criteria can rule out substantial portions of that family. Their framework uses stochastic complexity and minimum description length.

The central idea is an admissible model: a model whose complexity is appropriate for consideration under the available information. The factors affecting this judgment include the amount of training data, prior belief, and class entropy, which reflects uncertainty in the class labels. Complexity is therefore assessed in relation to the learning problem rather than treated as an isolated property of a network.

The authors describe how the structure of the minimum-description-length framework can eliminate many candidate models using only limited information about the data. They discuss consequences for neural architectures and demonstrate the approach on real medical-diagnosis data. The contribution is a principled way to narrow classifier selection, connecting properties of the data and prior assumptions to the range of models worth considering.
summary.tldr: Stochastic complexity provides criteria for narrowing neural classifier choices based on data quantity, class entropy, and prior belief.

title: On Stochastic Complexity and Admissible Models for Neural Network Classifiers

abstract: Reinforcement Learning methods based on approximating dynamic programming (DP) are receiving increased attention due to their utility in forming reactive control policies for systems embedded in dynamic environments. Environments are usually modeled as controlled Markov processes, but when the environment model is not known a priori, adaptive methods are necessary. Adaptive con(cid:173) trol methods are often classified as being direct or indirect. Direct methods directly adapt the control policy from experience, whereas indirect methods adapt a model of the controlled process and com(cid:173) pute control policies based on the latest model. Our focus is on indirect adaptive DP-based methods in this paper. We present a convergence result for indirect adaptive asynchronous value itera(cid:173) tion algorithms for the case in which a look-up table is used to store the value function. Our result implies convergence of several ex(cid:173) isting reinforcement learning algorithms such as adaptive real-time dynamic programming (ARTDP) (Barto, Bradtke, & Singh, 1993) and prioritized sweeping (Moore & Atkeson, 1993). Although the emphasis of researchers studying DP-based reinforcement learning has been on direct adaptive methods such as Q-Learning (Watkins, 1989) and methods using TD algorithms (Sutton, 1988), it is not clear that these direct methods are preferable in practice to indirect methods such as those analyzed in this paper.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning methods that learn an environment model and use it to compute control policies. These are indirect adaptive methods: experience updates the model, and planning uses the latest model. This approach is relevant when the controlled environment is represented as a Markov process but its dynamics are initially unknown.

The authors establish a convergence result for indirect adaptive asynchronous value iteration. The stated setting stores the value function in a lookup table. The result therefore concerns this explicit representation of values, rather than an unspecified function approximator. It gives a theoretical basis for a family of algorithms that combine model learning with value updates.

The theorem implies convergence for existing methods including adaptive real-time dynamic programming and prioritized sweeping. Its significance is to strengthen the foundations of model-based learning while the environment model is still being adapted. The authors also question whether direct methods deserve practical preference, but the abstract does not claim that the convergence result establishes a performance advantage over them.
summary.tldr: The paper proves convergence for a family of model-based asynchronous value-iteration algorithms using tabular value functions.

title: Convergence of Indirect Adaptive Asynchronous Value Iteration Algorithms

abstract: We implement a model of obstacle avoidance in flying insects on a small, monocular robot. The result is a system that is capable of rapid navigation through a dense obstacle field. The key to the system is the use of zigzag behavior to articulate the body during movement. It is shown that this behavior compensates for a parallax blind spot surrounding the focus of expansion nor(cid:173) mally found in systems without parallax behavior. The system models the coop(cid:173) eration of several behaviors: halteres-ocular response (similar to VOR), optomotor response, and the parallax field computation and mapping to motor system. The resulting system is neurally plausible, very simple, and should be easily hosted on a VLSI hardware.

The key to the system is the use of zigzag behavior to articulate the body during movement. It is shown that this behavior compensates for a parallax blind spot surrounding the focus of expansion nor(cid:173) mally found in systems without parallax behavior. The system models the coop(cid:173) eration of several behaviors: halteres-ocular response (similar to VOR), optomotor response, and the parallax field computation and mapping to motor system. paragraphs: The paper implements an insect-inspired obstacle-avoidance model on a small robot with one camera. The robot can navigate rapidly through a dense field of obstacles. Its distinctive feature is zigzag movement, which changes how the body moves through the scene and thereby changes the visual information available for avoiding obstacles.

The authors show that this behavior compensates for a parallax blind spot around the focus of expansion. That region is problematic in systems lacking the relevant parallax-producing behavior. Zigzag motion therefore serves a perceptual purpose: the robot's movement helps address a weakness in the visual information generated by its travel.

The system combines a halteres-ocular response, described as similar to the vestibulo-ocular reflex, an optomotor response, and computation of the parallax field linked to motor control. The resulting design is described as simple and neurally plausible, with potential for VLSI implementation. The main contribution is the cooperation between visual processing and deliberate body movement in a working navigation system.
summary.tldr: An insect-inspired robot uses zigzag movement to compensate for a visual parallax blind spot and avoid dense obstacles.

title: Visual Navigation in a Robot Using Zig-Zag Behavior

abstract: For many problems, the correct behavior of a model depends not only on its input-output mapping but also on properties of its Jacobian matrix, the matrix of partial derivatives of the model's outputs with respect to its in(cid:173) puts. We introduce the J-prop algorithm, an efficient general method for computing the exact partial derivatives of a variety of simple functions of the Jacobian of a model with respect to its free parameters. The algorithm applies to any parametrized feedforward model, including nonlinear re(cid:173) gression, multilayer perceptrons, and radial basis function networks.
originalAbstract: For many problems, the correct behavior of a model depends not only on its input-output mapping but also on properties of its Jacobian matrix, the matrix of partial derivatives of the model's outputs with respect to its in(cid:173) puts. We introduce the J-prop algorithm, an efficient general method for computing the exact partial derivatives of a variety of simple functions of the Jacobian of a model with respect to its free parameters. The algorithm applies to any parametrized feedforward model, including nonlinear re(cid:173) gression, multilayer perceptrons, and radial basis function networks.

paragraphs: The paper addresses models whose desired behavior depends on how their outputs respond to changes in their inputs. This local response is described by the Jacobian, a matrix containing the partial derivatives of outputs with respect to inputs. Specifying the desired input-output relationship can therefore also involve specifying properties of this matrix.

The authors introduce J-prop, an efficient method for computing exact derivatives of various simple functions of the Jacobian with respect to model parameters. There are two derivative relationships involved: the Jacobian describes sensitivity to inputs, and J-prop determines how a chosen measure of that sensitivity changes when the model's parameters change.

These parameter derivatives supply the information needed to adjust a model according to an objective involving its Jacobian. The method applies to any parameterized feedforward model, including nonlinear regression models, multilayer perceptrons, and radial basis function networks. Its contribution is a general computational procedure for this class of derivative calculations, allowing input sensitivity to be treated directly as a property to optimize.
summary.tldr: J-prop efficiently computes exact parameter derivatives for a variety of simple functions of a feedforward model's Jacobian.

title: Differentiating Functions of the Jacobian with Respect to the Weights

abstract: In this paper we propose a general framework to study the generalization properties of binary classiﬁers trained with data which may be depen- dent, but are deterministically generated upon a sample of independent examples. It provides generalization bounds for binary classiﬁcation and some cases of ranking problems, and clariﬁes the relationship between these learning tasks.
originalAbstract: In this paper we propose a general framework to study the generalization properties of binary classiﬁers trained with data which may be depen- dent, but are deterministically generated upon a sample of independent examples. It provides generalization bounds for binary classiﬁcation and some cases of ranking problems, and clariﬁes the relationship between these learning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to bound the generalization error of binary classifiers when their training examples may depend on one another. It considers a particular source of dependence: the training data are generated deterministically from an underlying sample of independent examples. Independence therefore remains present at the source, even though it need not hold among the derived training items.

The authors propose a general framework for analyzing this situation and derive generalization bounds for binary classification. Such bounds concern how training with the available observations relates to performance beyond them. The framework makes the construction of the dependent data part of the analysis, rather than assuming those derived examples are themselves independent.

The results also cover some ranking problems and clarify their relationship with binary classification. This extends the usefulness of the framework while preserving its stated scope: it addresses dependence produced through deterministic transformations of an independent sample. The contribution is a theoretical way to reason about these linked observations and learning tasks, rather than a claim covering every possible form of dependent data.
summary.tldr: A theoretical framework bounds classification and some ranking errors when dependent training data are deterministically derived from independent examples.

title: Generalization error bounds for classifiers trained with interdependent data

abstract: Kernel-based regularized learning seeks a model in a hypothesis space by minimizing the empirical error and the model's complexity. Based on the representer theorem, the solution consists of a linear combination of translates of a kernel. This paper investigates a generalized form of representer theorem for kernel-based learning. After mapping predefined features and translates of a kernel simultaneously onto a hypothesis space by a specific way of constructing kernels, we proposed a new algorithm by utilizing a generalized regularizer which leaves part of the space unregularized. Using a squared-loss function in calculating the empirical error, a simple convex solution is obtained which combines predefined features with translates of the kernel. Empirical evaluations have confirmed the effectiveness of the algorithm for supervised learning tasks.
originalAbstract: Kernel-based regularized learning seeks a model in a hypothesis space by minimizing the empirical error and the model's complexity. Based on the representer theorem, the solution consists of a linear combination of translates of a kernel. This paper investigates a generalized form of representer theorem for kernel-based learning. After mapping predefined features and translates of a kernel simultaneously onto a hypothesis space by a specific way of constructing kernels, we proposed a new algorithm by utilizing a generalized regularizer which leaves part of the space unregularized. Using a squared-loss function in calculating the empirical error, a simple convex solution is obtained which combines predefined features with translates of the kernel. Empirical evaluations have confirmed the effectiveness of the algorithm for supervised learning tasks.

paragraphs: Kernel-based learning balances fitting training observations against controlling model complexity. The representer theorem expresses the resulting solution using combinations of kernel functions anchored at data points. This paper extends that framework so that predefined features can participate in the same model, bringing supplied feature structure into kernel-based regularized learning.

The authors construct kernels that map both the predefined features and kernel translates into a common hypothesis space. They then introduce a generalized regularizer that leaves part of that space unpenalized. This allows different parts of the model to receive different treatment when complexity is controlled, while retaining a unified learning formulation.

With squared prediction error as the loss, the formulation yields a simple convex solution combining predefined features and kernel translates. The generalized representer theorem provides the theoretical support for that solution. Empirical evaluations confirm effectiveness on supervised learning tasks. The contribution is therefore a principled way to include predefined features within regularized kernel learning, together with an algorithm whose optimization remains convex.
summary.tldr: A generalized representer theorem supports convex least-squares learning that combines predefined features with kernel functions.

title: Generalized Regularized Least-Squares Learning with Predefined Features in a Hilbert Space

abstract: Using multiple regularization hyperparameters is an effective method for managing model complexity in problems where input features have varying amounts of noise. While algorithms for choosing multiple hyperparameters are often used in neural networks and support vector machines, they are not common in structured prediction tasks, such as sequence labeling or parsing. In this paper, we consider the problem of learning regularization hyperparameters for log-linear models, a class of probabilistic models for structured prediction tasks which includes conditional random fields (CRFs). Using an implicit differentiation trick, we derive an efficient gradient-based method for learning Gaussian regularization priors with multiple hyperparameters. In both simulations and the real-world task of computational RNA secondary structure prediction, we find that multiple hyperparameter learning provides a significant boost in accuracy compared to models learned using only a single regularization hyperparameter.
originalAbstract: Using multiple regularization hyperparameters is an effective method for managing model complexity in problems where input features have varying amounts of noise. While algorithms for choosing multiple hyperparameters are often used in neural networks and support vector machines, they are not common in structured prediction tasks, such as sequence labeling or parsing. In this paper, we consider the problem of learning regularization hyperparameters for log-linear models, a class of probabilistic models for structured prediction tasks which includes conditional random fields (CRFs). Using an implicit differentiation trick, we derive an efficient gradient-based method for learning Gaussian regularization priors with multiple hyperparameters. In both simulations and the real-world task of computational RNA secondary structure prediction, we find that multiple hyperparameter learning provides a significant boost in accuracy compared to models learned using only a single regularization hyperparameter.

paragraphs: Regularization controls model complexity, but different input features can contain different amounts of noise. A single regularization setting applies one overall level of control, while multiple settings can express different degrees of constraint. This paper develops a way to learn those settings for log-linear models used in structured prediction, including conditional random fields.

The authors focus on Gaussian regularization priors with multiple hyperparameters. They use implicit differentiation to derive an efficient gradient-based learning method. The relevant gradients account for how the learned model depends on its regularization settings, providing a computational route to adjusting several settings together. This brings multiple-hyperparameter learning into tasks such as sequence labeling and parsing.

The method is evaluated in simulations and in computational prediction of RNA secondary structure. In both settings, learning multiple hyperparameters yields a significant accuracy improvement over learning with only one. The findings support adapting regularization more finely when feature noise varies, and demonstrate that the proposed optimization method can make this useful for structured prediction.
summary.tldr: Implicit differentiation enables efficient learning of multiple regularization settings for log-linear models, improving accuracy in simulations and RNA structure prediction.

title: Efficient multiple hyperparameter learning for log-linear models

abstract: The Singular Value Decomposition is a key operation in many machine learning methods. Its computational cost, however, makes it unscalable and impractical for the massive-sized datasets becoming common in applications. We present a new method, QUIC-SVD, for fast approximation of the full SVD with automatic sample size minimization and empirical relative error control. Previous Monte Carlo approaches have not addressed the full SVD nor benefited from the efficiency of automatic, empirically-driven sample sizing. Our empirical tests show speedups of several orders of magnitude over exact SVD. Such scalability should enable QUIC-SVD to meet the needs of a wide array of methods and applications.
originalAbstract: The Singular Value Decomposition is a key operation in many machine learning methods. Its computational cost, however, makes it unscalable and impractical for the massive-sized datasets becoming common in applications. We present a new method, QUIC-SVD, for fast approximation of the full SVD with automatic sample size minimization and empirical relative error control. Previous Monte Carlo approaches have not addressed the full SVD nor benefited from the efficiency of automatic, empirically-driven sample sizing. Our empirical tests show speedups of several orders of magnitude over exact SVD. Such scalability should enable QUIC-SVD to meet the needs of a wide array of methods and applications.

paragraphs: Singular value decomposition is used in many machine learning methods, but its computational expense can make exact calculation impractical for very large datasets. The paper introduces QUIC-SVD as a fast approximation to the full decomposition. Its aim is to make this underlying operation more scalable for methods that depend on it.

The approach automatically adjusts sample size using empirical information and provides empirical relative-error control. Sample sizing matters because it determines how much work the approximation performs. By choosing that size automatically, the method seeks to avoid unnecessary sampling while keeping approximation quality under observation. The authors distinguish this combination from earlier Monte Carlo approaches that did not address the full SVD.

Empirical tests show speedups of several orders of magnitude compared with exact SVD. These findings establish a substantial computational advantage in the reported evaluations, while the error control is explicitly empirical. The authors argue that this scalability should support a broad range of methods and applications, treating that wider reach as an expected consequence of accelerating a common computational operation.
summary.tldr: QUIC-SVD approximates the full SVD with adaptive sample sizing and empirical error control, achieving large speedups in reported tests.

title: QUIC-SVD: Fast SVD Using Cosine Trees

abstract: We introduce skill chaining, a skill discovery method for reinforcement learning agents in continuous domains, that builds chains of skills leading to an end-of-task reward. We demonstrate experimentally that it creates skills that result in performance benefits in a challenging continuous domain.
originalAbstract: We introduce skill chaining, a skill discovery method for reinforcement learning agents in continuous domains, that builds chains of skills leading to an end-of-task reward. We demonstrate experimentally that it creates skills that result in performance benefits in a challenging continuous domain.

paragraphs: This paper introduces skill chaining, a method for discovering skills in reinforcement learning problems with continuous domains. Its organizing idea is to build chains of skills that lead toward a reward delivered at the end of a task. The connection among skills is central: discovery is directed toward assembling a route to the task’s rewarded outcome.

The approach gives skill discovery a task-oriented structure. A discovered skill contributes as part of a chain whose eventual destination is the end-of-task reward. This makes the relationship between skills and the overall objective explicit. The method is presented for continuous domains, placing the construction of these connected skills within that reinforcement learning setting.

The authors demonstrate experimentally that the resulting skills provide performance benefits in a challenging continuous domain. This supports the usefulness of skill chaining in the evaluated problem. The stated finding concerns the benefit of the skills the method creates, linking the proposed chain-building idea to improved task performance. The contribution is therefore both a method for organizing skill discovery and an experimental demonstration that its discovered skills can help an agent.
summary.tldr: Skill chaining discovers connected skills leading to an end-of-task reward and demonstrates performance benefits in a challenging continuous domain.

title: Skill Discovery in Continuous Reinforcement Learning Domains using Skill Chaining

abstract: Motivated by applications in electronic games as well as teaching systems, we investigate the problem of dynamic difficulty adjustment. The task here is to repeatedly find a game difficulty setting that is neither `too easy' and bores the player, nor `too difficult' and overburdens the player. The contributions of this paper are ($i$) formulation of difficulty adjustment as an online learning problem on partially ordered sets, ($ii$) an exponential update algorithm for dynamic difficulty adjustment, ($iii$) a bound on the number of wrong difficulty settings relative to the best static setting chosen in hindsight, and ($iv$) an empirical investigation of the algorithm when playing against adversaries.
originalAbstract: Motivated by applications in electronic games as well as teaching systems, we investigate the problem of dynamic difficulty adjustment. The task here is to repeatedly find a game difficulty setting that is neither `too easy' and bores the player, nor `too difficult' and overburdens the player. The contributions of this paper are ($i$) formulation of difficulty adjustment as an online learning problem on partially ordered sets, ($ii$) an exponential update algorithm for dynamic difficulty adjustment, ($iii$) a bound on the number of wrong difficulty settings relative to the best static setting chosen in hindsight, and ($iv$) an empirical investigation of the algorithm when playing against adversaries.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a system can repeatedly choose a suitable difficulty level for a user. The motivating applications are electronic games and teaching systems, where an easy setting may become boring while a difficult one may become overwhelming. The task is to adjust choices over time while avoiding settings that fall on either side of this desired balance.

The authors formulate difficulty adjustment as an online learning problem on partially ordered sets. This places the relationships among possible settings inside a formal learning framework. They propose an exponential update algorithm for making successive difficulty choices, turning the practical adjustment problem into a procedure that can be analyzed mathematically.

The theoretical result bounds the number of wrong difficulty settings relative to the best fixed setting chosen after seeing the full sequence. That hindsight comparator defines the scope of the guarantee: it evaluates the adaptive procedure against a single static choice. The paper also investigates the algorithm empirically against adversaries, connecting the formal analysis to tests of its behavior under challenging sequences.
summary.tldr: An online difficulty-adjustment algorithm bounds wrong settings relative to the best fixed setting chosen in hindsight.

title: Predicting Dynamic Difficulty

abstract: Probabilistic planning captures the uncertainty of plan execution by probabilistically modeling the effects of actions in the environment, and therefore the probability of reaching different states from a given state and action. In order to compute a solution for a probabilistic planning problem, planners need to manage the uncertainty associated with the different paths from the initial state to a goal state. Several approaches to manage uncertainty were proposed, e.g., consider all paths at once, perform determinization of actions, and sampling. In this paper, we introduce trajectory-based short-sighted Stochastic Shortest Path Problems (SSPs), a novel approach to manage uncertainty for probabilistic planning problems in which states reachable with low probability are substituted by artificial goals that heuristically estimate their cost to reach a goal state. We also extend the theoretical results of Short-Sighted Probabilistic Planner (SSiPP) [ref] by proving that SSiPP always finishes and is asymptotically optimal under sufficient conditions on the structure of short-sighted SSPs. We empirically compare SSiPP using trajectory-based short-sighted SSPs with the winners of the previous probabilistic planning competitions and other state-of-the-art planners in the triangle tireworld problems. Trajectory-based SSiPP outperforms all the competitors and is the only planner able to scale up to problem number 60, a problem in which the optimal solution contains approximately $10^{70}$ states.

This paper introduces trajectory-based short-sighted stochastic shortest-path problems, which simplify that uncertainty by replacing states reached with low probability with artificial goals.

These artificial goals carry heuristic estimates of the remaining cost to reach a real goal. The planner can therefore concentrate on a reduced problem while retaining estimated consequences for less likely outcomes. The authors also extend the theory of the Short-Sighted Probabilistic Planner, proving termination and asymptotic optimality under sufficient conditions on the structure of the short-sighted problems.

summary.tldr: Replacing unlikely states with heuristic artificial goals enables strong planning performance and conditional termination and asymptotic-optimality guarantees.

title: Trajectory-Based Short-Sighted Probabilistic Planning

abstract: We study two communication-efficient algorithms for distributed statistical optimization on large-scale data. The first algorithm is an averaging method that distributes the $N$ data samples evenly to $m$ machines, performs separate minimization on each subset, and then averages the estimates. We provide a sharp analysis of this average mixture algorithm, showing that under a reasonable set of conditions, the combined parameter achieves mean-squared error that decays as $\order(N^{-1}+(N/m)^{-2})$. Whenever $m \le \sqrt{N}$, this guarantee matches the best possible rate achievable by a centralized algorithm having access to all $N$ samples. The second algorithm is a novel method, based on an appropriate form of the bootstrap. Requiring only a single round of communication, it has mean-squared error that decays as $\order(N^{-1}+(N/m)^{-3})$, and so is more robust to the amount of parallelization. We complement our theoretical results with experiments on large-scale problems from the Microsoft Learning to Rank dataset.

paragraphs: Distributing statistical estimation across machines raises a practical question: how much accuracy can be retained with little communication? The paper studies two approaches that combine work performed on separate portions of a large dataset. Its analysis makes explicit how the number of machines interacts with the total amount of data.

The first method divides N samples evenly among m machines, minimizes an objective separately on each subset, and averages the resulting estimates. Under the stated conditions, its mean-squared error has order N⁻¹ + (N/m)⁻². When m is no larger than √N, this matches the best rate available to a centralized method using all samples.

The second method uses a suitable bootstrap construction and requires only one communication round. Its error has order N⁻¹ + (N/m)⁻³, making its guarantee more tolerant of increasing parallelization. The comparison shows why simply averaging local estimates can work well, and how the bootstrap method improves the dependence on local sample size. Experiments use large-scale problems from the Microsoft Learning to Rank dataset.
summary.tldr: Local averaging and a bootstrap-based alternative offer distributed estimation guarantees that quantify the accuracy cost of parallelization.

title: Communication-Efficient Algorithms for Statistical Optimization

abstract: As massively parallel computations have become broadly available with modern GPUs, deep architectures trained on very large datasets have risen in popularity. Discriminatively trained convolutional neural networks, in particular, were recently shown to yield state-of-the-art performance in challenging image classification benchmarks such as ImageNet. However, elements of these architectures are similar to standard hand-crafted representations used in computer vision. In this paper, we explore the extent of this analogy, proposing a version of the state-of-the-art Fisher vector image encoding that can be stacked in multiple layers. This architecture significantly improves on standard Fisher vectors, and obtains competitive results with deep convolutional networks at a significantly smaller computational cost. Our hybrid architecture allows us to measure the performance improvement brought by a deeper image classification pipeline, while staying in the realms of conventional SIFT features and FV encodings.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how much image classification can benefit from depth while retaining conventional visual features and encodings. Its starting observation is that parts of deep convolutional architectures resemble components of established handcrafted image representations. The authors use that resemblance to construct a deeper pipeline around Fisher vector encoding.

The main contribution is a version of Fisher vector encoding that can be stacked into multiple layers. The resulting hybrid architecture continues to use SIFT features and Fisher vector representations. This gives the authors a way to examine the performance contribution of a deeper classification pipeline within that familiar representation framework.

The paper reports a substantial improvement over standard Fisher vectors and results competitive with deep convolutional networks at a substantially smaller computational cost. These findings support the usefulness of adding depth to this conventional encoding approach in the reported comparisons. They also make the architecture informative beyond its immediate classification performance: it offers a concrete way to investigate depth without changing the pipeline entirely to convolutional neural networks.
summary.tldr: Stacking Fisher vector encodings improves image classification and yields results competitive with deep convolutional networks at lower reported computational cost.

title: Deep Fisher Networks for Large-Scale Image Classification

abstract: Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) is a popular data analysis method, the objective of which is to decompose a matrix with all nonnegative components into the product of two other nonnegative matrices. In this work, we describe a new simple and efficient algorithm for multi-factor nonnegative matrix factorization problem ({mfNMF}), which generalizes the original NMF problem to more than two factors. Furthermore, we extend the mfNMF algorithm to incorporate a regularizer based on Dirichlet distribution over normalized columns to encourage sparsity in the obtained factors. Our sparse NMF algorithm affords a closed form and an intuitive interpretation, and is more efficient in comparison with previous works that use fix point iterations. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithms on both synthetic and real data sets.

Furthermore, we extend the mfNMF algorithm to incorporate a regularizer based on Dirichlet distribution over normalized columns to encourage sparsity in the obtained factors. Our sparse NMF algorithm affords a closed form and an intuitive interpretation, and is more efficient in comparison with previous works that use fix point iterations. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithms on both synthetic and real data sets.

paragraphs: Nonnegative matrix factorization represents a matrix of nonnegative values as a product of nonnegative matrices. The usual formulation uses two factors. This paper develops a simple, efficient algorithm for the more general case with multiple factors, expanding the factorization structure while keeping the nonnegativity requirement on the components.

The authors also extend the algorithm to encourage sparse factors. Their regularizer is based on a Dirichlet distribution applied to normalized columns. Sparsity favors representations in which fewer components are active, so this extension changes the kind of factorization sought as well as how it is computed. The paper presents the sparse method in closed form with an intuitive interpretation.

The authors report greater efficiency than earlier approaches that rely on fixed-point iterations. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithms. The contribution thus joins two developments: a practical method for factorizing into more than two matrices and a sparsity-promoting extension designed to avoid the iterative burden of the compared approaches.
summary.tldr: An efficient multi-factor NMF algorithm gains a closed-form, Dirichlet-based extension that encourages sparse factors.

title: On Algorithms for Sparse Multi-factor NMF

abstract: We design and analyze minimax-optimal algorithms for online linear optimization games where the player's choice is unconstrained. The player strives to minimize regret, the difference between his loss and the loss of a post-hoc benchmark strategy. The standard benchmark is the loss of the best strategy chosen from a bounded comparator set, whereas we consider a broad range of benchmark functions. We consider the problem as a sequential multi-stage zero-sum game, and we give a thorough analysis of the minimax behavior of the game, providing characterizations for the value of the game, as well as both the player's and the adversary's optimal strategy. We show how these objects can be computed efficiently under certain circumstances, and by selecting an appropriate benchmark, we construct a novel hedging strategy for an unconstrained betting game.

paragraphs: Online linear optimization involves making choices sequentially and comparing the accumulated loss with a benchmark defined afterward. This difference is called regret. The paper studies games in which the player's choices are unconstrained and considers a broad range of benchmark functions beyond the usual best strategy in a bounded comparator set.

The authors formulate the problem as a sequential zero-sum game between a player and an adversary. Their minimax analysis characterizes the game's value together with optimal strategies for both sides. This establishes how the benchmark and the adversarial interaction determine the best worst-case performance, rather than evaluating only a single proposed update rule.

The paper also identifies circumstances in which these quantities and strategies can be computed efficiently. That computational claim is conditional, rather than an assertion that every benchmark leads to an efficient solution. As an application, selecting an appropriate benchmark yields a new hedging strategy for an unconstrained betting game. The result shows how a general analysis of benchmark functions can lead to a concrete sequential decision strategy.
summary.tldr: A minimax analysis of unconstrained online linear games characterizes optimal strategies and yields a new betting hedge through benchmark selection.

title: Minimax Optimal Algorithms for Unconstrained Linear Optimization

abstract: Most work on sequential learning assumes a fixed set of actions that are available all the time. However, in practice, actions can consist of picking subsets of readings from sensors that may break from time to time, road segments that can be blocked or goods that are out of stock. In this paper we study learning algorithms that are able to deal with stochastic availability of such unreliable composite actions. We propose and analyze algorithms based on the Follow-The-Perturbed-Leader prediction method for several learning settings differing in the feedback provided to the learner. Our algorithms rely on a novel loss estimation technique that we call Counting Asleep Times. We deliver regret bounds for our algorithms for the previously studied full information and (semi-)bandit settings, as well as a natural middle point between the two that we call the restricted information setting. A special consequence of our results is a significant improvement of the best known performance guarantees achieved by an efficient algorithm for the sleeping bandit problem with stochastic availability. Finally, we evaluate our algorithms empirically and show their improvement over the known approaches.

paragraphs: Sequential decision-making often assumes that the same actions are always available. This paper studies composite actions whose availability changes randomly, as when sensors fail, roads close, or products sell out. The learner must choose from the currently available combinations while dealing with adversarial losses.

The authors develop algorithms based on Follow-The-Perturbed-Leader and a new loss estimation technique called Counting Asleep Times. Their analysis covers several feedback settings: full information, bandit and semi-bandit feedback, and an intermediate restricted-information setting. This distinguishes uncertainty about an action's availability from uncertainty caused by how much loss information the learner receives.

The paper establishes regret bounds across these settings. One consequence is a significant improvement in the best known guarantees for an efficient sleeping-bandit algorithm under stochastic availability. Empirical evaluations also show improvements over known approaches. Together, the theoretical and experimental results support learning methods that explicitly accommodate unreliable action availability, rather than treating a fixed decision set as a prerequisite for sequential optimization.
summary.tldr: New loss estimation and perturbed-leader algorithms improve regret guarantees and empirical performance when composite actions are randomly unavailable.

title: Online combinatorial optimization with stochastic decision sets and adversarial losses

abstract: The Birkhoff polytope (the convex hull of the set of permutation matrices), which is represented using $\Theta(n^2)$ variables and constraints, is frequently invoked in formulating relaxations of optimization problems over permutations. Using a recent construction of Goemans (2010), we show that when optimizing over the convex hull of the permutation vectors (the permutahedron), we can reduce the number of variables and constraints to $\Theta(n \log n)$ in theory and $\Theta(n \log^2 n)$ in practice. We modify the recent convex formulation of the 2-SUM problem introduced by Fogel et al. (2013) to use this polytope, and demonstrate how we can attain results of similar quality in significantly less computational time for large $n$. To our knowledge, this is the first usage of Goemans' compact formulation of the permutahedron in a convex optimization problem. We also introduce a simpler regularization scheme for this convex formulation of the 2-SUM problem that yields good empirical results.

paragraphs: Optimization over permutations can be approached by replacing discrete choices with a continuous convex set. A common representation uses the Birkhoff polytope, the convex hull of permutation matrices, and requires a quadratic number of variables and constraints. This paper investigates a more compact representation when the relevant objects are permutation vectors.

The authors use a construction for the permutahedron, the convex hull of those vectors. It reduces the representation size to Θ(n log n) in theory and Θ(n log² n) in practice. They adapt an existing convex formulation of the 2-SUM problem to use this smaller polytope, making the representation itself the source of computational savings.

For large problems, the adapted formulation produces results of similar quality in substantially less computation time. The paper also introduces a simpler regularization scheme with good empirical results. The scope matters: the compact formulation concerns optimization over permutation vectors, and the demonstrated computational benefits come from applying it to the stated 2-SUM formulation.
summary.tldr: A compact permutahedron formulation reduces the size of vector-permutation relaxations and accelerates a convex 2-SUM method while preserving similar solution quality.

title: Beyond the Birkhoff Polytope: Convex Relaxations for Vector Permutation Problems

abstract: We show that the maximum-likelihood (ML) estimate of models derived from Luce's choice axiom (e.g., the Plackett-Luce model) can be expressed as the stationary distribution of a Markov chain. This conveys insight into several recently proposed spectral inference algorithms. We take advantage of this perspective and formulate a new spectral algorithm that is significantly more accurate than previous ones for the Plackett--Luce model. With a simple adaptation, this algorithm can be used iteratively, producing a sequence of estimates that converges to the ML estimate. The ML version runs faster than competing approaches on a benchmark of five datasets. Our algorithms are easy to implement, making them relevant for practitioners at large.

The ML version runs faster than competing approaches on a benchmark of five datasets. Our algorithms are easy to implement, making them relevant for practitioners at large.

paragraphs: This paper connects maximum-likelihood estimation for models derived from Luce's choice axiom with the stationary distribution of a Markov chain. The connection includes the Plackett–Luce model. A stationary distribution is a probability distribution that remains unchanged by the chain's transition rule, giving a different mathematical view of the estimation problem.

The authors use this perspective to explain several existing spectral inference algorithms and to develop a new one. For the Plackett–Luce model, the new spectral algorithm is reported to be significantly more accurate than previous spectral approaches. A simple modification also lets it run iteratively, producing estimates that converge to the maximum-likelihood solution.

On a benchmark comprising five datasets, the iterative maximum-likelihood version runs faster than competing approaches. The authors also emphasize that the algorithms are easy to implement. The contribution therefore combines a structural explanation of estimation with practical algorithms: the Markov-chain connection supports both a more accurate spectral estimate and an iterative route to maximum likelihood.
summary.tldr: A Markov-chain view yields more accurate spectral estimates for Plackett–Luce models and a fast iterative method converging to maximum likelihood.

title: Fast and Accurate Inference of Plackett–Luce Models

abstract: Boltzmann machines are able to learn highly complex, multimodal, structured and multiscale real-world data distributions. Parameters of the model are usually learned by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence from training samples to the learned model. We propose in this work a novel approach for Boltzmann machine training which assumes that a meaningful metric between observations is known. This metric between observations can then be used to define the Wasserstein distance between the distribution induced by the Boltzmann machine on the one hand, and that given by the training sample on the other hand. We derive a gradient of that distance with respect to the model parameters. Minimization of this new objective leads to generative models with different statistical properties. We demonstrate their practical potential on data completion and denoising, for which the metric between observations plays a crucial role.

Their parameters are usually learned by minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence between the training data and the model distribution. This paper proposes a different training objective that incorporates a meaningful distance between individual observations.

The approach assumes that this observation-level metric is known. It uses the metric to define a Wasserstein distance between the distribution represented by the model and the distribution given by the training sample. The authors derive a gradient of this distance with respect to model parameters, providing a way to optimize the proposed objective.

Training with the new objective yields generative models with different statistical properties. The authors demonstrate their practical potential on data completion and denoising, tasks where the metric between observations plays a crucial role. The contribution connects the chosen notion of similarity in data space with the objective used to fit a generative model, and shows applications in which that connection is useful.
summary.tldr: Wasserstein training uses a known metric between observations to fit Boltzmann machines, with demonstrated potential for completion and denoising.

title: Wasserstein Training of Restricted Boltzmann Machines

abstract: In recent years, structured matrix recovery problems have gained considerable attention for its real world applications, such as recommender systems and computer vision. Much of the existing work has focused on matrices with low-rank structure, and limited progress has been made on matrices with other types of structure. In this paper we present non-asymptotic analysis for estimation of generally structured matrices via the generalized Dantzig selector based on sub-Gaussian measurements. We show that the estimation error can always be succinctly expressed in terms of a few geometric measures such as Gaussian widths of suitable sets associated with the structure of the underlying true matrix. Further, we derive general bounds on these geometric measures for structures characterized by unitarily invariant norms, a large family covering most matrix norms of practical interest. Examples are provided to illustrate the utility of our theoretical development.

paragraphs: Recovering a matrix from measurements is useful in applications such as recommendation and computer vision. Much of the associated theory emphasizes low-rank matrices, leaving other kinds of structure less developed. This paper studies a broader matrix-recovery setting using an estimator called the generalized Dantzig selector.

The authors provide a non-asymptotic analysis under sub-Gaussian measurements, meaning their results concern finite amounts of data rather than only a limiting regime. They express estimation error using a small collection of geometric quantities associated with the true matrix's structure. These include Gaussian widths, which serve as measures of the relevant sets' geometric complexity.

The paper then derives general bounds on these quantities for structures described by unitarily invariant norms, a broad family containing many practically relevant matrix norms. Examples illustrate how the theory can be applied. The contribution is a common way to analyze recovery across matrix structures: characterize the appropriate geometry, bound its complexity, and use those quantities to express estimation error within the stated measurement setting.
summary.tldr: Finite-sample recovery bounds express error through geometric complexity for broadly structured matrices under sub-Gaussian measurements.

title: Structured Matrix Recovery via the Generalized Dantzig Selector

abstract: The importance of studying the robustness of learners to malicious data is well established. While much work has been done establishing both robust estimators and effective data injection attacks when the attacker is omniscient, the ability of an attacker to provably harm learning while having access to little information is largely unstudied. We study the potential of a “blind attacker” to provably limit a learner’s performance by data injection attack without observing the learner’s training set or any parameter of the distribution from which it is drawn. We provide examples of simple yet effective attacks in two settings: firstly, where an “informed learner” knows the strategy chosen by the attacker, and secondly, where a “blind learner” knows only the proportion of malicious data and some family to which the malicious distribution chosen by the attacker belongs. For each attack, we analyze minimax rates of convergence and establish lower bounds on the learner’s minimax risk, exhibiting limits on a learner’s ability to learn under data injection attack even when the attacker is “blind”.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much damage malicious training data can cause when the attacker knows very little. The attacker cannot inspect the learner's training set and does not know any parameter of the distribution generating it. The issue is whether this lack of information still permits attacks with provable consequences for learning.

The authors construct simple data-injection attacks under two different assumptions about the learner's knowledge. An informed learner knows the attacker's chosen strategy. A blind learner knows only the fraction of malicious observations and a family containing the attacker's malicious distribution. These settings separate the attacker's limited information from the information available to the defender.

For each attack, the analysis establishes lower bounds on minimax risk and examines convergence rates. These bounds describe unavoidable worst-case estimation difficulty, rather than merely showing that a particular learning algorithm performs poorly. The examples demonstrate that an attacker need not observe the training data to create fundamental obstacles to learning. They also show why knowing the attack strategy and knowing only its broad characteristics are meaningfully different defensive settings.
summary.tldr: Simple data-injection attacks can impose provable learning limits even without access to training data or distribution parameters.

title: Blind Attacks on Machine Learners

abstract: Given recent deep learning results that demonstrate the ability to effectively optimize high-dimensional non-convex functions with gradient descent optimization on GPUs, we ask in this paper whether symbolic gradient optimization tools such as Tensorflow can be effective for planning in hybrid (mixed discrete and continuous) nonlinear domains with high dimensional state and action spaces? To this end, we demonstrate that hybrid planning with Tensorflow and RMSProp gradient descent is competitive with mixed integer linear program (MILP) based optimization on piecewise linear planning domains (where we can compute optimal solutions) and substantially outperforms state-of-the-art interior point methods for nonlinear planning domains. Furthermore, we remark that Tensorflow is highly scalable, converging to a strong plan on a large-scale concurrent domain with a total of 576,000 continuous action parameters distributed over a horizon of 96 time steps and 100 parallel instances in only 4 minutes. We provide a number of insights that clarify such strong performance including observations that despite long horizons, RMSProp avoids both the vanishing and exploding gradient problems. Together these results suggest a new frontier for highly scalable planning in nonlinear hybrid domains by leveraging GPUs and the power of recent advances in gradient descent with highly optimized toolkits like Tensorflow.

The authors use Tensorflow and RMSProp to optimize plans, drawing on GPU computation and efficient gradient-based tooling.

On piecewise-linear planning domains, where optimal solutions can be computed, the approach is competitive with mixed-integer linear programming. On nonlinear domains, it substantially outperforms the tested state-of-the-art interior-point methods. A large concurrent example reaches a strong plan in four minutes, involving 576,000 continuous action parameters over 96 time steps and 100 parallel instances.

The authors investigate why this approach works well and observe that RMSProp avoids vanishing and exploding gradients despite long planning horizons. These are reported observations about the studied problems, not an unconditional guarantee for every planning domain. The results suggest that optimized gradient tools and GPUs offer a promising route to large-scale planning in nonlinear hybrid systems.
summary.tldr: Tensorflow with RMSProp produces competitive, scalable plans in tested hybrid and nonlinear planning domains.

title: Scalable Planning with Tensorflow for Hybrid Nonlinear Domains

abstract: Decoding sensory stimuli from neural signals can be used to reveal how we sense our physical environment, and is valuable for the design of brain-machine interfaces. However, existing linear techniques for neural decoding may not fully reveal or exploit the fidelity of the neural signal. Here we develop a new approximate Bayesian method for decoding natural images from the spiking activity of populations of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs). We sidestep known computational challenges with Bayesian inference by exploiting artificial neural networks developed for computer vision, enabling fast nonlinear decoding that incorporates natural scene statistics implicitly. We use a decoder architecture that first linearly reconstructs an image from RGC spikes, then applies a convolutional autoencoder to enhance the image. The resulting decoder, trained on natural images and simulated neural responses, significantly outperforms linear decoding, as well as simple point-wise nonlinear decoding. These results provide a tool for the assessment and optimization of retinal prosthesis technologies, and reveal that the retina may provide a more accurate representation of the visual scene than previously appreciated.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an image from retinal neuron activity can help reveal how faithfully the retina represents visual scenes. Linear decoding methods may fail to recover all the usable information in those signals. This paper develops an approximate Bayesian decoder that uses neural networks to make nonlinear image reconstruction computationally efficient.

The architecture has two stages. First, it creates a linear image reconstruction from spikes produced by populations of retinal ganglion cells. A convolutional autoencoder then enhances that reconstruction. Training on natural images and simulated neural responses allows the decoder to incorporate natural-scene statistics implicitly, avoiding known computational difficulties of Bayesian inference while using structure learned from images.

The resulting decoder significantly outperforms both linear decoding and a simple nonlinear method that operates point by point. These findings suggest that the retina may support more accurate visual reconstruction than simpler decoders reveal. The authors also identify the decoder as a tool for assessing and optimizing retinal prosthesis technologies, connecting the reconstruction method to an application in neural interface design.
summary.tldr: A two-stage neural decoder improves image reconstruction from simulated retinal responses, suggesting richer recoverable visual information than simpler decoders reveal.

title: Neural Networks for Efficient Bayesian Decoding of Natural Images from Retinal Neurons

abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) is a notoriously challenging problem because it involves various heterogeneous tasks defined by questions within a unified framework. Learning specialized models for individual types of tasks is intuitively attracting but surprisingly difficult; it is not straightforward to outperform naive independent ensemble approach. We present a principled algorithm to learn specialized models with knowledge distillation under a multiple choice learning (MCL) framework, where training examples are assigned dynamically to a subset of models for updating network parameters. The assigned and non-assigned models are learned to predict ground-truth answers and imitate their own base models before specialization, respectively. Our approach alleviates the limitation of data deficiency in existing MCL frameworks, and allows each model to learn its own specialized expertise without forgetting general knowledge. The proposed framework is model-agnostic and applicable to any tasks other than VQA, e.g., image classification with a large number of labels but few per-class examples, which is known to be difficult under existing MCL schemes. Our experimental results indeed demonstrate that our method outperforms other baselines for VQA and image classification.

paragraphs: Visual question answering combines many different tasks because different questions require different kinds of reasoning about images. Specialized models are appealing, but training specialists does not straightforwardly outperform an independently trained ensemble. This paper proposes a way to develop specialized expertise while preserving the general knowledge models had before specialization.

The method combines multiple choice learning with knowledge distillation. Training examples are dynamically assigned to a subset of models. Assigned models learn to predict the correct answers, while models not assigned those examples learn to imitate their own earlier base models. This gives the unassigned models a learning signal that preserves prior knowledge.

The approach alleviates data deficiency in existing multiple choice learning frameworks, where specialization can leave individual models with too little training data. It is model-agnostic and is also applied to image classification with many labels and few examples per class. Experiments show improvements over the compared baselines in both visual question answering and image classification, supporting the combination of specialization with continued retention of general knowledge.
summary.tldr: Knowledge distillation helps models specialize through dynamic example assignment while retaining their earlier general knowledge.

title: Learning to Specialize with Knowledge Distillation for Visual Question Answering

abstract: Understanding and interpreting how machine learning (ML) models make decisions have been a big challenge. While recent research has proposed various technical approaches to provide some clues as to how an ML model makes individual predictions, they cannot provide users with an ability to inspect a model as a complete entity. In this work, we propose a novel technical approach that augments a Bayesian non-parametric regression mixture model with multiple elastic nets. Using the enhanced mixture model, we can extract generalizable insights for a target model through a global approximation. To demonstrate the utility of our approach, we evaluate it on different ML models in the context of image recognition. The empirical results indicate that our proposed approach not only outperforms the state-of-the-art techniques in explaining individual decisions but also provides users with an ability to discover the vulnerabilities of the target ML models.

paragraphs: An explanation of one prediction can help a person understand a particular decision, but it does not necessarily reveal how a model behaves across many inputs. This paper targets that broader view by constructing a global approximation of a trained model. The aim is to extract insights that extend beyond a single example.

The proposed approach combines a Bayesian nonparametric regression mixture model with multiple elastic nets. A mixture represents behavior through several components, while elastic nets supply regularized regression models within the approach. Together, these elements form an approximation intended to make the target model's behavior easier to inspect as a whole.

The authors evaluate the method on different machine-learning models used for image recognition. Their empirical results report better explanations of individual decisions than the state-of-the-art techniques considered, alongside the ability to discover vulnerabilities in the target models. The significance is that a global explanatory model can also support analysis of particular predictions, linking broad behavioral inspection with the examination of specific weaknesses.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian mixture approach builds global model approximations that support individual explanations and help reveal model vulnerabilities.

title: Explaining Deep Learning Models -- A Bayesian Non-parametric Approach

abstract: We describe a neural network-based system for text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis that is able to generate speech audio in the voice of many different speakers, including those unseen during training. Our system consists of three independently trained components: (1) a speaker encoder network, trained on a speaker verification task using an independent dataset of noisy speech from thousands of speakers without transcripts, to generate a fixed-dimensional embedding vector from seconds of reference speech from a target speaker; (2) a sequence-to-sequence synthesis network based on Tacotron 2, which generates a mel spectrogram from text, conditioned on the speaker embedding; (3) an auto-regressive WaveNet-based vocoder that converts the mel spectrogram into a sequence of time domain waveform samples. We demonstrate that the proposed model is able to transfer the knowledge of speaker variability learned by the discriminatively-trained speaker encoder to the new task, and is able to synthesize natural speech from speakers that were not seen during training. We quantify the importance of training the speaker encoder on a large and diverse speaker set in order to obtain the best generalization performance. Finally, we show that randomly sampled speaker embeddings can be used to synthesize speech in the voice of novel speakers dissimilar from those used in training, indicating that the model has learned a high quality speaker representation.

paragraphs: This paper presents a text-to-speech system that can generate speech in voices absent from its training data. It transfers information learned through speaker verification into speech synthesis, using seconds of reference speech to specify the target voice. The system separates speaker representation, speech generation, and waveform generation into independently trained components.

A speaker encoder learns from noisy, untranscribed speech from thousands of speakers and produces a fixed-dimensional voice embedding. A Tacotron 2-based synthesis network uses the text and embedding to generate a mel spectrogram. An autoregressive WaveNet-based vocoder then converts that representation into waveform samples. This arrangement lets speaker knowledge learned from an independent dataset condition the synthesis process.

The authors demonstrate natural-sounding synthesis for previously unseen speakers and quantify the importance of training the encoder on a large, diverse speaker collection. They also generate novel voices from randomly sampled embeddings, with voices dissimilar to those in training. These findings support the usefulness of the learned speaker representation both for transferring a reference voice and for generating new voice characteristics.
summary.tldr: Speaker-verification embeddings condition a text-to-speech system that generates natural speech in previously unseen voices.

title: Transfer Learning from Speaker Verification to Multispeaker Text-To-Speech Synthesis

abstract: Beyond local convolution networks, we explore how to harness various external human knowledge for endowing the networks with the capability of semantic global reasoning. Rather than using separate graphical models (e.g. CRF) or constraints for modeling broader dependencies, we propose a new Symbolic Graph Reasoning (SGR) layer, which performs reasoning over a group of symbolic nodes whose outputs explicitly represent different properties of each semantic in a prior knowledge graph. To cooperate with local convolutions, each SGR is constituted by three modules: a) a primal local-to-semantic voting module where the features of all symbolic nodes are generated by voting from local representations; b) a graph reasoning module propagates information over knowledge graph to achieve global semantic coherency; c) a dual semantic-to-local mapping module learns new associations of the evolved symbolic nodes with local representations, and accordingly enhances local features. The SGR layer can be injected between any convolution layers and instantiated with distinct prior graphs. Extensive experiments show incorporating SGR significantly improves plain ConvNets on three semantic segmentation tasks and one image classification task. More analyses show the SGR layer learns shared symbolic representations for domains/datasets with the different label set given a universal knowledge graph, demonstrating its superior generalization capability.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks build local visual representations, while semantic relationships can span an entire image. This paper introduces a Symbolic Graph Reasoning layer that brings external human knowledge into the network. Its symbolic nodes represent semantic properties associated with a prior knowledge graph, providing a place for global reasoning.

The layer has three parts. Local features first vote to generate representations for symbolic nodes. Information then propagates through the knowledge graph to encourage coherent semantic representations. Finally, the evolved nodes are mapped back to local features through learned associations, enhancing the visual representation. The layer can be inserted between convolutional layers and instantiated with different prior graphs.

Experiments report significant improvements over plain convolutional networks on three semantic segmentation tasks and one image classification task. Further analysis finds shared symbolic representations across datasets with different label sets when a universal knowledge graph is provided. These results support linking local visual computation with explicit semantic structure to improve prediction and cross-domain representation sharing.
summary.tldr: A graph reasoning layer exchanges information between local visual features and symbolic knowledge, improving convolutional networks across several tasks.

title: Symbolic Graph Reasoning Meets Convolutions

abstract: Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) is an objective function for end-to-end sequence learning, which adopts dynamic programming algorithms to directly learn the mapping between sequences. CTC has shown promising results in many sequence learning applications including speech recognition and scene text recognition. However, CTC tends to produce highly peaky and overconfident distributions, which is a symptom of overfitting. To remedy this, we propose a regularization method based on maximum conditional entropy which penalizes peaky distributions and encourages exploration. We also introduce an entropy-based pruning method to dramatically reduce the number of CTC feasible paths by ruling out unreasonable alignments. Experiments on scene text recognition show that our proposed methods consistently improve over the CTC baseline without the need to adjust training settings. Code has been made publicly available at: https://github.com/liuhu-bigeye/enctc.crnn.
