paragraphs: Connectionist Temporal Classification, or CTC, trains models to map one sequence to another using dynamic programming. It has been useful for tasks such as recognizing speech and text in images. The paper focuses on a weakness of this objective: its predicted distributions can become sharply concentrated and overconfident, which the authors identify as a symptom of overfitting.

The proposed remedy adds regularization based on maximum conditional entropy. This discourages overly concentrated distributions and encourages the model to explore alternatives during learning. A second contribution uses entropy to prune feasible CTC paths, removing alignments judged unreasonable. These two changes address different parts of the problem: confidence in the learned distribution and the collection of possible sequence alignments.

Experiments on scene text recognition show consistent improvements over the CTC baseline without changing the training settings. The findings support the usefulness of adjusting the learning objective and alignment handling within an existing sequence-learning framework. The stated experimental evidence concerns scene text recognition, even though CTC itself is used in other sequence tasks.
summary.tldr: Entropy regularization and entropy-based alignment pruning improve CTC scene text recognition in the reported experiments.

title: Connectionist Temporal Classification with Maximum Entropy Regularization

paragraphs: A visual question-answering system can exploit patterns in question wording instead of grounding its answer in the image. Such shortcuts can fail when the relationship between questions and answers changes at test time. This paper targets that failure by changing the training objective to favor answers supported by influential visual evidence.

The self-critical objective compares visual explanations for the correct answer with explanations for competing answer candidates. It requires the correct answer’s explanation to align more strongly with influential image regions. Those regions can be identified from human visual or textual explanations, or automatically using significant words in the question and answer. The comparison makes visual support part of how competing answers are judged during training.

The paper evaluates generalization on VQA-CP and reports a new state-of-the-art result of 49.5% using textual explanations. This supports the value of supervising how an answer relates to image evidence when question-answer distributions shift. The supplied abstract also reports 48.5% for an automatic variant, although its final description is truncated. The central contribution is the comparative explanation-based training objective.
summary.tldr: A self-critical training objective improves visual question answering by making correct answers align with influential image regions more than competing answers do.

title: Self-Critical Reasoning for Robust Visual Question Answering

abstract: Natural gradient descent, which preconditions a gradient descent update with the Fisher information matrix of the underlying statistical model, is a way to capture partial second-order information. Several highly visible works have advocated an approximation known as the empirical Fisher, drawing connections between approximate second-order methods and heuristics like Adam. We dispute this argument by showing that the empirical Fisher---unlike the Fisher---does not generally capture second-order information. We further argue that the conditions under which the empirical Fisher approaches the Fisher (and the Hessian) are unlikely to be met in practice, and that, even on simple optimization problems, the pathologies of the empirical Fisher can have undesirable effects.

paragraphs: Natural gradient descent modifies a gradient update using the Fisher information matrix of the statistical model. This provides a way to incorporate partial second-order information into optimization. The paper examines the empirical Fisher, an approximation that has been used to motivate connections between approximate second-order optimization and methods such as Adam.

The authors challenge that interpretation by showing that the empirical Fisher does not generally capture second-order information in the way the Fisher does. The distinction matters because using a matrix to rescale gradients does not, by itself, establish that the matrix represents the relevant curvature. Claims about second-order behavior therefore depend on which matrix is actually being used.

The paper further argues that the conditions needed for the empirical Fisher to approach the Fisher and the Hessian are unlikely to hold in practice. It shows that problematic behavior can have undesirable effects even on simple optimization problems. The conclusion is a qualified challenge to the approximation and its justification, rather than a claim that every method using it must fail.
summary.tldr: The empirical Fisher generally lacks the Fisher's second-order interpretation and can produce undesirable optimization behavior.

title: Limitations of the empirical Fisher approximation for natural gradient descent

abstract: We take initial steps in studying PAC-MDP algorithms with limited adaptivity, that is, algorithms that change its exploration policy as infrequently as possible during regret minimization. This is motivated by the difficulty of running fully adaptive algorithms in real-world applications (such as medical domains), and we propose to quantify adaptivity using the notion of \emph{local switching cost}. Our main contribution, Q-Learning with UCB2 exploration, is a model-free algorithm for $H$-step episodic MDP that achieves sublinear regret whose local switching cost in $K$ episodes is $O(H^3SA\log K)$, and we provide a lower bound of $\Omega(HSA)$ on the local switching cost for any no-regret algorithm. Our algorithm can be naturally adapted to the concurrent setting \citep{guo2015concurrent}, which yields nontrivial results that improve upon prior work in certain aspects.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning algorithms often change their exploration policy as new data arrive. Frequent adaptation can be difficult to implement in real applications. This paper studies how an agent can keep learning effectively while changing its policy infrequently, using local switching cost to quantify that aspect of adaptivity.

The main algorithm combines model-free Q-learning with UCB2 exploration in episodic Markov decision processes of H steps. Over K episodes, it achieves sublinear regret with local switching cost O(H^3SA log K), where S and A count states and actions. Sublinear regret means that the cumulative performance shortfall grows more slowly than the number of episodes.

The authors also prove a lower bound of Omega(HSA) on local switching cost for any no-regret algorithm, showing that some switching is unavoidable in this setting. They adapt their algorithm to concurrent learning, obtaining improvements over prior work in certain aspects. Together, the results make policy-change frequency an explicit theoretical consideration alongside learning performance.
summary.tldr: Q-learning with UCB2 achieves sublinear regret with bounded local switching cost, while a lower bound shows some switching is unavoidable.

title: Provably Efficient Q-Learning with Low Switching Cost

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of unsupervised discovery of object landmarks. We take a different path compared to existing works, based on 2 novel perspectives: (1) Self-training: starting from generic keypoints, we propose a self-training approach where the goal is to learn a detector that improves itself, becoming more and more tuned to object landmarks. (2) Correspondence: we identify correspondence as a key objective for unsupervised landmark discovery and propose an optimization scheme which alternates between recovering object landmark correspondence across different images via clustering and learning an object landmark descriptor without labels. Compared to previous works, our approach can learn landmarks that are more flexible in terms of capturing large changes in viewpoint. We show the favourable properties of our method on a variety of difficult datasets including LS3D, BBCPose and Human3.6M. Code is available at https://github.com/malldimi1/UnsupervisedLandmarks.

paragraphs: Discovering object landmarks without labels requires identifying points that remain meaningfully related across images. This paper makes correspondence central to that task. It begins with generic keypoints and uses self-training to develop a detector that becomes increasingly tuned to object landmarks as its own learning process progresses.

The optimization alternates between two activities. Clustering recovers landmark correspondences across different images, and an unlabeled learning step trains a landmark descriptor. These activities connect the discovery of matching points with the representation used to describe them, providing a repeated process for improving the detector without supplied landmark labels.

The authors report that the resulting landmarks are more flexible in handling large viewpoint changes than those learned by previous approaches. They demonstrate favorable properties on challenging datasets including LS3D, BBCPose, and Human3.6M. The contribution is a route from generic starting points to object-specific landmarks through cross-image correspondence, with the reported viewpoint flexibility addressing an important source of variation in how objects appear.
summary.tldr: Alternating correspondence discovery and descriptor learning turns generic keypoints into unsupervised object landmarks that better handle large viewpoint changes.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Object Landmarks via Self-Training Correspondence

abstract: Hybrid Privacy-Preserving Neural Network (HPPNN) implementing linear layers by Homomorphic Encryption (HE) and nonlinear layers by Garbled Circuit (GC) is one of the most promising secure solutions to emerging Machine Learning as a Service (MLaaS). Unfortunately, a HPPNN suffers from long inference latency, e.g., $\sim100$ seconds per image, which makes MLaaS unsatisfactory. Because HE-based linear layers of a HPPNN cost $93\%$ inference latency, it is critical to select a set of HE parameters to minimize computational overhead of linear layers. Prior HPPNNs over-pessimistically select huge HE parameters to maintain large noise budgets, since they use the same set of HE parameters for an entire network and ignore the error tolerance capability of a network. In this paper, for fast and accurate secure neural network inference, we propose an automated layer-wise parameter selector, AutoPrivacy, that leverages deep reinforcement learning to automatically determine a set of HE parameters for each linear layer in a HPPNN. The learning-based HE parameter selection policy outperforms conventional rule-based HE parameter selection policy. Compared to prior HPPNNs, AutoPrivacy-optimized HPPNNs reduce inference latency by $53\%\sim70\%$ with negligible loss of accuracy.

paragraphs: Hybrid privacy-preserving neural networks combine homomorphic encryption for linear layers with garbled circuits for nonlinear layers. These systems enable secure inference, but their latency can be substantial. The paper identifies encrypted linear computation as the dominant cost, accounting for 93% of inference latency in the setting described.

Earlier systems use one set of encryption parameters throughout the network, conservatively preserving a large noise budget. The authors argue that this overlooks differences between layers and the network's ability to tolerate errors. AutoPrivacy instead uses deep reinforcement learning to choose encryption parameters separately for each linear layer, targeting the computational overhead where it is largest.

The learned selection policy outperforms a conventional rule-based policy in the reported comparison. Relative to prior hybrid systems, networks optimized with AutoPrivacy reduce inference latency by 53–70%, with negligible accuracy loss. The finding shows that parameter selection is an important part of practical secure inference: adapting cryptographic computation across layers can substantially improve speed while largely preserving the network's predictive performance.
summary.tldr: AutoPrivacy learns encryption parameters for individual network layers, reducing reported secure-inference latency by 53–70% with negligible accuracy loss.

title: AutoPrivacy: Automated Layer-wise Parameter Selection for Secure Neural Network Inference

abstract: Discriminatively localizing sounding objects in cocktail-party, i.e., mixed sound scenes, is commonplace for humans, but still challenging for machines. In this paper, we propose a two-stage learning framework to perform self-supervised class-aware sounding object localization. First, we propose to learn robust object representations by aggregating the candidate sound localization results in the single source scenes. Then, class-aware object localization maps are generated in the cocktail-party scenarios by referring the pre-learned object knowledge, and the sounding objects are accordingly selected by matching audio and visual object category distributions, where the audiovisual consistency is viewed as the self-supervised signal. Experimental results in both realistic and synthesized cocktail-party videos demonstrate that our model is superior in filtering out silent objects and pointing out the location of sounding objects of different classes. Code is available at https://github.com/DTaoo/Discriminative-Sounding-Objects-Localization.
originalAbstract: Discriminatively localizing sounding objects in cocktail-party, i.e., mixed sound scenes, is commonplace for humans, but still challenging for machines. In this paper, we propose a two-stage learning framework to perform self-supervised class-aware sounding object localization. First, we propose to learn robust object representations by aggregating the candidate sound localization results in the single source scenes. Then, class-aware object localization maps are generated in the cocktail-party scenarios by referring the pre-learned object knowledge, and the sounding objects are accordingly selected by matching audio and visual object category distributions, where the audiovisual consistency is viewed as the self-supervised signal. Experimental results in both realistic and synthesized cocktail-party videos demonstrate that our model is superior in filtering out silent objects and pointing out the location of sounding objects of different classes. Code is available at https://github.com/DTaoo/Discriminative-Sounding-Objects-Localization.

paragraphs: A video can contain several visible objects while its soundtrack mixes sounds from only some of them. The task is to locate the objects that are actually producing sound and distinguish their categories. This is especially difficult in mixed sound scenes, where a single audio track must be related to several possible visual sources.

The paper proposes a two-stage framework. First, it aggregates candidate localization results from scenes with a single sound source to learn robust object representations. It then uses that object knowledge to produce category-aware localization maps in mixed scenes. Matching the category distributions inferred from audio and visual objects helps select which visible objects are sounding.

Agreement between the audio and visual information supplies the self-supervised learning signal. Experiments on both realistic and synthesized mixed sound videos report better filtering of silent objects and better localization of sounding objects from different classes. The approach matters because it combines learned object knowledge with cross-modal agreement, addressing both where a possible source is located and whether it is supported by the audio.
summary.tldr: A two-stage audiovisual model learns object knowledge from single-source scenes and uses category agreement to locate sounding objects in mixed scenes.

title: Discriminative Sounding Objects Localization via Self-supervised Audiovisual Matching

abstract: Discrete latent spaces in variational autoencoders have been shown to effectively capture the data distribution for many real-world problems such as natural language understanding, human intent prediction, and visual scene representation. However, discrete latent spaces need to be sufficiently large to capture the complexities of real-world data, rendering downstream tasks computationally challenging. For instance, performing motion planning in a high-dimensional latent representation of the environment could be intractable. We consider the problem of sparsifying the discrete latent space of a trained conditional variational autoencoder, while preserving its learned multimodality. As a post hoc latent space reduction technique, we use evidential theory to identify the latent classes that receive direct evidence from a particular input condition and filter out those that do not. Experiments on diverse tasks, such as image generation and human behavior prediction, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed technique at reducing the discrete latent sample space size of a model while maintaining its learned multimodality.

paragraphs: A discrete latent space lets a generative model represent multiple possible explanations or outcomes for an input. Complex data may require many latent classes, but that size can make downstream computation difficult. The paper highlights motion planning as an example where reasoning over a large latent representation of the environment could become intractable.

The proposed method reduces the discrete latent space of an already trained conditional variational autoencoder. Using evidential theory, it identifies which latent classes receive direct support from the particular input condition and filters out classes that lack that support. The reduction is therefore conditional on the input and is applied after training.

Experiments involving image generation and human behavior prediction show that the technique can shrink the latent sample space while maintaining this diversity. The contribution is a way to simplify downstream use of a trained model without treating compression as a reason to collapse its predictions into a single outcome.
summary.tldr: An evidence-based post-training filter reduces a conditional autoencoder’s discrete latent space while empirically preserving its multiple learned possibilities.

title: Evidential Sparsification of Multimodal Latent Spaces in Conditional Variational Autoencoders

abstract: Self- and semi-supervised learning frameworks have made significant progress in training machine learning models with limited labeled data in image and language domains. These methods heavily rely on the unique structure in the domain datasets (such as spatial relationships in images or semantic relationships in language). They are not adaptable to general tabular data which does not have the same explicit structure as image and language data. In this paper, we fill this gap by proposing novel self- and semi-supervised learning frameworks for tabular data, which we refer to collectively as VIME (Value Imputation and Mask Estimation). We create a novel pretext task of estimating mask vectors from corrupted tabular data in addition to the reconstruction pretext task for self-supervised learning. We also introduce a novel tabular data augmentation method for self- and semi-supervised learning frameworks. In experiments, we evaluate the proposed framework in multiple tabular datasets from various application domains, such as genomics and clinical data. VIME exceeds state-of-the-art performance in comparison to the existing baseline methods.

paragraphs: Learning from unlabeled data can reduce dependence on expensive labels, but successful image and language methods often exploit structure that ordinary tables do not share. VIME develops self-supervised and semi-supervised learning specifically for tabular data, where columns lack the same explicit spatial or semantic relationships.

The framework creates training tasks from corrupted table entries. Alongside reconstructing the data, it asks the model to estimate a mask indicating which values were corrupted. These complementary tasks make both value recovery and recognition of corruption part of representation learning. The authors also introduce a tabular augmentation method for use in their self-supervised and semi-supervised frameworks.

The paper evaluates VIME across multiple tabular datasets, including genomics and clinical applications, and reports performance above the existing state-of-the-art baselines tested. Its contribution is a concrete learning signal designed around tabular inputs rather than the structures of images or text. The results support this combination of value imputation, mask estimation, and augmentation as a way to use unlabeled tables when labeled data are limited.
summary.tldr: VIME learns from unlabeled tables by reconstructing corrupted values and predicting corruption masks, improving performance in reported tabular benchmarks.

title: VIME: Extending the Success of Self- and Semi-supervised Learning to Tabular Domain

abstract: On-device learning enables edge devices to continually adapt the AI models to new data, which requires a small memory footprint to fit the tight memory constraint of edge devices. Existing work solves this problem by reducing the number of trainable parameters. However, this doesn't directly translate to memory saving since the major bottleneck is the activations, not parameters. In this work, we present Tiny-Transfer-Learning (TinyTL) for memory-efficient on-device learning. TinyTL freezes the weights while only learns the bias modules, thus no need to store the intermediate activations. To maintain the adaptation capacity, we introduce a new memory-efficient bias module, the lite residual module, to refine the feature extractor by learning small residual feature maps adding only 3.8% memory overhead. Extensive experiments show that TinyTL significantly saves the memory (up to 6.5x) with little accuracy loss compared to fine-tuning the full network. Compared to fine-tuning the last layer, TinyTL provides significant accuracy improvements (up to 34.1%) with little memory overhead. Furthermore, combined with feature extractor adaptation, TinyTL provides 7.3-12.9x memory saving without sacrificing accuracy compared to fine-tuning the full Inception-V3.

summary.tldr: TinyTL reduces on-device training memory by freezing weights and learning compact bias and residual modules that preserve useful adaptation capacity.

title: TinyTL: Reduce Memory, Not Parameters for Efficient On-Device Learning

abstract: Disentanglement is at the forefront of unsupervised learning, as disentangled representations of data improve generalization, interpretability, and performance in downstream tasks. Current unsupervised approaches remain inapplicable for real-world datasets since they are highly variable in their performance and fail to reach levels of disentanglement of (semi-)supervised approaches. We introduce population-based training (PBT) for improving consistency in training variational autoencoders (VAEs) and demonstrate the validity of this approach in a supervised setting (PBT-VAE). We then use Unsupervised Disentanglement Ranking (UDR) as an unsupervised heuristic to score models in our PBT-VAE training and show how models trained this way tend to consistently disentangle only a subset of the generative factors. Building on top of this observation we introduce the recursive rPU-VAE approach. We train the model until convergence, remove the learned factors from the dataset and reiterate. In doing so, we can label subsets of the dataset with the learned factors and consecutively use these labels to train one model that fully disentangles the whole dataset. With this approach, we show striking improvement in state-of-the-art unsupervised disentanglement performance and robustness across multiple datasets and metrics.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate the underlying factors that generate data, making learned features easier to interpret and use. The paper addresses the inconsistent performance of unsupervised disentanglement methods. It first applies population-based training to variational autoencoders and demonstrates improved training consistency in a supervised setting.

The authors then use Unsupervised Disentanglement Ranking as a heuristic for scoring models during population-based training. The paper reports substantial improvements in unsupervised disentanglement performance and robustness across multiple datasets and metrics. Its central contribution is turning consistent partial disentanglement into a staged process for learning a more complete representation.
summary.tldr: rPU-VAE repeatedly learns subsets of generative factors and uses the resulting labels to train a more fully disentangled model.

title: Robust Disentanglement of a Few Factors at a Time using rPU-VAE

abstract: The rapid evolution of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) has led to a growing number of new architectures as well as novel applications. However, current research focuses on proposing and evaluating specific architectural designs of GNNs, such as GCN, GIN, or GAT, as opposed to studying the more general design space of GNNs that consists of a Cartesian product of different design dimensions, such as the number of layers or the type of the aggregation function. Additionally, GNN designs are often specialized to a single task, yet few efforts have been made to understand how to quickly find the best GNN design for a novel task or a novel dataset. Here we define and systematically study the architectural design space for GNNs which consists of 315,000 different designs over 32 different predictive tasks. Our approach features three key innovations: (1) A general GNN design space; (2) a GNN task space with a similarity metric, so that for a given novel task/dataset, we can quickly identify/transfer the best performing architecture; (3) an efficient and effective design space evaluation method which allows insights to be distilled from a huge number of model-task combinations. Our key results include: (1) A comprehensive set of guidelines for designing well-performing GNNs; (2) while best GNN designs for different tasks vary significantly, the GNN task space allows for transferring the best designs across different tasks; (3) models discovered using our design space achieve state-of-the-art performance. Overall, our work offers a principled and scalable approach to transition from studying individual GNN designs for specific tasks, to systematically studying the GNN design space and the task space. Finally, we release GraphGym, a powerful platform for exploring different GNN designs and tasks. GraphGym features modularized GNN implementation, standardized GNN evaluation, and reproducible and scalable experiment management.

paragraphs: Graph neural network research often evaluates individual architectures on particular tasks. This paper instead organizes architecture choices into a shared design space, including dimensions such as layer count and aggregation function. The resulting space contains 315,000 designs, which the authors systematically study across 32 predictive tasks using an efficient evaluation approach.

The work also defines a task space with a similarity measure. Its purpose is to help identify which architecture choices may transfer to a new task or dataset. This addresses the authors' finding that the strongest designs vary considerably across tasks: useful architectural guidance needs to account for the task rather than simply select one universally preferred design.

The study produces design guidelines, demonstrates transfer of strong designs across tasks, and discovers models achieving state-of-the-art performance. The authors also release GraphGym, a platform combining modular implementations, standardized evaluation, and reproducible experiment management. Together, the framework and platform support studying relationships between architecture and task at a broader scale than isolated model comparisons.
summary.tldr: A systematic study of GNN architectures and task similarity yields design guidelines, transferable architecture choices, and the GraphGym platform.

title: Design Space for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: In this paper, we propose polynomial forms to represent distributions of state variables over time for discrete-time stochastic dynamical systems. This problem arises in a variety of applications in areas ranging from biology to robotics. Our approach allows us to rigorously represent the probability distribution of state variables over time, and provide guaranteed bounds on the expectations, moments and probabilities of tail events involving the state variables. First, we recall ideas from interval arithmetic, and use them to rigorously represent the state variables at time t as a function of the initial state variables and noise symbols that model the random exogenous inputs encountered before time t. Next, we show how concentration of measure inequalities can be employed to prove rigorous bounds on the tail probabilities of these state variables. We demonstrate interesting applications that demonstrate how our approach can be useful in some situations to establish mathematically guaranteed bounds that are of a different nature from those obtained through simulations with pseudo-random numbers.

paragraphs: In a stochastic dynamical system, uncertainty in the starting state and later random inputs influences how the system evolves. This paper introduces polynomial forms for representing state-variable distributions over discrete time. The aim is to obtain mathematically guaranteed information about uncertainty as it propagates through the dynamics.

Building on interval arithmetic, the method expresses a state at a given time as a function of initial variables and symbols for earlier external noise. This retains an explicit relationship between the current state and the uncertain quantities that produced it. The representation supports rigorous bounds on expectations, moments, and probabilities of events involving the state.

The authors use concentration inequalities to bound tail probabilities, which describe outcomes in the extremes of a distribution. Applications illustrate situations where the method supplies guarantees of a different nature from estimates obtained through pseudo-random simulation. The contribution is therefore a way to reason formally about evolving uncertainty, with demonstrated usefulness in some settings rather than a claim that it replaces simulation generally.
summary.tldr: Polynomial forms track uncertainty through stochastic dynamics and provide rigorous bounds on state statistics and tail-event probabilities.

title: Reasoning about Uncertainties in Discrete-Time Dynamical Systems using Polynomial Forms.

abstract: Recently significant progress has been made in pedestrian detection, but it remains challenging to achieve high performance in occluded and crowded scenes. It could be mostly attributed to the widely used representation of pedestrians, i.e., 2Daxis-aligned bounding box, which just describes the approximate location and size of the object. Bounding box models the object as a uniform distribution within the boundary, making pedestrians indistinguishable in occluded and crowded scenes due to much noise. To eliminate the problem, we propose a novel representation based on 2D beta distribution, named Beta Representation. It pictures a pedestrianby explicitly constructing the relationship between full-body and visible boxes, and emphasizes the center of visual mass by assigning different probability valuesto pixels. As a result, Beta Representation is much better for distinguishing highly-overlapped instances in crowded scenes with a new NMS strategy named BetaNMS. What’s more, to fully exploit Beta Representation, a novel pipeline Beta R-CNN equipped with BetaHead and BetaMask is proposed, leading to high detection performance in occluded and crowded scenes.

paragraphs: Pedestrian detection becomes difficult when people overlap or hide parts of one another. The paper attributes much of this difficulty to representing each person with an axis-aligned rectangle. Such a box gives an approximate location and size, but treats the enclosed region uniformly, making it hard to distinguish overlapping people from the surrounding visual noise.

The authors introduce Beta Representation, which describes a pedestrian using a two-dimensional beta distribution. It explicitly relates the full-body box to the visible box and gives different pixels different probability values. This emphasizes the center of visible mass, providing more information about where the person’s visible evidence lies than a uniform rectangle supplies.

A companion suppression strategy, BetaNMS, uses the representation to better distinguish heavily overlapping instances. The full Beta R-CNN pipeline adds BetaHead and BetaMask components to exploit it. The reported outcome is improved detection in crowded and occluded scenes. The contribution ties the object representation to the process of distinguishing competing detections, addressing the ambiguity that arises when several people occupy much of the same image region.
summary.tldr: Beta R-CNN represents pedestrians with spatial probability distributions to better distinguish overlapping people in crowded and occluded scenes.

title: Beta R-CNN: Looking into Pedestrian Detection from Another Perspective

abstract: Distribution alignment has many applications in deep learning, including domain adaptation and unsupervised image-to-image translation. Most prior work on unsupervised distribution alignment relies either on minimizing simple non-parametric statistical distances such as maximum mean discrepancy or on adversarial alignment. However, the former fails to capture the structure of complex real-world distributions, while the latter is difficult to train and does not provide any universal convergence guarantees or automatic quantitative validation procedures. In this paper, we propose a new distribution alignment method based on a log-likelihood ratio statistic and normalizing flows. We show that, under certain assumptions, this combination yields a deep neural likelihood-based minimization objective that attains a known lower bound upon convergence. We experimentally verify that minimizing the resulting objective results in domain alignment that preserves the local structure of input domains.

paragraphs: Distribution alignment attempts to bring different data distributions into agreement, with applications including domain adaptation and unsupervised image translation. This paper addresses weaknesses in two common approaches: simple statistical distances can miss complex distribution structure, while adversarial alignment can be difficult to train and lacks automatic quantitative validation and universal convergence guarantees.

The proposed method combines normalizing flows with a log-likelihood ratio statistic. Together, they define a neural likelihood-based minimization objective. Under certain assumptions, the authors show that this objective reaches a known lower bound upon convergence. Having a known target value gives the optimization an explicit quantitative reference for assessing its result.

Experiments verify that minimizing the objective produces alignment while preserving local structure within the input domains. This supports the usefulness of the objective beyond merely making distributions agree according to a numerical score. The theoretical result remains conditional on its assumptions and on convergence; it supplies a characterized endpoint, while the experiments provide evidence that the learned alignment retains local relationships in the evaluated data.
summary.tldr: Normalizing flows and a log-likelihood ratio yield a distribution-alignment objective with a known lower bound under stated assumptions.

title: Log-Likelihood Ratio Minimizing Flows: Towards Robust and Quantifiable Neural Distribution Alignment

abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have shown impressive performance in computer vision tasks such as image classification, detection, and segmentation. Moreover, recent work in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has highlighted the importance of learning by progressively increasing the difficulty of a learning task Kerras et al. When learning a network from scratch, the information propagated within the network during the earlier stages of training can contain distortion artifacts due to noise which can be detrimental to training. In this paper, we propose an elegant curriculum-based scheme that smoothes the feature embedding of a CNN using anti-aliasing or low-pass filters. We propose to augment the training of CNNs by controlling the amount of high frequency information propagated within the CNNs as training progresses, by convolving the output of a CNN feature map of each layer with a Gaussian kernel. By decreasing the variance of the Gaussian kernel, we gradually increase the amount of high-frequency information available within the network for inference. As the amount of information in the feature maps increases during training, the network is able to progressively learn better representations of the data. Our proposed augmented training scheme significantly improves the performance of CNNs on various vision tasks without either adding additional trainable parameters or an auxiliary regularization objective. The generality of our method is demonstrated through empirical performance gains in CNN architectures across four different tasks: transfer learning, cross-task transfer learning, and generative models.

paragraphs: Early in training, a convolutional network can propagate noisy, distorted information through its internal features. This paper proposes a curriculum that controls the detail available inside the network as learning progresses. The aim is to let the model learn from smoother representations before exposing it to more high-frequency information.

The method applies a Gaussian filter to the output feature map of each convolutional layer. Initially, stronger smoothing suppresses high-frequency content. Decreasing the Gaussian kernel’s variance over training gradually permits more of that content to pass through. The curriculum therefore operates on intermediate representations, directly changing what information later computations receive.

The authors report that this progressive increase in detail helps networks learn better representations and improves performance across several vision tasks and architectures. The scheme introduces neither additional trainable parameters nor an auxiliary regularization objective. Reported gains include transfer learning, transfer across tasks, and generative modeling, supporting the usefulness of smoothing as an augmentation to training across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Gradually reducing smoothing inside CNNs creates a training curriculum that improves visual representations without adding trainable parameters.

title: Curriculum By Smoothing

abstract: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) data has become a critical component in ensuring the safe deployment of machine learning models in the real world. Existing OOD detection approaches primarily rely on the output or feature space for deriving OOD scores, while largely overlooking information from the gradient space. In this paper, we present GradNorm, a simple and effective approach for detecting OOD inputs by utilizing information extracted from the gradient space. GradNorm directly employs the vector norm of gradients, backpropagated from the KL divergence between the softmax output and a uniform probability distribution. Our key idea is that the magnitude of gradients is higher for in-distribution (ID) data than that for OOD data, making it informative for OOD detection. GradNorm demonstrates superior performance, reducing the average FPR95 by up to 16.33% compared to the previous best method.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input differs from the data a model is intended to handle. Many existing approaches derive a detection score from model outputs or internal features. This paper investigates another source of information: the gradients produced when a prediction-related quantity is backpropagated through the model.

The proposed method, GradNorm, computes the KL divergence between the model's softmax output and a uniform probability distribution, backpropagates it, and uses the resulting gradient vector's norm as the score. The motivating observation is that gradient magnitudes are higher for in-distribution data than for out-of-distribution data. The score converts that observed difference into a signal for identifying unfamiliar inputs.

GradNorm reports superior detection performance, reducing average FPR95 by up to 16.33% relative to the previous best method. This is an empirical result for the evaluated comparisons, rather than a guarantee that gradient magnitudes always separate the two groups. The contribution is a simple scoring approach demonstrating that backward-pass information can be useful for distribution-shift detection alongside the more commonly studied output and feature information.
summary.tldr: GradNorm detects distribution shifts using gradient magnitudes derived from divergence between model predictions and a uniform distribution.

title: On the Importance of Gradients for Detecting Distributional Shifts in the Wild

abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher --- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student network to imitate a larger teacher, which may itself be an ensemble. The usual explanation is that the student benefits by reproducing the teacher's predictions. This paper investigates that explanation by separating two outcomes: matching the teacher and generalizing well to new data.

The authors find that distillation can improve student generalization even while the student's predictive distribution remains surprisingly different from the teacher's. Such discrepancies can persist when the student has enough capacity to match the teacher perfectly. They identify optimization difficulties as a key reason: having a model capable of representing the teacher does not ensure that training finds that representation.

The data used for distillation also influence how closely the student reproduces the teacher. Yet closer agreement does not always yield better generalization. This makes teacher imitation and student performance distinct measures of success. The results challenge a common account of why distillation works while preserving its practical benefit: a student can improve without faithfully copying the teacher, and better copying is not always better learning.
summary.tldr: Knowledge distillation can improve generalization even when students poorly match their teachers, and closer matching does not always help.

title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?

abstract: Causal effect identification is concerned with determining whether a causal effect is computable from a combination of qualitative assumptions about the underlying system (e.g., a causal graph) and distributions collected from this system. Many identification algorithms exclusively rely on graphical criteria made of a non-trivial combination of probability axioms, do-calculus, and refined c-factorization (e.g., Lee & Bareinboim, 2020). In a sequence of increasingly sophisticated results, it has been shown how proxy variables can be used to identify certain effects that would not be otherwise recoverable in challenging scenarios through solving matrix equations (e.g., Kuroki & Pearl, 2014; Miao et al., 2018). In this paper, we develop a new causal identification algorithm which utilizes both graphical criteria and matrix equations. Specifically, we first characterize the relationships between certain graphically-driven formulae and matrix multiplications. With such characterizations, we broaden the spectrum of proxy variable based identification conditions and further propose novel intermediary criteria based on the pseudoinverse of a matrix. Finally, we devise a causal effect identification algorithm, which accepts as input a collection of marginal, conditional, and interventional distributions, integrating enriched matrix-based criteria into a graphical identification approach.

Many algorithms answer this through graphical rules. Other results show that proxy variables can recover certain otherwise inaccessible effects by solving matrix equations. This paper develops an algorithm that combines these two approaches.

The authors first characterize connections between particular formulas derived from causal graphs and matrix multiplication. Those connections let them expand the conditions under which proxy variables support identification. They also introduce intermediate criteria based on a matrix pseudoinverse, adding algebraic tools to the reasoning process used to establish whether an effect is recoverable.

The resulting algorithm accepts a collection of marginal, conditional, and interventional distributions and integrates the enriched matrix criteria into graphical identification. Its contribution is a broader route from causal assumptions and available evidence to identifiable effects. Recovery remains tied to the relevant identification conditions; the advance is in the range of conditions the algorithm can use.
summary.tldr: A causal identification algorithm combines graphical reasoning with matrix equations to broaden the use of proxy variables.

title: Causal Identification with Matrix Equations

abstract: We consider the problem of embedding a dynamic network, to obtain time-evolving vector representations of each node, which can then be used to describe changes in behaviour of individual nodes, communities, or the entire graph. Given this open-ended remit, we argue that two types of stability in the spatio-temporal positioning of nodes are desirable: to assign the same position, up to noise, to nodes behaving similarly at a given time (cross-sectional stability) and a constant position, up to noise, to a single node behaving similarly across different times (longitudinal stability). Similarity in behaviour is defined formally using notions of exchangeability under a dynamic latent position network model. By showing how this model can be recast as a multilayer random dot product graph, we demonstrate that unfolded adjacency spectral embedding satisfies both stability conditions. We also show how two alternative methods, omnibus and independent spectral embedding, alternately lack one or the other form of stability.

paragraphs: Dynamic network embeddings assign each node a vector that can change over time. Those vectors can help describe changes in individual nodes, communities, or a whole graph. This paper argues that interpreting them requires stability: positions should remain comparable when the underlying behavior is similar, both across nodes and across time.

The authors distinguish two requirements. Cross-sectional stability places similarly behaving nodes at the same position, up to noise, at a given time. Longitudinal stability keeps a node's position constant, up to noise, when its behavior stays similar across times. They formalize behavioral similarity through exchangeability in a dynamic latent position network model.

By expressing that model as a multilayer random dot product graph, they show that unfolded adjacency spectral embedding satisfies both requirements. Two alternatives, omnibus and independent spectral embedding, each lack one form of stability. The contribution supplies a formal basis for choosing an embedding whose movements can be interpreted consistently under the stated model, rather than relying only on the appearance of its coordinates.
summary.tldr: Under a dynamic latent position model, unfolded adjacency spectral embedding provides stability both across similarly behaving nodes and across time.

title: Spectral embedding for dynamic networks with stability guarantees

abstract: Due to the broad range of applications of reinforcement learning (RL), understanding the effects of adversarial attacks against RL model is essential for the safe applications of this model. Prior theoretical works on adversarial attacks against RL mainly focus on either reward poisoning attacks or environment poisoning attacks. In this paper, we introduce a new class of attacks named action poisoning attacks, where an adversary can change the action signal selected by the agent. Compared with existing attack models, the attacker’s ability in the proposed action poisoning attack model is more restricted, which brings some design challenges. We study the action poisoning attack in both white-box and black-box settings. We introduce an adaptive attack scheme called LCB-H, which works for most RL agents in the black-box setting. We prove that LCB-H attack can force any efficient RL agent, whose dynamic regret scales sublinearly with the total number of steps taken, to choose actions according to a policy selected by the attacker very frequently, with only sublinear cost. In addition, we apply LCB-H attack against a very popular model-free RL algorithm: UCB-H. We show that, even in black-box setting, by spending only logarithm cost, the proposed LCB-H attack scheme can force the UCB-H agent to choose actions according to the policy selected by the attacker very frequently.

They show why analyzing only attacks on rewards or environments leaves an additional mechanism of interference unaddressed.
summary.tldr: LCB-H can steer qualifying reinforcement-learning agents through black-box action poisoning with sublinear cost, and logarithmic cost for UCB-H.

title: Provably Efficient Black-Box Action Poisoning Attacks Against Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Implementations of the exponential mechanism in differential privacy often require sampling from intractable distributions. When approximate procedures like Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) are used, the end result incurs costs to both privacy and accuracy. Existing work has examined these effects asymptotically, but implementable finite sample results are needed in practice so that users can specify privacy budgets in advance and implement samplers with exact privacy guarantees. In this paper, we use tools from ergodic theory and perfect simulation to design exact finite runtime sampling algorithms for the exponential mechanism by introducing an intermediate modified target distribution using artificial atoms. We propose an additional modification of this sampling algorithm that maintains its $\epsilon$-DP guarantee and has improved runtime at the cost of some utility. We then compare these methods in scenarios where we can explicitly calculate a $\delta$ cost (as in $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP) incurred when using standard MCMC techniques. Much as there is a well known trade-off between privacy and utility, we demonstrate that there is also a trade-off between privacy guarantees and runtime.

This paper addresses the practical need to specify a privacy budget before running a sampler and obtain a guarantee for its actual finite execution.

The authors combine tools from ergodic theory and perfect simulation to construct exact sampling algorithms with finite runtime. Their construction introduces an intermediate modified target distribution using artificial atoms. The purpose is to make exact sampling available within a Markov-chain implementation, so the privacy analysis need not rely only on eventual convergence.

They also propose a modification that preserves an epsilon-differential-privacy guarantee while improving runtime at some cost to utility. Comparisons consider situations where the additional delta privacy cost of standard MCMC can be calculated explicitly. The results make runtime part of the privacy design problem: the strength of the privacy guarantee, computational cost, and usefulness of the output must be considered together.
summary.tldr: Exact finite-runtime samplers provide explicit privacy guarantees for the exponential mechanism while exposing trade-offs with runtime and utility.

title: Exact Privacy Guarantees for Markov Chain Implementations of the Exponential Mechanism with Artificial Atoms

abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization is widely used to handle challenging tasks, such as query-based black-box adversarial attacks and reinforcement learning. Various attempts have been made to integrate prior information into the gradient estimation procedure based on finite differences, with promising empirical results. However, their convergence properties are not well understood. This paper makes an attempt to fill up this gap by analyzing the convergence of prior-guided ZO algorithms under a greedy descent framework with various gradient estimators. We provide a convergence guarantee for the prior-guided random gradient-free (PRGF) algorithms. Moreover, to further accelerate over greedy descent methods, we present a new accelerated random search (ARS) algorithm that incorporates prior information, together with a convergence analysis. Finally, our theoretical results are confirmed by experiments on several numerical benchmarks as well as adversarial attacks.

The authors also introduce an accelerated random search algorithm that incorporates prior information, together with its own convergence analysis. This extends the investigation beyond greedy descent toward faster search. Experiments on numerical benchmarks and adversarial attacks support the theoretical results. The contribution combines analysis of existing prior-guided methods with a new accelerated method, linking the use of prior knowledge to formally studied optimization progress.
summary.tldr: The paper proves convergence results for prior-guided zeroth-order optimization and introduces an analyzed accelerated random search method.

title: On the Convergence of Prior-Guided Zeroth-Order Optimization Algorithms

abstract: We consider a variant of the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem where arms are known to be organized into different groups having the same mean. The groups are unknown but a lower bound $q$ on their size is known. This situation typically appears when each arm can be described with a list of categorical attributes, and the (unknown) mean reward function only depends on a subset of them, the others being redundant. In this case, $q$ is linked naturally to the number of attributes considered redundant, and the number of categories of each attribute. For this structured problem of practical relevance, we first derive the asymptotic regret lower bound and corresponding constrained optimization problem. They reveal the achievable regret can be substantially reduced when compared to the unstructured setup, possibly by a factor $q$. However, solving exactly the exact constrained optimization problem involves a combinatorial problem. We introduce a lower-bound inspired strategy involving a computationally efficient relaxation that is based on a sorting mechanism. We further prove it achieves a lower bound close to the optimal one up to a controlled factor, and achieves an asymptotic regret $q$ times smaller than the unstructured one. We believe this shows it is a valuable strategy for the practitioner. Last, we illustrate the performance of the considered strategy on numerical experiments involving a large number of arms.

summary.tldr: A sorting-based bandit strategy exploits unknown equal-mean groups with known minimum size q to achieve a factor-q asymptotic regret reduction.

title: Stochastic bandits with groups of similar arms.

abstract: Many experts argue that the future of artificial intelligence is limited by the field’s ability to integrate symbolic logical reasoning into deep learning architectures. The recently proposed differentiable MAXSAT solver, SATNet, was a breakthrough in its capacity to integrate with a traditional neural network and solve visual reasoning problems. For instance, it can learn the rules of Sudoku purely from image examples. Despite its success, SATNet was shown to succumb to a key challenge in neurosymbolic systems known as the Symbol Grounding Problem: the inability to map visual inputs to symbolic variables without explicit supervision ("label leakage"). In this work, we present a self-supervised pre-training pipeline that enables SATNet to overcome this limitation, thus broadening the class of problems that SATNet architectures can solve to include datasets where no intermediary labels are available at all. We demonstrate that our method allows SATNet to attain full accuracy even with a harder problem setup that prevents any label leakage. We additionally introduce a proofreading method that further improves the performance of SATNet architectures, beating the state-of-the-art on Visual Sudoku.

Earlier success depended on explicit intermediate supervision, creating a label-leakage concern.

The paper introduces a self-supervised pretraining pipeline that enables SATNet to handle this mapping without intermediate labels. This expands the range of datasets to which the architecture can be applied. The change targets the connection between perception and logical reasoning, which must work for the solver to reason correctly about what it sees.

The authors demonstrate full accuracy in a harder experimental setup designed to prevent label leakage. They also introduce a proofreading method that further improves SATNet architectures and exceeds the reported state of the art on Visual Sudoku. These findings show that the proposed training pipeline can overcome the demonstrated grounding barrier, with proofreading providing an additional improvement in the evaluated visual reasoning task.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised pretraining enables SATNet to ground visual symbols without intermediate labels, while proofreading further improves Visual Sudoku performance.

title: Techniques for Symbol Grounding with SATNet

abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are the go-to model for computer vision. Recently, attention-based networks, such as the Vision Transformer, have also become popular. In this paper we show that while convolutions and attention are both sufficient for good performance, neither of them are necessary. We present MLP-Mixer, an architecture based exclusively on multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). MLP-Mixer contains two types of layers: one with MLPs applied independently to image patches (i.e. "mixing" the per-location features), and one with MLPs applied across patches (i.e. "mixing" spatial information). When trained on large datasets, or with modern regularization schemes, MLP-Mixer attains competitive scores on image classification benchmarks, with pre-training and inference cost comparable to state-of-the-art models. We hope that these results spark further research beyond the realms of well established CNNs and Transformers.

paragraphs: MLP-Mixer asks whether strong image classification requires either convolutions or attention. The paper presents an architecture built entirely from multilayer perceptrons, showing that these familiar vision mechanisms are not necessary for competitive performance in the evaluated training settings. Its contribution is a different architectural route to combining visual information.

The model uses two types of layers. One applies multilayer perceptrons independently within image patches, mixing features at each location. The other operates across patches, mixing information between spatial locations. Separating these two operations lets the network combine local feature information and information distributed across the image using the same basic family of building blocks.

With large training datasets or modern regularization schemes, MLP-Mixer achieves competitive image-classification results. Its pretraining and inference costs are comparable to those of leading models. These conditions matter: the claim is about performance with the stated training support, not superiority in every setting. The findings broaden the set of architectures worth investigating beyond the established convolutional and attention-based approaches.
summary.tldr: MLP-Mixer achieves competitive image classification using only multilayer perceptrons that mix within-patch features and information across patches.

title: MLP-Mixer: An all-MLP Architecture for Vision

abstract: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) is a set of procedural tasks that tests an agent's ability to flexibly solve novel problems. While most ARC tasks are easy for humans, they are challenging for state-of-the-art AI. What makes building intelligent systems that can generalize to novel situations such as ARC difficult? We posit that the answer might be found by studying the difference of $\textit{language}$: While humans readily generate and interpret instructions in a general language, computer systems are shackled to a narrow domain-specific language that they can precisely execute. We present LARC, the $\textit{Language-complete ARC}$: a collection of natural language descriptions by a group of human participants who instruct each other on how to solve ARC tasks using language alone, which contains successful instructions for 88\% of the ARC tasks. We analyze the collected instructions as `natural programs', finding that while they resemble computer programs, they are distinct in two ways: First, they contain a wide range of primitives; Second, they frequently leverage communicative strategies beyond directly executable codes. We demonstrate that these two distinctions prevent current program synthesis techniques from leveraging LARC to its full potential, and give concrete suggestions on how to build the next-generation program synthesizers.

paragraphs: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus tests whether an agent can solve unfamiliar procedural problems. Many tasks are easy for people but difficult for AI systems. This paper investigates language as a possible part of that gap: people can exchange flexible instructions, whereas computer systems often depend on a narrow set of precisely executable operations.

The authors introduce Language-complete ARC, or LARC, by asking human participants to explain task solutions to one another using language alone. The collection includes successful instructions for 88% of ARC tasks. They analyze these descriptions as natural programs: instructions that convey a procedure without necessarily following the rigid form of executable code.

Two distinctions emerge. Human instructions draw on a broad range of basic operations, and they use communication strategies that go beyond directly specifying executable steps. The authors demonstrate that these properties limit how fully current program synthesis methods can use LARC. The dataset and analysis therefore offer concrete guidance for designing synthesizers that better accommodate how people communicate procedures.
summary.tldr: LARC captures human instructions for ARC tasks and exposes ways natural-language procedures exceed the capabilities of current program synthesis methods.

title: Communicating Natural Programs to Humans and Machines

abstract: Multi-agent collaborative perception could significantly upgrade the perception performance by enabling agents to share complementary information with each other through communication. It inevitably results in a fundamental trade-off between perception performance and communication bandwidth. To tackle this bottleneck issue, we propose a spatial confidence map, which reflects the spatial heterogeneity of perceptual information. It empowers agents to only share spatially sparse, yet perceptually critical information, contributing to where to communicate. Based on this novel spatial confidence map, we propose Where2comm, a communication-efficient collaborative perception framework. Where2comm has two distinct advantages: i) it considers pragmatic compression and uses less communication to achieve higher perception performance by focusing on perceptually critical areas; and ii) it can handle varying communication bandwidth by dynamically adjusting spatial areas involved in communication. To evaluate Where2comm, we consider 3D object detection in both real-world and simulation scenarios with two modalities (camera/LiDAR) and two agent types (cars/drones) on four datasets: OPV2V, V2X-Sim, DAIR-V2X, and our original CoPerception-UAVs. Where2comm consistently outperforms previous methods; for example, it achieves more than $100,000 \times$ lower communication volume and still outperforms DiscoNet and V2X-ViT on OPV2V. Our code is available at~\url{https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/where2comm}.

Our code is available at~\url{https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/where2comm}.

paragraphs: Collaborative perception lets agents share complementary observations, but sending more information consumes bandwidth. Where2comm addresses this tradeoff by asking which spatial regions are most useful to communicate. Its spatial confidence map represents differences in perceptual information across locations, allowing communication to focus on a sparse set of important regions.

The framework uses these maps to select perceptually critical information and supports practical compression. It can also adjust the spatial areas involved in communication as available bandwidth changes. This makes the amount and location of transmitted information responsive to the communication budget while preserving the goal of improving perception.

The authors evaluate 3D object detection in real and simulated settings involving cameras, LiDAR, cars, and drones across four datasets. They report consistent improvements over previous methods. On OPV2V, one highlighted result uses more than 100,000 times less communication volume while outperforming DiscoNet and V2X-ViT. That comparison illustrates the potential of spatial selection in the evaluated setting, rather than a universal reduction for every deployment.
summary.tldr: Where2comm uses spatial confidence maps to share critical regions, improving evaluated collaborative perception while sharply reducing communication.

title: Where2comm: Communication-Efficient Collaborative Perception via Spatial Confidence Maps

abstract: Understanding the consequences of mutation for molecular fitness and function is a fundamental problem in biology. Recently, generative probabilistic models have emerged as a powerful tool for estimating fitness from evolutionary sequence data, with accuracy sufficient to predict both laboratory measurements of function and disease risk in humans, and to design novel functional proteins. Existing techniques rest on an assumed relationship between density estimation and fitness estimation, a relationship that we interrogate in this article. We prove that fitness is not identifiable from observational sequence data alone, placing fundamental limits on our ability to disentangle fitness landscapes from phylogenetic history. We show on real datasets that perfect density estimation in the limit of infinite data would, with high confidence, result in poor fitness estimation; current models perform accurate fitness estimation because of, not despite, misspecification. Our results challenge the conventional wisdom that bigger models trained on bigger datasets will inevitably lead to better fitness estimation, and suggest novel estimation strategies going forward.

paragraphs: Probabilistic models of evolutionary sequences are used to estimate molecular fitness and function. These applications rely on a relationship between how likely a sequence is under a model and how fit it is biologically. This paper investigates whether increasingly accurate sequence-probability estimates necessarily improve fitness estimates.

The authors prove that fitness cannot be uniquely identified from observational sequence data alone. In particular, the observations do not suffice to disentangle the fitness landscape from evolutionary history. This creates a fundamental information limit that cannot be removed simply by fitting the observed sequence distribution more accurately.

On real datasets, the analysis indicates with high confidence that even perfect density estimation in the infinite-data limit would produce poor fitness estimation. The authors attribute current models’ accurate fitness estimates to their misspecification: their imperfect representation of the sequence distribution is beneficial for this target. The finding challenges inevitable improvement through model and dataset scaling, while suggesting that fitness estimation needs objectives or strategies beyond density accuracy alone.
summary.tldr: Fitness is not identifiable from sequence observations alone, and imperfect density models can estimate it better than perfect density estimation.

title: Non-identifiability and the Blessings of Misspecification in Models of Molecular Fitness

abstract: Neural diffusion on graphs is a novel class of graph neural networks that has attracted increasing attention recently. The capability of graph neural partial differential equations (PDEs) in addressing common hurdles of graph neural networks (GNNs), such as the problems of over-smoothing and bottlenecks, has been investigated but not their robustness to adversarial attacks. In this work, we explore the robustness properties of graph neural PDEs. We empirically demonstrate that graph neural PDEs are intrinsically more robust against topology perturbation as compared to other GNNs. We provide insights into this phenomenon by exploiting the stability of the heat semigroup under graph topology perturbations. We discuss various graph diffusion operators and relate them to existing graph neural PDEs. Furthermore, we propose a general graph neural PDE framework based on which a new class of robust GNNs can be defined. We verify that the new model achieves comparable state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Graph neural diffusion models process information on a graph through dynamics described by partial differential equations. Previous research had investigated their ability to address problems such as over-smoothing and information bottlenecks. This paper turns to a different question: how these models respond when an adversary perturbs the graph's topology, changing its connection structure.

The authors empirically find that graph neural PDEs are intrinsically more robust to these perturbations than other graph neural networks in their comparisons. To explain this behavior, they draw on the stability of the heat semigroup under changes to graph topology. This connects observed robustness to mathematical properties of diffusion as graph structure changes.

The paper also examines several graph diffusion operators and relates them to existing neural PDE models. From this analysis, it proposes a general framework for defining a new class of robust graph networks. The resulting model achieves performance comparable to the state of the art on several benchmarks, supporting diffusion as a route to robustness while retaining competitive predictive performance.
summary.tldr: The paper links graph neural diffusion's observed robustness to diffusion stability and introduces a robust PDE-based graph-network framework.

title: On the Robustness of Graph Neural Diffusion to Topology Perturbations

abstract: Temporal-difference learning is a popular algorithm for policy evaluation. In this paper, we study the convergence of the regularized non-parametric TD(0) algorithm, in both the independent and Markovian observation settings. In particular, when TD is performed in a universal reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), we prove convergence of the averaged iterates to the optimal value function, even when it does not belong to the RKHS. We provide explicit convergence rates that depend on a source condition relating the regularity of the optimal value function to the RKHS. We illustrate this convergence numerically on a simple continuous-state Markov reward process.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning estimates value functions for policy evaluation. This paper examines a regularized, non-parametric version of TD(0), asking how its estimates converge as observations accumulate. It treats both independent observations and Markovian observations, so the analysis includes data whose successive samples are linked through a state-transition process.

The method represents value estimates in a universal reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS. The main result proves convergence of averaged iterates to the target value function even when that function is not itself an element of the RKHS. This distinction matters: the convergence claim does not require the exact target to belong to the space used to represent the individual estimates.

The authors also provide explicit convergence rates. Those rates depend on a source condition connecting the target function's regularity to the chosen RKHS, making that relationship part of the guarantee. A numerical example on a simple continuous-state Markov reward process illustrates the convergence. Together, the results describe both eventual convergence and how quickly finite sequences of estimates approach the target under the stated conditions.
summary.tldr: Regularized kernel TD(0) receives explicit convergence guarantees, including when the target value function lies outside its RKHS.

title: A Non-asymptotic Analysis of Non-parametric Temporal-Difference Learning

abstract: We give a method for proactively identifying small, plausible shifts in distribution which lead to large differences in model performance. These shifts are defined via parametric changes in the causal mechanisms of observed variables, where constraints on parameters yield a "robustness set" of plausible distributions and a corresponding worst-case loss over the set. While the loss under an individual parametric shift can be estimated via reweighting techniques such as importance sampling, the resulting worst-case optimization problem is non-convex, and the estimate may suffer from large variance. For small shifts, however, we can construct a local second-order approximation to the loss under shift and cast the problem of finding a worst-case shift as a particular non-convex quadratic optimization problem, for which efficient algorithms are available. We demonstrate that this second-order approximation can be estimated directly for shifts in conditional exponential family models, and we bound the approximation error. We apply our approach to a computer vision task (classifying gender from images), revealing sensitivity to shifts in non-causal attributes.

paragraphs: A model can perform well on its evaluation data yet be sensitive to small changes in the data distribution. This paper develops a way to search proactively for plausible changes that cause large performance differences. It describes shifts through parameter changes in the causal mechanisms governing observed variables, with parameter constraints defining the distributions considered plausible.

The objective is to find the worst loss within this robustness set. Estimating each shifted loss by reweighting data is possible, but the search is non-convex and estimates can have high variance. For small shifts, the authors instead approximate the loss locally to second order. This turns the search into a particular quadratic optimization problem for which efficient algorithms exist.

For shifts in conditional exponential-family models, the paper shows how to estimate the approximation directly and bounds its error. An image-based gender classification application reveals sensitivity to changes in non-causal attributes. The result illustrates how a structured, local robustness analysis can expose vulnerabilities to specified distribution changes.
summary.tldr: The paper searches for damaging small distribution shifts using constrained causal parameters and an efficiently optimized second-order loss approximation.

title: Evaluating Robustness to Dataset Shift via Parametric Robustness Sets

abstract: Recently, Miller et al. showed that a model's in-distribution (ID) accuracy has a strong linear correlation with its out-of-distribution (OOD) accuracy, on several OOD benchmarks, a phenomenon they dubbed ``accuracy-on-the-line''. While a useful tool for model selection (i.e., the model most likely to perform the best OOD is the one with highest ID accuracy), this fact does not help to estimate the actual OOD performance of models without access to a labeled OOD validation set. In this paper, we show a similar surprising phenomena also holds for the agreement between pairs of neural network classifiers: whenever accuracy-on-the-line holds, we observe that the OOD agreement between the predictions of any two pairs of neural networks (with potentially different architectures) also observes a strong linear correlation with their ID agreement. Furthermore, we observe that the slope and bias of OOD vs ID agreement closely matches that of OOD vs ID accuracy. This phenomenon which we call agreement-on-the-line, has important practical applications: without any labeled data, we can predict the OOD accuracy of classifiers, since OOD agreement can be estimated with just unlabeled data. Our prediction algorithm outperforms previous methods both in shifts where agreement-on-the-line holds and, surprisingly, when accuracy is not on the line. This phenomenon also provides new insights into neural networks: unlike accuracy-on-the-line, agreement-on-the-line only appears to hold for neural network classifiers.
