paragraphs: Structured sparsity encourages whole groups of neural-network weights to disappear, producing more compact models. The penalties used to induce this behavior are often non-differentiable, complicating ordinary gradient-based training. D-Gating tackles that difficulty by representing each weight group through a primary vector and several scalar gates, yielding a fully differentiable objective.

The authors prove a specific connection to the original sparsity problem: every local minimum under D-Gating is also a local minimum for the corresponding non-smooth structured L2,2/D penalty. They additionally show that, in the gradient-flow limit, the D-Gating objective approaches the regularized loss at least exponentially fast. These results give the smooth formulation a formal relationship to structured penalization.

Despite that relationship, its training trajectory differs: optimization begins in a non-sparse regime and evolves toward sparse optimization. Experiments across vision, language, and tabular tasks report strong tradeoffs between predictive performance and sparsity, outperforming direct structured-penalty optimization and conventional pruning baselines. The contribution combines a differentiable training mechanism with guarantees about the sparsity objective it represents.
summary.tldr: D-Gating provides a differentiable route to structured sparsity with theoretical links to non-smooth penalties and strong empirical performance–sparsity tradeoffs.

title: Differentiable Sparsity via $D$-Gating: Simple and Versatile Structured Penalization

abstract: Diffusion models have advanced image stylization significantly, yet two core challenges persist: (1) maintaining consistent stylization in complex scenes, particularly identity, composition, and fine details, and (2) preventing style degradation in image-to-image pipelines with style LoRAs. GPT-4o's exceptional stylization consistency highlights the performance gap between open-source methods and proprietary models. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{OmniConsistency}, a universal consistency plugin leveraging large-scale Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). OmniConsistency contributes: (1) an in-context consistency learning framework trained on aligned image pairs for robust generalization; (2) a two-stage progressive learning strategy decoupling style learning from consistency preservation to mitigate style degradation; and (3) a fully plug-and-play design compatible with arbitrary style LoRAs under the Flux framework. Extensive experiments show that OmniConsistency significantly enhances visual coherence and aesthetic quality, achieving performance comparable to commercial state-of-the-art model GPT-4o.

paragraphs: Image stylization must change an image’s appearance while retaining identity, composition, and fine details. Diffusion-based pipelines can lose that consistency, especially in complex scenes, and can weaken the intended style when using style LoRAs. OmniConsistency is a plugin designed to improve content preservation while maintaining the requested visual style.

The method uses large diffusion transformers and learns consistency from aligned image pairs through an in-context framework. Its two-stage progressive training separates style learning from consistency preservation, aiming to reduce style degradation. The resulting plugin is designed to work with arbitrary style LoRAs within the Flux framework, giving the consistency mechanism a reusable role across styles.

The authors report substantial improvements in visual coherence and aesthetic quality, with performance comparable to GPT-4o in their experiments. The contribution is therefore both a training approach and a modular component: paired examples teach what should remain stable, while separating training stages helps keep that stability from interfering with stylization. The compatibility claim is specifically situated within Flux.
summary.tldr: OmniConsistency learns from aligned image pairs to preserve content and style across Flux stylization pipelines.

title: OmniConsistency: Learning Style-Agnostic Consistency from Paired Stylization Data

abstract: Robotic manipulation systems benefit from complementary sensing modalities, where each provides unique environmental information. Point clouds capture detailed geometric structure, while RGB images provide rich semantic context. Current point cloud methods struggle to capture fine-grained detail, especially for complex tasks, which RGB methods lack geometric awareness, which hinders their precision and generalization. We introduce PointMapPolicy, a novel approach that conditions diffusion policies on structured grids of points without downsampling. The resulting data type makes it easier to extract shape and spatial relationships from observations, and can be transformed between reference frames. Yet due to their structure in a regular grid, we enable the use of established computer vision techniques directly to 3D data. Using xLSTM as a backbone, our model efficiently fuses the point maps with RGB data for enhanced multi-modal perception. Through extensive experiments on the RoboCasa and CALVIN benchmarks and real robot evaluations, we demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse manipulation tasks. The overview and demos are available on our project page: https://point-map.github.io/Point-Map/

paragraphs: Robotic manipulation benefits from both geometric and visual information. Point clouds describe spatial structure, while RGB images provide semantic context. The paper identifies complementary weaknesses in existing approaches: point-cloud methods can miss fine detail, and image-based methods lack geometric awareness needed for precise and generalizable behavior.

PointMapPolicy conditions diffusion policies on point maps, which arrange 3D points in structured grids without downsampling. This preserves detailed observations while making shape and spatial relationships easier to extract. The maps can also be transformed between reference frames. Their regular grid structure enables established computer vision techniques to operate directly on the 3D information.

The authors evaluate the approach on RoboCasa, CALVIN, and real robots, reporting state-of-the-art performance across diverse manipulation tasks. The results support the usefulness of the chosen representation: structured 3D observations can retain detail while fitting naturally into techniques for processing visual data.
summary.tldr: PointMapPolicy combines full-resolution structured 3D point grids with RGB observations to improve diffusion policies for robotic manipulation.

title: PointMapPolicy: Structured Point Cloud Processing for Multi-Modal Imitation Learning

abstract: We propose LangHOPS, the first Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)-based framework for open-vocabulary object–part instance segmentation. Given an image, LangHOPS can jointly detect and segment hierarchical object and part instances from open-vocabulary candidate categories. Unlike prior approaches that rely on heuristic or learnable visual grouping, our approach grounds object–part hierarchies in language space. It integrates the MLLM into the object-part parsing pipeline to leverage rich knowledge and reasoning capabilities, and link multi-granularity concepts within the hierarchies. We evaluate LangHOPS across multiple challenging scenarios, including in-domain and cross-dataset object-part instance segmentation, and zero-shot semantic segmentation. LangHOPS achieves state-of-the-art results, surpassing previous methods by 5.5% Average Precision(AP) (in-domain) and 4.8% (cross-dataset) on the PartImageNet dataset and by 2.5% mIOU on unseen object parts in ADE20K (zero-shot). Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the language-grounded hierarchy and MLLM-driven part query refinement strategy. Our results establish LangHOPS as a strong foundation for advancing open-vocabulary fine-grained visual understanding applicable in multiple scenarios.

paragraphs: LangHOPS identifies objects and their individual parts in images while preserving the hierarchy connecting them. Given candidate categories expressed through an open vocabulary, it jointly detects instances and segments their image regions. This links fine-grained visual recognition to the larger objects those parts belong to, rather than treating every region as an unrelated category.

The framework grounds object–part hierarchies in language space using a multimodal large language model. Its knowledge and reasoning connect concepts at different levels of detail within the parsing pipeline. The method also uses model-driven refinement of part queries. This approach makes language-grounded relationships central to organizing the visual predictions.

Evaluation covers in-domain and cross-dataset instance segmentation, plus zero-shot semantic segmentation. The reported improvements are 5.5% and 4.8% in Average Precision on PartImageNet, and 2.5% in mIOU for unseen ADE20K object parts. Ablation studies support the contributions of both the language-grounded hierarchy and query refinement. Together, the results demonstrate gains across several forms of fine-grained visual understanding.
summary.tldr: LangHOPS uses language-grounded object–part hierarchies to improve open-vocabulary segmentation, including recognition of unseen parts.

title: LangHOPS: Language Grounded Hierarchical Open-Vocabulary Part Segmentation

abstract: In recent years, a number of probabilistic inference and counting techniques have been proposed that exploit pairwise independent hash functions to infer properties of succinctly defined high-dimensional sets. While providing desirable statistical guarantees, typical constructions of such hash functions are themselves not amenable to efficient inference. Inspired by the success of LDPC codes, we propose the use of low-density parity constraints to make inference more tractable in practice. While not strongly universal, we show that such sparse constraints belong to a new class of hash functions that we call Average Universal. These weaker hash functions retain the desirable statistical guarantees needed by most such probabilistic inference methods. Thus, they continue to provide provable accuracy guarantees while at the same time making a number of algorithms significantly more scalable in practice. Using this technique, we provide new, tighter bounds for challenging discrete integration and model counting problems.

paragraphs: Hashing-based inference and counting methods use randomized functions to learn about high-dimensional sets that have compact descriptions. Standard constructions offer useful statistical guarantees, but the hash constraints themselves can make inference computationally difficult. This paper targets that obstacle by using sparse parity constraints inspired by low-density parity-check codes.

The proposed constraints belong to a new class called Average Universal hash functions. They do not satisfy the stronger universality property of conventional constructions. The authors nevertheless show that this weaker class preserves the statistical guarantees needed by most of the relevant probabilistic inference methods. The analysis establishes that those methods can retain provable accuracy while using more tractable constraints.

In practice, the change makes a number of algorithms significantly more scalable. The authors use it to obtain tighter bounds on challenging discrete integration and model-counting problems. The contribution shows that a weaker hashing property can be sufficient for the desired inference guarantees, allowing computational improvements without abandoning the accuracy guarantees established for the applicable methods.
summary.tldr: Sparse Average Universal hash constraints preserve useful accuracy guarantees while making discrete integration and model counting more scalable.

title: Low-density Parity Constraints for Hashing-Based Discrete Integration

abstract: Recovering a low-rank tensor from incomplete information is a recurring problem in signal processing and machine learning. The most popular convex relaxation of this problem minimizes the sum of the nuclear norms (SNN) of the unfolding matrices of the tensor. We show that this approach can be substantially suboptimal: reliably recovering a K-way n\timesn\times⋯\times n tensor of Tucker rank (r, r, \ldots, r) from Gaussian measurements requires Ω( r n^K-1 ) observations. In contrast, a certain (intractable) nonconvex formulation needs only O(r^K + nrK) observations. We introduce a simple, new convex relaxation, which partially bridges this gap. Our new formulation succeeds with O(r^⌊K/2 ⌋n^⌈K/2 ⌉) observations. The lower bound for the SNN model follows from our new result on recovering signals with multiple structures (e.g. sparse, low rank), which indicates the significant suboptimality of the common approach of minimizing the sum of individual sparsity inducing norms (e.g. \ell_1, nuclear norm). Our new tractable formulation for low-rank tensor recovery shows how the sample complexity can be reduced by designing convex regularizers that exploit several structures jointly.

paragraphs: Recovering a low-rank tensor means reconstructing a multidimensional array from incomplete measurements. A common convex approach sums the nuclear norms of matrices formed by unfolding the tensor. This paper proves that this sum-of-norms formulation can require substantially more information than the tensor’s structure would otherwise suggest.

For a K-way tensor with side length n and Tucker rank (r, …, r), reliable recovery from Gaussian measurements using that formulation requires on the order of r n^(K−1) observations. An intractable nonconvex formulation needs only O(r^K + nrK). The authors introduce a tractable convex relaxation that succeeds with O(r^floor(K/2) n^ceil(K/2)) observations, partially closing the gap.

The lower bound follows from a broader result about signals possessing several structures at once. Adding separate structure-promoting norms can be significantly suboptimal because the resulting penalty may not exploit those structures jointly. The new tensor formulation demonstrates that designing the regularizer around their combination can reduce sample requirements. Its improvement narrows the gap without claiming to match the intractable formulation’s measurement count.
summary.tldr: The paper proves weaknesses in sum-of-nuclear-norm tensor recovery and introduces a convex relaxation with improved measurement requirements.

title: Square Deal: Lower Bounds and Improved Relaxations for Tensor Recovery

abstract: How should we present training examples to learners to teach them classification rules? This is a natural problem when training workers for crowdsourcing labeling tasks, and is also motivated by challenges in data-driven online education. We propose a natural stochastic model of the learners, modeling them as randomly switching among hypotheses based on observed feedback. We then develop STRICT, an efficient algorithm for selecting examples to teach to workers. Our solution greedily maximizes a submodular surrogate objective function in order to select examples to show to the learners. We prove that our strategy is competitive with the optimal teaching policy. Moreover, for the special case of linear separators, we prove that an exponential reduction in error probability can be achieved. Our experiments on simulated workers as well as three real image annotation tasks on Amazon Mechanical Turk show the effectiveness of our teaching algorithm.

It asks how a teacher should choose what a learner sees when learning behavior is uncertain.

Their algorithm, STRICT, selects teaching examples by greedily maximizing a submodular surrogate objective. The surrogate gives an efficient objective to optimize within the proposed learner model, connecting individual example choices to the overall teaching task.

summary.tldr: STRICT efficiently selects teaching examples and offers guarantees and empirical evidence for improving workers’ classification learning.

title: Near-Optimally Teaching the Crowd to Classify

abstract: LogitBoost, MART and their variant can be viewed as additive tree regression using logistic loss and boosting style optimization. We analyze their convergence rates based on a new weak learnability formulation. We show that it has O(\frac1T) rate when using gradient descent only, while a linear rate is achieved when using Newton descent. Moreover, introducing Newton descent when growing the trees, as LogitBoost does, leads to a faster linear rate. Empirical results on UCI datasets support our analysis.

Moreover, introducing Newton descent when growing the trees, as LogitBoost does, leads to a faster linear rate. Empirical results on UCI datasets support our analysis.

paragraphs: This paper studies how quickly LogitBoost, MART, and a related variant improve their optimization objectives. It treats these methods within a common framework: they build an additive collection of regression trees, use logistic loss to measure prediction errors, and optimize through boosting. This shared view makes it possible to compare the consequences of their different update choices.

The analysis introduces a new formulation of weak learnability, the condition underlying its convergence results. Under this formulation, using only gradient descent yields an O(1/T) convergence rate, where T represents the number of iterations. Using Newton descent instead gives a linear convergence rate, meaning that the remaining optimization gap contracts geometrically rather than decreasing inversely with the iteration count.

The analysis further distinguishes where Newton descent enters the procedure. Incorporating it while growing trees, as LogitBoost does, produces a faster linear rate. Experiments on UCI datasets support these theoretical comparisons. The findings connect specific optimization choices to convergence speed under the paper’s formulation.
summary.tldr: Under a new weak learnability formulation, Newton updates give faster convergence guarantees for tree boosting than gradient updates alone.

title: A Convergence Rate Analysis for LogitBoost, MART and Their Variant

abstract: This paper considers estimating the leading k principal components with at most s non-zero attributes from p-dimensional samples collected sequentially in memory limited environments. We develop and analyze two memory and computational efficient algorithms called streaming sparse PCA and streaming sparse ECA for analyzing data generated according to the spike model and the elliptical model respectively. In particular, the proposed algorithms have memory complexity O(pk), computational complexity O(pk mink,slogp) and sample complexity Θ(s \log p). We provide their finite sample performance guarantees, which implies statistical consistency in the high dimensional regime. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate good empirical performance of the proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper considers estimating leading principal components when high-dimensional samples arrive sequentially and memory is limited. The desired components are sparse, involving at most s nonzero attributes among p available dimensions. The task therefore combines structural estimation with the practical need to process data as a stream.

The authors develop two algorithms: streaming sparse PCA for data generated by a spike model, and streaming sparse ECA for an elliptical model. For k leading components, the stated memory requirement is O(pk), and the sample complexity is Θ(s log p). The algorithms are also designed for computational efficiency, making both storage and processing costs central to the contribution.

Finite-sample guarantees describe performance with a limited amount of data and imply statistical consistency in the high-dimensional regime under the analyzed models. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report good empirical performance. The result matters because it connects sparse component recovery with streaming constraints, showing how model-specific guarantees can accompany algorithms intended for memory-limited analysis.
summary.tldr: Two efficient streaming algorithms estimate sparse principal components with finite-sample guarantees under spike and elliptical data models.

title: Streaming Sparse Principal Component Analysis

abstract: Convolution is a critical component in modern deep neural networks, thus several algorithms for convolution have been developed. Direct convolution is simple but suffers from poor performance. As an alternative, multiple indirect methods have been proposed including im2col-based convolution, FFT-based convolution, or Winograd-based algorithm. However, all these indirect methods have high memory overhead, which creates performance degradation and offers a poor trade-off between performance and memory consumption. In this work, we propose a memory-efficient convolution or MEC with compact lowering, which reduces memory overhead substantially and accelerates convolution process. MEC lowers the input matrix in a simple yet efficient/compact way (i.e., much less memory overhead), and then executes multiple small matrix multiplications in parallel to get convolution completed. Additionally, the reduced memory footprint improves memory sub-system efficiency, improving performance. Our experimental results show that MEC reduces memory consumption significantly with good speedup on both mobile and server platforms, compared with other indirect convolution algorithms.

paragraphs: Convolution is a major operation in deep neural networks, and its implementation affects both speed and memory use. The paper describes a tension among existing approaches: direct convolution has poor performance, while indirect methods can require substantial extra memory. That overhead can itself reduce performance, making memory consumption part of the computational problem.

MEC addresses this through compact lowering, a way of arranging the input for computation while using much less intermediate memory. After this compact transformation, the method performs several small matrix multiplications in parallel to complete the convolution. The design connects a smaller working representation with a parallel computation strategy.

The reduced memory footprint also improves the efficiency of the memory subsystem, contributing to speed gains. Experiments on both mobile and server platforms show substantial memory reductions and good speedups compared with other indirect convolution algorithms. The stated results indicate that reducing intermediate storage can improve the memory–performance tradeoff for convolution in the evaluated implementations.
summary.tldr: MEC uses compact input lowering and parallel small matrix multiplications to reduce convolution memory overhead and improve speed on mobile and server platforms.

title: MEC: Memory-efficient Convolution for Deep Neural Network

abstract: Backpropagation algorithm is indispensable for the training of feedforward neural networks. It requires propagating error gradients sequentially from the output layer all the way back to the input layer. The backward locking in backpropagation algorithm constrains us from updating network layers in parallel and fully leveraging the computing resources. Recently, several algorithms have been proposed for breaking the backward locking. However, their performances degrade seriously when networks are deep. In this paper, we propose decoupled parallel backpropagation algorithm for deep learning optimization with convergence guarantee. Firstly, we decouple the backpropagation algorithm using delayed gradients, and show that the backward locking is removed when we split the networks into multiple modules. Then, we utilize decoupled parallel backpropagation in two stochastic methods and prove that our method guarantees convergence to critical points for the non-convex problem. Finally, we perform experiments for training deep convolutional neural networks on benchmark datasets. The experimental results not only confirm our theoretical analysis, but also demonstrate that the proposed method can achieve significant speedup without loss of accuracy.

paragraphs: Ordinary backpropagation creates a dependency between layers during training: an earlier layer must wait for error information to travel backward from later layers. This backward locking limits how much updating can happen in parallel. The paper targets that dependency, especially in deep networks where previous attempts to remove it have suffered substantial performance degradation.

The proposed method divides a network into modules and uses delayed gradients to decouple their backward computations. This removes the locking between modules and makes parallel updates possible. The authors incorporate this mechanism into two stochastic optimization methods, connecting the parallel execution scheme to algorithms that can be analyzed mathematically.

For the nonconvex problem studied, they prove convergence to critical points. This is a convergence guarantee, not a claim that training always reaches a globally best solution. Experiments with deep convolutional networks on benchmark datasets support the analysis and show significant training speedups without accuracy loss in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: Delayed gradients enable parallel training across network modules, with critical-point convergence guarantees and reported speedups without accuracy loss.

title: Decoupled Parallel Backpropagation with Convergence Guarantee

abstract: We present PredRNN++, a recurrent network for spatiotemporal predictive learning. In pursuit of a great modeling capability for short-term video dynamics, we make our network deeper in time by leveraging a new recurrent structure named Causal LSTM with cascaded dual memories. To alleviate the gradient propagation difficulties in deep predictive models, we propose a Gradient Highway Unit, which provides alternative quick routes for the gradient flows from outputs back to long-range previous inputs. The gradient highway units work seamlessly with the causal LSTMs, enabling our model to capture the short-term and the long-term video dependencies adaptively. Our model achieves state-of-the-art prediction results on both synthetic and real video datasets, showing its power in modeling entangled motions.

The gradient highway units work seamlessly with the causal LSTMs, enabling our model to capture the short-term and the long-term video dependencies adaptively. Our model achieves state-of-the-art prediction results on both synthetic and real video datasets, showing its power in modeling entangled motions.

paragraphs: PredRNN++ is a recurrent network for predicting data that varies across both space and time, evaluated here on video. The design addresses a tension between modeling detailed short-term motion and preserving learning signals over longer intervals. Making a predictive network deeper in time can strengthen its modeling capacity while making gradient propagation more difficult.

The authors introduce a Causal LSTM with two memories arranged in a cascade to increase temporal depth. They pair it with a Gradient Highway Unit, which gives gradients faster alternative routes from outputs back to distant inputs. Together, these components let the model adaptively capture both short-term and long-term video dependencies.

The reported evaluations achieve state-of-the-art prediction results on synthetic and real video datasets. These findings support the combination of richer recurrent computation and additional gradient routes for modeling entangled motions. The contribution lies in how the two architectural components work together to address the competing demands of temporal depth and learning across long intervals.
summary.tldr: PredRNN++ combines deeper recurrent memory with gradient highways to improve prediction of short-term and long-term video dynamics.

title: PredRNN++: Towards A Resolution of the Deep-in-Time Dilemma in Spatiotemporal Predictive Learning

abstract: Randomly initialized first-order optimization algorithms are the method of choice for solving many high-dimensional nonconvex problems in machine learning, yet general theoretical guarantees cannot rule out convergence to critical points of poor objective value. For some highly structured nonconvex problems however, the success of gradient descent can be understood by studying the geometry of the objective. We study one such problem – complete orthogonal dictionary learning, and provide converge guarantees for randomly initialized gradient descent to the neighborhood of a global optimum. The resulting rates scale as low order polynomials in the dimension even though the objective possesses an exponential number of saddle points. This efficient convergence can be viewed as a consequence of negative curvature normal to the stable manifolds associated with saddle points, and we provide evidence that this feature is shared by other nonconvex problems of importance as well.

paragraphs: Gradient descent often works well on nonconvex learning problems, even though general theory cannot exclude convergence to poor critical points. This paper investigates why it can succeed in the structured setting of complete orthogonal dictionary learning. The authors analyze the geometry of the objective to connect the optimization landscape with algorithmic behavior.

They prove that randomly initialized gradient descent converges to a neighborhood of a global optimum. The convergence rates grow as low-order polynomials in dimension, despite the objective having exponentially many saddle points. The result shows that a large number of saddles does not, by itself, force inefficient optimization in this particular problem.

The explanation centers on negative curvature in directions normal to the stable manifolds associated with saddle points. This geometric feature helps account for efficient convergence despite the saddles. The paper also provides evidence that other important nonconvex problems share this feature. That broader evidence suggests a useful perspective, while the stated convergence guarantee concerns complete orthogonal dictionary learning.
summary.tldr: For complete orthogonal dictionary learning, randomly initialized gradient descent efficiently approaches a global optimum despite exponentially many saddles.

title: Efficient Dictionary Learning with Gradient Descent

abstract: In many practical applications, heuristic or approximation algorithms are used to efficiently solve the task at hand. However their solutions frequently do not satisfy natural monotonicity properties expected to hold in the optimum. In this work we develop algorithms that are able to restore monotonicity in the parameters of interest. Specifically, given oracle access to a possibly non monotone function, we provide an algorithm that restores monotonicity while degrading the expected value of the function by at most $\epsilon$. The number of queries required is at most logarithmic in $1/\epsilon$ and exponential in the number of parameters. We also give a lower bound showing that this exponential dependence is necessary. Finally, we obtain improved query complexity bounds for restoring the weaker property of $k$-marginal monotonicity. Under this property, every $k$-dimensional projection of the function is required to be monotone. The query complexity we obtain only scales exponentially with $k$ and is polynomial in the number of parameters.

paragraphs: An efficient heuristic can produce outputs that violate a monotonic relationship expected of an optimal solution. For example, a parameter may have an intended direction of influence that the approximation fails to respect. This paper studies how to restore such monotonicity using only oracle access to the function, so the correction operates through queries rather than its internal implementation.

The authors give an algorithm that restores monotonicity while reducing the function's expected value by at most epsilon. Its query requirement grows at most logarithmically with the inverse of epsilon but exponentially with the number of parameters. A lower bound shows that the exponential dependence on dimension is necessary for the full restoration problem.

The paper also considers a weaker requirement called k-marginal monotonicity, where every k-dimensional projection must be monotone. For this requirement, the query cost is exponential only in k and polynomial in the total number of parameters. The results expose a tradeoff between the scope of the monotonicity requirement and the cost of enforcing it.
summary.tldr: Black-box algorithms restore monotonicity with bounded expected-value loss, while a weaker projection-based requirement reduces the dependence on dimension.

title: Black-Box Methods for Restoring Monotonicity

abstract: Log-loss (also known as cross-entropy loss) metric is ubiquitously used across machine learning applications to assess the performance of classification algorithms. In this paper, we investigate the problem of inferring the labels of a dataset from single (or multiple) log-loss score(s), without any other access to the dataset. Surprisingly, we show that for any finite number of label classes, it is possible to accurately infer the labels of the dataset from the reported log-loss score of a single carefully constructed prediction vector if we allow arbitrary precision arithmetic. Additionally, we present label inference algorithms (attacks) that succeed even under addition of noise to the log-loss scores and under limited precision arithmetic. All our algorithms rely on ideas from number theory and combinatorics and require no model training. We run experimental simulations on some real datasets to demonstrate the ease of running these attacks in practice.

Surprisingly, we show that for any finite number of label classes, it is possible to accurately infer the labels of the dataset from the reported log-loss score of a single carefully constructed prediction vector if we allow arbitrary precision arithmetic. paragraphs: Log-loss is commonly reported as a summary of a classifier's performance. This paper investigates whether that summary can reveal the underlying dataset labels even when the dataset is otherwise inaccessible. The central finding is that carefully chosen predictions can make a reported score carry enough information to recover much more than an overall assessment of accuracy.

For any finite number of label classes, the authors show that one carefully constructed prediction vector and its log-loss score can enable accurate label inference when arbitrary-precision arithmetic is available. That arithmetic condition is central to this single-score result. The paper also develops attacks that succeed with noisy scores and limited numerical precision.

The algorithms use number-theoretic and combinatorial ideas and require no model training. Simulations on real datasets demonstrate that the attacks can be practical. The findings identify the evaluation score itself as a potential channel for exposing labels: restricting direct access to a dataset does not, by itself, eliminate the information that a scoring interface may reveal through constructed submissions.
summary.tldr: Carefully constructed predictions can expose dataset labels through log-loss scores, including a single-score result under arbitrary-precision arithmetic.

title: Label Inference Attacks from Log-loss Scores

abstract: We study episodic reinforcement learning under unknown adversarial corruptions in both the rewards and the transition probabilities of the underlying system. We propose new algorithms which, compared to the existing results in \cite{lykouris2020corruption}, achieve strictly better regret bounds in terms of total corruptions for the tabular setting. To be specific, firstly, our regret bounds depend on more precise numerical values of total rewards corruptions and transition corruptions, instead of only on the total number of corrupted episodes. Secondly, our regret bounds are the first of their kind in the reinforcement learning setting to have the number of corruptions show up additively with respect to $\min\{ \sqrt{T},\text{PolicyGapComplexity} \}$ rather than multiplicatively. Our results follow from a general algorithmic framework that combines corruption-robust policy elimination meta-algorithms, and plug-in reward-free exploration sub-algorithms. Replacing the meta-algorithm or sub-algorithm may extend the framework to address other corrupted settings with potentially more structure.

Secondly, our regret bounds are the first of their kind in the reinforcement learning setting to have the number of corruptions show up additively with respect to $\min\{ \sqrt{T},\text{PolicyGapComplexity} \}$ rather than multiplicatively. Our results follow from a general algorithmic framework that combines corruption-robust policy elimination meta-algorithms, and plug-in reward-free exploration sub-algorithms. paragraphs: This paper studies episodic reinforcement learning when an adversary can corrupt both rewards and transition probabilities, with the corruption unknown to the learner. In the tabular setting, the authors develop algorithms with improved regret bounds. Regret measures the performance cost accumulated while learning, so these bounds describe how corruption affects that cost.

The guarantees improve how corruption enters the analysis in two ways. They use the numerical amounts of reward and transition corruption, rather than simply counting episodes containing corruption. They also make the corruption contribution additive with respect to the smaller of √T and PolicyGapComplexity, where previous results had a multiplicative relationship. This yields a more precise dependence on the adversary's interference.

The algorithms arise from a framework combining corruption-robust policy elimination with reward-free exploration components. This separates the mechanism for managing candidate policies from the mechanism for gathering information. The authors suggest that replacing either component may extend the framework to other structured corruption settings; this is presented as a possible extension, not an established guarantee.
summary.tldr: New tabular reinforcement-learning algorithms provide sharper regret guarantees under unknown reward and transition corruption.

title: Improved Corruption Robust Algorithms for Episodic Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Modern machine learning increasingly requires training on a large collection of data from multiple sources, not all of which can be trusted. A particularly frightening scenario is when a small fraction of corrupted data changes the behavior of the trained model when triggered by an attacker-specified watermark. Such a compromised model will be deployed unnoticed as the model is accurate otherwise. There has been promising attempts to use the intermediate representations of such a model to separate corrupted examples from clean ones. However, these methods require a significant fraction of the data to be corrupted, in order to have strong enough signal for detection. We propose a novel defense algorithm using robust covariance estimation to amplify the spectral signature of corrupted data. This defense is able to completely remove backdoors whenever the benchmark backdoor attacks are successful, even in regimes where previous methods have no hope for detecting poisoned examples.

Such a compromised model will be deployed unnoticed as the model is accurate otherwise. There has been promising attempts to use the intermediate representations of such a model to separate corrupted examples from clean ones. However, these methods require a significant fraction of the data to be corrupted, in order to have strong enough signal for detection. paragraphs: A backdoor attack corrupts a small part of a training set so that the trained model behaves differently when an attacker’s watermark appears. The model can remain accurate on ordinary inputs, allowing the compromise to go unnoticed. This paper addresses detecting poisoned examples when their small number makes their signal difficult to distinguish.

Earlier defenses examine intermediate model representations to separate poisoned and clean data. Their effectiveness can depend on having enough corrupted examples to create a visible spectral signature, a pattern in the representations’ variation. SPECTRE uses robust covariance estimation to amplify that signature, making the structure associated with corruption easier to detect.

The authors report that the defense completely removes backdoors whenever the evaluated benchmark attacks succeed, including regimes where previous methods cannot detect the poisoned examples. That claim is tied to the benchmark attacks rather than all possible attacks. The contribution is a statistical method for strengthening a weak corruption signal, addressing the difficulty of finding a small poisoned subset within mostly clean training data.
summary.tldr: SPECTRE amplifies poisoned-data signatures with robust covariance estimation and removes successful backdoors across the evaluated benchmark attacks.

title: SPECTRE: defending against backdoor attacks using robust statistics

abstract: Motivated by objects such as electric fields or fluid streams, we study the problem of learning stochastic fields, i.e. stochastic processes whose samples are fields like those occurring in physics and engineering. Considering general transformations such as rotations and reflections, we show that spatial invariance of stochastic fields requires an inference model to be equivariant. Leveraging recent advances from the equivariance literature, we study equivariance in two classes of models. Firstly, we fully characterise equivariant Gaussian processes. Secondly, we introduce Steerable Conditional Neural Processes (SteerCNPs), a new, fully equivariant member of the Neural Process family. In experiments with Gaussian process vector fields, images, and real-world weather data, we observe that SteerCNPs significantly improve the performance of previous models and equivariance leads to improvements in transfer learning tasks.

Considering general transformations such as rotations and reflections, we show that spatial invariance of stochastic fields requires an inference model to be equivariant. Leveraging recent advances from the equivariance literature, we study equivariance in two classes of models. Firstly, we fully characterise equivariant Gaussian processes. paragraphs: The paper studies learning uncertain fields, such as electric fields or fluid flows. Here, an outcome is a field spread across space rather than a single value. Rotations and reflections matter because changing the spatial frame also changes how observations and predictions should be expressed.

The authors show that spatial invariance of a stochastic field requires an equivariant inference model. In plain terms, transforming the observations should transform the inferred field in the corresponding way. They investigate this requirement for two model families: fully characterizing equivariant Gaussian processes and introducing Steerable Conditional Neural Processes, or SteerCNPs, as a fully equivariant neural-process model.

Experiments cover Gaussian-process vector fields, images, and real weather data. The authors report significant improvements over previous models and better transfer-learning performance from equivariance. These findings connect the theoretical symmetry requirement to practical learning benefits in the evaluated settings: the model’s treatment of transformed data is built into its structure rather than left entirely to learning.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes equivariant Gaussian processes and introduces symmetry-preserving neural processes that improve field prediction and transfer in experiments.

title: Equivariant Learning of Stochastic Fields: Gaussian Processes and Steerable Conditional Neural Processes

abstract: We consider Bayesian optimization in settings where observations can be adversarially biased, for example by an uncontrolled hidden confounder. Our first contribution is a reduction of the confounded setting to the dueling bandit model. Then we propose a novel approach for dueling bandits based on information-directed sampling (IDS). Thereby, we obtain the first efficient kernelized algorithm for dueling bandits that comes with cumulative regret guarantees. Our analysis further generalizes a previously proposed semi-parametric linear bandit model to non-linear reward functions, and uncovers interesting links to doubly-robust estimation.

Our first contribution is a reduction of the confounded setting to the dueling bandit model. Then we propose a novel approach for dueling bandits based on information-directed sampling (IDS). Thereby, we obtain the first efficient kernelized algorithm for dueling bandits that comes with cumulative regret guarantees. Our analysis further generalizes a previously proposed semi-parametric linear bandit model to non-linear reward functions, and uncovers interesting links to doubly-robust estimation.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good choices using observations of an unknown objective. This paper considers settings where those observations can be adversarially biased, including bias caused by an uncontrolled hidden confounder. The challenge is that an observed outcome can reflect both the choice being evaluated and an outside influence, complicating the search for the best choice.

The authors first reduce this confounded optimization problem to a dueling-bandit problem, which frames learning around comparisons between alternatives. They then introduce a dueling-bandit approach based on information-directed sampling. The resulting method uses kernels to handle nonlinear reward structure and comes with guarantees on cumulative regret, a measure of the performance lost while learning.

The paper presents this as the first efficient kernelized dueling-bandit algorithm with such guarantees. Its analysis also extends an earlier semiparametric linear-bandit model to nonlinear rewards and identifies connections to doubly robust estimation. Together, these contributions provide a theoretical route from optimization with biased observations to comparison-based learning with controlled cumulative loss.
summary.tldr: The paper converts Bayesian optimization with adversarially biased observations into a kernelized dueling-bandit problem with cumulative-regret guarantees.

title: Bias-Robust Bayesian Optimization via Dueling Bandits

abstract: In many real world problems, we want to infer some property of an expensive black-box function f, given a budget of T function evaluations. One example is budget constrained global optimization of f, for which Bayesian optimization is a popular method. Other properties of interest include local optima, level sets, integrals, or graph-structured information induced by f. Often, we can find an algorithm A to compute the desired property, but it may require far more than T queries to execute. Given such an A, and a prior distribution over f, we refer to the problem of inferring the output of A using T evaluations as Bayesian Algorithm Execution (BAX). To tackle this problem, we present a procedure, InfoBAX, that sequentially chooses queries that maximize mutual information with respect to the algorithm’s output. Applying this to Dijkstra’s algorithm, for instance, we infer shortest paths in synthetic and real-world graphs with black-box edge costs. Using evolution strategies, we yield variants of Bayesian optimization that target local, rather than global, optima. On these problems, InfoBAX uses up to 500 times fewer queries to f than required by the original algorithm. Our method is closely connected to other Bayesian optimal experimental design procedures such as entropy search methods and optimal sensor placement using Gaussian processes.

paragraphs: An expensive black-box function may contain information needed to find a shortest path, locate an optimum, or calculate an integral. An existing algorithm might compute the desired answer but require too many function evaluations. Bayesian Algorithm Execution frames the alternative: infer that algorithm's output within a fixed evaluation budget, using a prior distribution over the function.

In plain terms, it asks which measurement is expected to reveal the most about the answer being sought. This directs limited evaluations toward the desired property rather than treating every aspect of the unknown function as equally important.

That reported maximum demonstrates the potential efficiency of estimating an algorithm's answer under a budget.
summary.tldr: InfoBAX selects expensive function evaluations to learn an algorithm's output, achieving up to 500-fold query savings on the studied problems.

title: Bayesian Algorithm Execution: Estimating Computable Properties of Black-box Functions Using Mutual Information

abstract: Despite the considerable success of neural networks in security settings such as malware detection, such models have proved vulnerable to evasion attacks, in which attackers make slight changes to inputs (e.g., malware) to bypass detection. We propose a novel approach, Fourier stabilization, for designing evasion-robust neural networks with binary inputs. This approach, which is complementary to other forms of defense, replaces the weights of individual neurons with robust analogs derived using Fourier analytic tools. The choice of which neurons to stabilize in a neural network is then a combinatorial optimization problem, and we propose several methods for approximately solving it. We provide a formal bound on the per-neuron drop in accuracy due to Fourier stabilization, and experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in boosting robustness of neural networks in several detection settings. Moreover, we show that our approach effectively composes with adversarial training.

This makes neuron selection part of the defense design, alongside the mathematical construction of the replacement weights themselves.

Experiments in several detection settings show improved network robustness, and the approach also combines effectively with adversarial training. The contribution joins a targeted change to neuron weights with an explicit analysis of its local accuracy cost and empirical evidence that it can complement another established form of defense.
summary.tldr: Fourier stabilization replaces selected neurons' weights to improve evasion robustness in binary-input networks and combines effectively with adversarial training.

title: Enhancing Robustness of Neural Networks through Fourier Stabilization

abstract: We study multi-objective reinforcement learning (RL) where an agent’s reward is represented as a vector. In settings where an agent competes against opponents, its performance is measured by the distance of its average return vector to a target set. We develop statistically and computationally efficient algorithms to approach the associated target set. Our results extend Blackwell’s approachability theorem \citep{blackwell1956analog} to tabular RL, where strategic exploration becomes essential. The algorithms presented are adaptive; their guarantees hold even without Blackwell’s approachability condition. If the opponents use fixed policies, we give an improved rate of approaching the target set while also tackling the more ambitious goal of simultaneously minimizing a scalar cost function. We discuss our analysis for this special case by relating our results to previous works on constrained RL. To our knowledge, this work provides the first provably efficient algorithms for vector-valued Markov games and our theoretical guarantees are near-optimal.

This paper studies competitive settings where success is measured by how close an agent’s average return vector comes to a target set. They relate this case to constrained reinforcement learning. The paper presents near-optimal theoretical guarantees and, to the authors’ knowledge, the first provably efficient algorithms for vector-valued Markov games.
summary.tldr: The paper develops efficient competitive reinforcement-learning algorithms with near-optimal guarantees for approaching target sets of vector-valued returns.

title: Provably Efficient Algorithms for Multi-Objective Competitive RL

abstract: In many areas, we have well-founded insights about causal structure that would be useful to bring into our trained models while still allowing them to learn in a data-driven fashion. To achieve this, we present the new method of interchange intervention training (IIT). In IIT, we (1) align variables in a causal model (e.g., a deterministic program or Bayesian network) with representations in a neural model and (2) train the neural model to match the counterfactual behavior of the causal model on a base input when aligned representations in both models are set to be the value they would be for a source input. IIT is fully differentiable, flexibly combines with other objectives, and guarantees that the target causal model is a causal abstraction of the neural model when its loss is zero. We evaluate IIT on a structural vision task (MNIST-PVR), a navigational language task (ReaSCAN), and a natural language inference task (MQNLI). We compare IIT against multi-task training objectives and data augmentation. In all our experiments, IIT achieves the best results and produces neural models that are more interpretable in the sense that they more successfully realize the target causal model.

paragraphs: This paper introduces interchange intervention training, or IIT, to incorporate a chosen causal structure into a neural network while preserving data-driven learning. The starting point is a causal model, such as a deterministic program or Bayesian network. Variables in that model are aligned with representations inside the neural network.

Training compares how the two models behave under matched interventions. For a base input, aligned variables and representations are replaced with the values they would have on a source input. The neural model is then trained to reproduce the causal model’s counterfactual behavior. IIT is fully differentiable and can be combined with other objectives. When its loss is zero, the target causal model is guaranteed to be a causal abstraction of the neural model.

The authors evaluate IIT on structural vision, navigational language, and natural language inference tasks. It achieves the best results in their comparisons with multitask training objectives and data augmentation. The resulting networks also realize the intended causal structure more successfully, giving a concrete behavioral meaning to the claimed improvement in interpretability.
summary.tldr: IIT trains neural representations to match a target causal model’s intervention behavior, with a causal-abstraction guarantee when its loss reaches zero.

title: Inducing Causal Structure for Interpretable Neural Networks

abstract: Despite the empirical success of meta reinforcement learning (meta-RL), there are still a number poorly-understood discrepancies between theory and practice. Critically, biased gradient estimates are almost always implemented in practice, whereas prior theory on meta-RL only establishes convergence under unbiased gradient estimates. In this work, we investigate such a discrepancy. In particular, (1) We show that unbiased gradient estimates have variance $\Theta(N)$ which linearly depends on the sample size $N$ of the inner loop updates; (2) We propose linearized score function (LSF) gradient estimates, which have bias $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{N})$ and variance $\mathcal{O}(1/N)$; (3) We show that most empirical prior work in fact implements variants of the LSF gradient estimates. This implies that practical algorithms "accidentally" introduce bias to achieve better performance; (4) We establish theoretical guarantees for the LSF gradient estimates in meta-RL regarding its convergence to stationary points, showing better dependency on $N$ than prior work when $N$ is large.

paragraphs: Meta reinforcement learning has a gap between common implementations and earlier convergence theory. Practical methods usually use biased gradient estimates, while the theory had established convergence using unbiased estimates. This paper investigates why the biased choices can work well and supplies guarantees that better match those choices.

The key result concerns the number N of samples used in inner-loop updates. The unbiased estimates studied have variance proportional to N, so increasing this sample size increases their variability. The proposed linearized score function estimates instead have bias bounded on the order of one over the square root of N and variance bounded on the order of one over N.

The authors also show that most prior empirical work implements variants of these estimates. This explains those implementations as introducing bias while substantially reducing variance. They establish convergence guarantees toward stationary points, with better dependence on N than prior work when N is large. The contribution connects a practical estimation choice to a quantified tradeoff and supporting optimization theory.
summary.tldr: Linearized score function estimates explain how biased meta-RL gradients can sharply reduce variance and retain stationary-point convergence guarantees.

title: Biased Gradient Estimate with Drastic Variance Reduction for Meta Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has been widely explored in recent years, and it is an effective way of leveraging unlabeled data to reduce the reliance on labeled data. In this work, we adjust neural processes (NPs) to the semi-supervised image classification task, resulting in a new method named NP-Match. NP-Match is suited to this task for two reasons. Firstly, NP-Match implicitly compares data points when making predictions, and as a result, the prediction of each unlabeled data point is affected by the labeled data points that are similar to it, which improves the quality of pseudolabels. Secondly, NP-Match is able to estimate uncertainty that can be used as a tool for selecting unlabeled samples with reliable pseudo-labels. Compared with uncertainty-based SSL methods implemented with Monte Carlo (MC) dropout, NP-Match estimates uncertainty with much less computational overhead, which can save time at both the training and the testing phases. We conducted extensive experiments on four public datasets, and NP-Match outperforms state-of-theart (SOTA) results or achieves competitive results on them, which shows the effectiveness of NPMatch and its potential for SSL.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised image classification uses unlabeled images alongside labeled examples to reduce dependence on annotation. One challenge is deciding which model-generated labels are trustworthy enough to use during learning. The paper adapts neural processes to this setting through a method called NP-Match, combining relationships between examples with uncertainty estimation.

NP-Match implicitly compares data points when predicting labels. Similar labeled examples therefore influence the prediction for an unlabeled image, improving the quality of its pseudolabel. The method also estimates uncertainty, which can guide selection of unlabeled examples whose pseudolabels are reliable. These two capabilities address both generating useful training targets and choosing which targets to trust.

Compared with uncertainty-based methods using Monte Carlo dropout, NP-Match estimates uncertainty with substantially less computational overhead, potentially saving time during training and testing. Across four public datasets, it either exceeds state-of-the-art results or performs competitively. The findings support neural processes as a useful approach to semi-supervised classification, with benefits spanning predictive quality and uncertainty-estimation cost.
summary.tldr: NP-Match uses neural processes to improve pseudolabels and estimate uncertainty efficiently for semi-supervised image classification.

title: NP-Match: When Neural Processes meet Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: Algorithms for min-max optimization and variational inequalities are often studied under monotonicity assumptions. Motivated by non-monotone machine learning applications, we follow the line of works (Diakonikolas et al., 2021; Lee & Kim, 2021; Pethick et al., 2022; Bohm,2022) aiming at going beyond monotonicity by considering the weaker negative comonotonicity assumption. In this work, we provide tight complexity analyses for the Proximal Point (PP), Extragradient (EG), and Optimistic Gradient (OG) methods in this setup, closing several questions on their working guarantees beyond monotonicity. In particular, we derive the first non-asymptotic convergence rates for PP under negative comonotonicity and star-negative comonotonicity and show their tightness via constructing worst-case examples; we also relax the assumptions for the last-iterate convergence guarantees for EG and OG and prove the tightness of the existing best-iterate guarantees for EG and OG via constructing counter-examples.

paragraphs: Algorithms for min-max problems and variational inequalities often rely on monotonicity assumptions to establish convergence. Motivated by machine-learning problems that do not satisfy those assumptions, this paper studies a weaker condition called negative comonotonicity. It asks what convergence guarantees remain available for Proximal Point, Extragradient, and Optimistic Gradient methods.

For Proximal Point, the authors derive the first non-asymptotic convergence rates under negative comonotonicity and its star variant. These rates describe progress after a finite number of iterations, rather than only eventual behavior. They also construct worst-case examples showing that the rates are tight within the analyzed setting.

For Extragradient and Optimistic Gradient, the paper weakens assumptions needed to guarantee convergence of the final iterate. Separately, counterexamples establish the tightness of existing guarantees for the best iterate encountered during optimization. This distinction matters because the final output and the best point in a sequence are different objects. Together, the results sharpen both the reach and the boundaries of these methods beyond monotonicity.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes tight convergence guarantees for three optimization methods under weaker conditions than monotonicity.

title: Convergence of Proximal Point and Extragradient-Based Methods Beyond Monotonicity: the Case of Negative Comonotonicity

abstract: The Bellman-Ford algorithm is a basic primitive for computing single source shortest paths in graphs with negative weight edges. Its running time is governed by the order the algorithm examines vertices for iterative updates on the value of their shortest path. In this work we study this problem through the lens of ’Algorithms with predictions,’ and show how to leverage auxiliary information from similar instances to improve the running time. We do this by identifying the key problem of Minimum Violation Permutations, and give algorithms with strong approximation guarantees as well as formal lower bounds. We complement the theoretical analysis with an empirical evaluation, showing that this approach can lead to a significant speed up in practice.

paragraphs: Bellman-Ford computes shortest paths from a single source in graphs that can contain negative edge weights. Its running time depends on the order in which vertices are examined as distance estimates are repeatedly updated. This paper treats that ordering choice as an opportunity to improve the algorithm using information from related problem instances.

The authors work within the algorithms-with-predictions framework, where auxiliary information guides an algorithm. They identify Minimum Violation Permutations as the key ordering problem and develop algorithms for it with strong approximation guarantees. They also provide formal lower bounds, pairing constructive methods with results about the limits of what can be achieved.

An empirical evaluation shows that the resulting approach can produce a significant practical speedup for Bellman-Ford. The findings connect a familiar graph algorithm's runtime to a separate permutation problem that can use evidence from similar instances. The contribution includes both a theoretical treatment of that ordering problem and experimental support for using the resulting orderings to reduce shortest-path computation time.
summary.tldr: The paper uses information from similar graph instances to improve Bellman-Ford's vertex ordering, with approximation guarantees and demonstrated practical speedups.

title: Speeding Up Bellman Ford via Minimum Violation Permutations

abstract: Controlling artificial agents from visual sensory data is an arduous task. Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms can succeed but require large amounts of interactions between the agent and the environment. To alleviate the issue, unsupervised RL proposes to employ self-supervised interaction and learning, for adapting faster to future tasks. Yet, as shown in the Unsupervised RL Benchmark (URLB; Laskin et al. 2021), whether current unsupervised strategies can improve generalization capabilities is still unclear, especially in visual control settings. In this work, we study the URLB and propose a new method to solve it, using unsupervised model-based RL, for pre-training the agent, and a task-aware fine-tuning strategy combined with a new proposed hybrid planner, Dyna-MPC, to adapt the agent for downstream tasks. On URLB, our method obtains 93.59% overall normalized performance, surpassing previous baselines by a staggering margin. The approach is empirically evaluated through a large-scale empirical study, which we use to validate our design choices and analyze our models. We also show robust performance on the Real-Word RL benchmark, hinting at resiliency to environment perturbations during adaptation. Project website: https://masteringurlb.github.io/

paragraphs: Learning control from visual observations can require many interactions with an environment. Unsupervised reinforcement learning attempts to make those interactions more reusable by letting an agent learn before it receives a particular downstream task. This paper investigates that approach on the Unsupervised RL Benchmark, where the benefits of existing unsupervised methods were especially uncertain for visual control.

The proposed system uses unsupervised model-based reinforcement learning for pretraining. It then adapts to downstream tasks through task-aware fine-tuning combined with a hybrid planner called Dyna-MPC. This connects the initial learning phase with a task-specific adaptation procedure, treating both stages as important parts of the overall method.

The method reaches 93.59% overall normalized performance on the benchmark and substantially exceeds the previous baselines. A large empirical study examines the design choices and learned models. Additional robust performance on the Real-World RL benchmark suggests resilience to environmental perturbations during adaptation. These results provide empirical support for this combination of unsupervised pretraining, task-aware fine-tuning, and planning.
summary.tldr: Unsupervised model-based pretraining, task-aware fine-tuning, and Dyna-MPC planning achieve strong benchmark results for control from pixels.

title: Mastering the Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning Benchmark from Pixels

abstract: Recent breakthroughs in synthetic data generation approaches made it possible to produce highly photorealistic images which are hardly distinguishable from real ones. Furthermore, synthetic generation pipelines have the potential to generate an unlimited number of images. The combination of high photorealism and scale turn synthetic data into a promising candidate for improving various machine learning (ML) pipelines. Thus far, a large body of research in this field has focused on using synthetic images for training, by augmenting and enlarging training data. In contrast to using synthetic data for training, in this work we explore whether synthetic data can be beneficial for model selection. Considering the task of image classification, we demonstrate that when data is scarce, synthetic data can be used to replace the held out validation set, thus allowing to train on a larger dataset. We also introduce a novel method to calibrate the synthetic error estimation to fit that of the real domain. We show that such calibration significantly improves the usefulness of synthetic data for model selection.

paragraphs: When labeled images are scarce, reserving some for validation leaves fewer available for training. This paper investigates whether synthetic images can support model selection instead. The idea gives generated data a different role from the usual practice of adding synthetic examples to the training set.

For image classification, the authors demonstrate that synthetic data can replace a held-out validation set in data-scarce conditions. This makes it possible to train on a larger collection of real examples. Model selection then depends on how well performance measured on generated images reflects performance in the real domain, making the quality of that error estimate central to the approach.

The paper introduces a calibration method to align synthetic error estimates with real-domain errors. This calibration significantly improves the usefulness of synthetic data for selecting models. The findings support synthetic validation as a way to use scarce data more effectively, with calibrated error estimates helping connect evaluation on generated images to the real task.
summary.tldr: Calibrated synthetic validation data can support image-classifier selection while freeing scarce real examples for training.

title: Synthetic data for model selection

abstract: With the arrival of the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era and the fast development of machine learning, variational quantum algorithms (VQA) including Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and quantum neural network (QNN) have received increasing attention with wide potential applications in foreseeable near future. We study the problem of quantum architecture search (QAS) for VQA to automatically design parameterized quantum circuits (PQC). We devise a differentiable searching algorithm based on Gumbel-Softmax in contrast to peer methods that often require numerous circuit sampling and evaluation. Two versions of our algorithm are provided, namely macro search and micro search, where macro search directly searches for the whole circuit like other literature while the innovative micro search is able to infer the sub-circuit structure from a small-scale and then transfer that to a large-scale problem. We conduct intensive experiments on unweighted Max-Cut, ground state energy estimation, and image classification. The superior performance shows the efficiency and capability of macro search, which requires little prior knowledge. Moreover, the experiments on micro search show the potential of our algorithm for large-scale QAS problems.

paragraphs: Variational quantum algorithms depend on the design of parameterized quantum circuits. This paper studies how to automate that design through quantum architecture search. The authors aim to reduce reliance on approaches that require sampling and evaluating many candidate circuits, proposing a differentiable search algorithm based on Gumbel-Softmax.

QuantumDARTS offers two search modes. Macro search directly searches for the structure of an entire circuit. Micro search instead learns a sub-circuit structure on a smaller problem and transfers it to a larger one. That distinction gives the method two ways to organize architecture discovery: whole-circuit design and reuse of structures identified at a smaller scale.

Experiments cover unweighted Max-Cut, ground-state energy estimation, and image classification. The reported performance supports the efficiency and capability of macro search while requiring little prior knowledge. The micro-search experiments suggest potential for larger-scale quantum architecture search, rather than establishing a universal scaling result. Together, the two modes explore how differentiable architecture selection and transferable circuit components can support the automatic design of variational quantum algorithms.
summary.tldr: QuantumDARTS uses differentiable search to design whole quantum circuits or transfer sub-circuit structures learned on smaller problems.

title: QuantumDARTS: Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search for Variational Quantum Algorithms

abstract: Unsupervised object-centric representation (OCR) learning has recently drawn attention as a new paradigm of visual representation. This is because of its potential of being an effective pre-training technique for various downstream tasks in terms of sample efficiency, systematic generalization, and reasoning. Although image-based reinforcement learning (RL) is one of the most important and thus frequently mentioned such downstream tasks, the benefit in RL has surprisingly not been investigated systematically thus far. Instead, most of the evaluations have focused on rather indirect metrics such as segmentation quality and object property prediction accuracy. In this paper, we investigate the effectiveness of OCR pre-training for image-based reinforcement learning via empirical experiments. For systematic evaluation, we introduce a simple object-centric visual RL benchmark and conduct experiments to answer questions such as "Does OCR pre-training improve performance on object-centric tasks?" and "Can OCR pre-training help with out-of-distribution generalization?". Our results provide empirical evidence for valuable insights into the effectiveness of OCR pre-training for RL and the potential limitations of its use in certain scenarios. Additionally, this study also examines the critical aspects of incorporating OCR pre-training in RL, including performance in a visually complex environment and the appropriate pooling layer to aggregate the object representations.

paragraphs: Object-centric representation learning organizes visual information around objects and has been proposed as useful preparation for reinforcement learning from images. However, much of its evaluation has focused on indirect measures, such as segmentation quality or predicting object properties. Those measures do not directly establish whether the representations help an agent learn to act.

This paper investigates that connection through reinforcement-learning experiments. The authors introduce a simple visual benchmark organized around objects and use it to examine whether object-centric pretraining improves task performance and helps generalization outside the training distribution. This shifts evaluation toward the downstream decisions that the representation is intended to support.

The study also examines visually complex environments and the choice of pooling layer used to combine separate object representations. Its findings provide empirical insights into both usefulness and potential limitations in particular scenarios. The abstract does not establish a universal benefit; its contribution is a systematic examination of when object-centric pretraining helps and which integration choices deserve attention.
summary.tldr: A systematic empirical study examines the benefits, limits, and integration choices of object-centric pretraining for visual reinforcement learning.

title: An Investigation into Pre-Training Object-Centric Representations for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Transformers are the backbone of powerful foundation models for many Vision and Natural Language Processing tasks. But their compute and memory/storage footprint is large, and so, serving such models is expensive often requiring high-end hardware. To mitigate this difficulty, Post-Training Quantization seeks to modify a pre-trained model and quantize it to eight bits or lower, significantly boosting compute/memory/latency efficiency. Such models have been successfully quantized to four bits with some performance loss. In this work, we outline a simple scheme to quantize Transformer-based models to just two bits (plus some overhead) with only a small drop in accuracy. Key to our formulation is a concept borrowed from Harmonic analysis called Fusion Frames. Our main finding is that the quantization must take place not in the original weight space, but instead in the Fusion Frame representations. If quantization is interpreted as the addition of noise, our casting of the problem allows invoking an extensive body of known consistent recovery and noise robustness guarantees. Further, if desired, de-noising filters are known in closed form. We show empirically, via a variety of experiments, that (almost) two-bit quantization for Transformer models promises sizable efficiency gains. The code is available at https://github.com/vsingh-group/FrameQuant
