paragraphs: Transformer models can be expensive to serve because their parameters and computations demand substantial resources. Post-training quantization reduces the precision used to represent a pretrained model. This paper introduces FrameQuant, a scheme that reaches approximately two-bit precision, with additional overhead, while reporting only a small loss in accuracy.

The method changes the representation in which quantization occurs. It uses fusion frames, a concept from harmonic analysis, rather than directly quantizing the original weights. Interpreting quantization as added noise lets the authors connect this formulation to established results on consistent recovery and robustness to noise. Closed-form denoising filters are also available if desired.

Experiments across transformer models support the promise of substantial efficiency gains from this representation. The important distinction is that very low precision is applied within the fusion-frame formulation; the reported scheme includes overhead beyond the nominal two bits. The contribution combines a practical quantization approach with a mathematical perspective explaining why the choice of representation matters when reducing numerical precision so aggressively.
summary.tldr: FrameQuant quantizes fusion-frame representations of transformers to roughly two bits plus overhead with a small reported accuracy drop.

title: FrameQuant: Flexible Low-Bit Quantization for Transformers

abstract: Certification for machine learning is proving that no adversarial sample can evade a model within a range under certain conditions, a necessity for safety-critical domains. Common certification methods for segmentation use a flat set of fine-grained classes, leading to high abstain rates due to model uncertainty across many classes. We propose a novel, more practical setting, which certifies pixels within a multi-level hierarchy, and adaptively relaxes the certification to a coarser level for unstable components classic methods would abstain from, effectively lowering the abstain rate whilst providing more certified semantically meaningful information. We mathematically formulate the problem setup, introduce an adaptive hierarchical certification algorithm and prove the correctness of its guarantees. Since certified accuracy does not take the loss of information into account for coarser classes, we introduce the Certified Information Gain ($\mathrm{CIG}$) metric, which is proportional to the class granularity level. Our extensive experiments on the datasets Cityscapes, PASCAL-Context, ACDC and COCO-Stuff demonstrate that our adaptive algorithm achieves a higher $\mathrm{CIG}$ and lower abstain rate compared to the current state-of-the-art certification method. Our code can be found here: https://github.com/AlaaAnani/adaptive-certify.

paragraphs: Robustness certification for image segmentation asks whether pixel labels remain protected against adversarial changes within a specified range and under stated conditions. When certification uses only fine-grained classes, uncertainty between similar categories can force the method to abstain. This paper explores how a hierarchy of categories can preserve useful certified information in those cases.

The proposed algorithm adaptively moves to a broader category when a more specific label is unstable. This allows a pixel to receive a semantically meaningful guarantee even when its finest classification cannot be certified. The authors formulate this hierarchical setting mathematically and prove the correctness of the algorithm’s guarantees. The tradeoff is explicit: broader labels retain less information.

To evaluate that tradeoff, the paper introduces Certified Information Gain, which accounts for class granularity instead of treating all certified labels as equally informative. Experiments on Cityscapes, PASCAL-Context, ACDC, and COCO-Stuff report higher information gain and fewer abstentions than the compared state-of-the-art method. The results support adapting the specificity of a guarantee to the model’s stability.
summary.tldr: Adaptive hierarchical certification reduces abstentions by certifying broader pixel categories when fine-grained labels are unstable, while accounting for lost specificity.

title: Adaptive Hierarchical Certification for Segmentation using Randomized Smoothing

abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) obtain their answers? The ability to explain and control an LLM’s reasoning process is key for reliability, transparency, and future model developments. We propose SelfIE (Self-Interpretation of Embeddings), a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own embeddings in natural language by leveraging their ability to respond to inquiries about a given passage. Capable of interpreting open-world concepts in the hidden embeddings, SelfIE reveals LLM internal reasoning in cases such as making ethical decisions, internalizing prompt injection, and recalling harmful knowledge. SelfIE’s text descriptions on hidden embeddings open avenues to control LLM reasoning. We propose Supervised Control, which allows editing open-ended concepts while only requiring gradient computation of individual layer. We extend RLHF to hidden embeddings and propose Reinforcement Control that erases harmful knowledge in LLM without supervision targets.

paragraphs: SelfIE addresses the challenge of understanding what a language model represents internally while producing an answer. It enables a model to describe its own hidden embeddings in natural language, drawing on its existing ability to answer questions about a passage. The goal is to make internal representations accessible through explanations expressed as text.

The framework interprets open-world concepts rather than restricting interpretation to a fixed inventory of predefined categories. The paper presents cases involving ethical decisions, the internalization of prompt injection, and the recall of harmful knowledge. These descriptions provide a basis for examining internal reasoning and for designing interventions that target the represented concepts.

The authors introduce two control methods built on this approach. Supervised Control edits open-ended concepts while requiring gradient computation for only an individual layer. Reinforcement Control extends reinforcement learning from human feedback to hidden embeddings and is presented as erasing harmful knowledge without supervision targets. The paper thus connects natural-language interpretation of embeddings with methods for changing the model’s internal behavior.
summary.tldr: SelfIE turns hidden language-model embeddings into natural-language interpretations and uses them to support interventions on internal concepts.

title: SelfIE: Self-Interpretation of Large Language Model Embeddings

abstract: Transformers to do reasoning and few-shot learning, without any fine-tuning, is widely conjectured to stem from their ability to implicitly simulate a multi-step algorithms – such as gradient descent – with their weights in a single forward pass. Recently, there has been progress in understanding this complex phenomenon from an expressivity point of view, by demonstrating that Transformers can express such multi-step algorithms. However, our knowledge about the more fundamental aspect of its learnability, beyond single layer models, is very limited. In particular, can training Transformers enable convergence to algorithmic solutions? In this work we resolve this for in context linear regression with linear looped Transformers – a multi-layer model with weight sharing that is conjectured to have an inductive bias to learn fix-point iterative algorithms. More specifically, for this setting we show that the global minimizer of the population training loss implements multi-step preconditioned gradient descent, with a preconditioner that adapts to the data distribution. Furthermore, we show a fast convergence for gradient flow on the regression loss, despite the non-convexity of the landscape, by proving a novel gradient dominance condition. To our knowledge, this is the first theoretical analysis for multi-layer Transformer in this setting. We further validate our theoretical findings through synthetic experiments.

paragraphs: A transformer might solve a task from examples in its input by internally carrying out an iterative learning algorithm. Showing that its architecture can represent such an algorithm leaves an important question unanswered: can training actually find that solution? This paper addresses that learning question for in-context linear regression using linear looped transformers, whose layers share weights.

The authors show that the global minimizer of the population training loss performs multiple steps of preconditioned gradient descent. The preconditioner adapts to the data distribution, so the learned procedure adjusts the geometry of its updates to the regression problems it encounters. This connects the best solution to an identifiable iterative algorithm.

They also prove fast convergence for gradient flow on the regression loss, despite its nonconvex landscape, using a gradient dominance condition. Synthetic experiments support the theoretical findings. The contribution is a learnability result for the specified linear, weight-sharing setting: it explains both the algorithm implemented by an optimum and how the analyzed training dynamics can converge.
summary.tldr: For in-context linear regression, linear looped transformers have an optimal solution that implements multi-step preconditioned gradient descent, with a fast gradient-flow convergence guarantee.

title: Can Looped Transformers Learn to Implement Multi-step Gradient Descent for In-context Learning?

abstract: While alignment algorithms are commonly used to tune pre-trained language models towards user preferences, we lack explanations for the underlying mechanisms in which models become “aligned”, thus making it difficult to explain phenomena like jailbreaks. In this work we study a popular algorithm, direct preference optimization (DPO), and the mechanisms by which it reduces toxicity. Namely, we first study how toxicity is represented and elicited in pre-trained language models (GPT2-medium, Llama2-7b). We then apply DPO with a carefully crafted pairwise dataset to reduce toxicity. We examine how the resulting models avert toxic outputs, and find that capabilities learned from pre-training are not removed, but rather bypassed. We use this insight to demonstrate a simple method to un-align the models, reverting them back to their toxic behavior.

paragraphs: Alignment methods can make a language model produce responses that better match user preferences, but improved behavior does not by itself explain what changed inside the model. This paper examines that question for direct preference optimization, or DPO, focusing on how the method reduces toxic language and what that reveals about alignment.

The authors first investigate how toxicity is represented and triggered in GPT2-medium and Llama2-7b before alignment. They then apply DPO using a carefully constructed dataset of paired responses. Studying the resulting models allows them to connect the change in outward behavior with the internal mechanisms responsible for avoiding toxic outputs.

Their finding is that capabilities acquired during pre-training remain present after this alignment procedure; the models bypass them when producing responses. Using that insight, the authors demonstrate a simple way to reverse the alignment and restore toxic behavior. In this case study, reducing toxic output therefore does not amount to removing the underlying capability, which helps explain how apparently aligned behavior can be undone.
summary.tldr: In a toxicity case study, DPO makes models bypass existing capabilities, and that retained capacity enables the alignment to be reversed.

title: A Mechanistic Understanding of Alignment Algorithms: A Case Study on DPO and Toxicity

abstract: The advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to increasing concerns about the misuse of AI-generated text, and watermarking LLM-generated text has emerged as a potential solution. However, it is challenging to generate high-quality watermarked text while maintaining robustness, security, and the ability to detect watermarks without prior knowledge of the prompt and model. This paper proposes an adaptive text watermarking strategy to address such a challenge. To improve the text quality and maintain robustness, we adaptively add watermarking to token distributions with high entropy measured by an auxiliary model and keep the low-entropy token distributions untouched. For the sake of security and to further minimize the watermark’s impact on text quality, instead of using a fixed green/red list generated from a random secret key, which can be vulnerable to decryption and forgery, we adaptively scale up the output logits based on the semantic embedding of previously generated text using a well designed semantic mapping model. Our experiments involving various LLMs demonstrate that our approach achieves comparable robustness performance to existing watermark methods. Additionally, the text generated by our method has perplexity comparable to that of un-watermarked LLMs while maintaining sufficient security.

paragraphs: Text watermarking introduces a detectable pattern into generated language, but changing token choices can harm text quality. This paper develops an adaptive strategy intended to balance quality, robustness, and security while addressing the challenge of detection without prior knowledge of the prompt or generating model.

The method uses an auxiliary model to measure uncertainty in token distributions. It adds a watermark where entropy is high, meaning there is more flexibility in the next token, and leaves low-entropy distributions untouched. It also adjusts output scores using a semantic embedding of previously generated text. This replaces a fixed division of tokens into favored and disfavored lists with a mechanism conditioned on the text's meaning.

Experiments across several language models report robustness comparable to existing watermarking methods and perplexity comparable to generation without watermarks, while maintaining sufficient security. These findings support selectively placing the watermark where the model has room to vary its output. The reported security result is qualified; it does not establish immunity to every possible forgery or removal attempt.
summary.tldr: An adaptive watermark modifies uncertain token choices using semantic context, reporting comparable robustness with perplexity close to unwatermarked text.

title: Adaptive Text Watermark for Large Language Models

abstract: Causal models and methods have great promise, but their progress has been stalled. Proposals using causality get squeezed between two opposing worldviews. Scientific perfectionism--an insistence on only using ``correct'' models--slows the adoption of causal methods in knowledge generating applications. Pushing in the opposite direction, the academic discipline of computer science prefers algorithms with no or few assumptions, and technologies based on automation and scalability are often selected for economic and business applications. We argue that these system-centric inductive biases should be replaced with a human-centric philosophy we refer to as scientific pragmatism. The machine learning community must strike the right balance to make space for the causal revolution to prosper.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that causal methods have considerable promise but face conflicting expectations that impede progress. One expectation is scientific perfectionism: using a causal model only when it can be regarded as correct. The authors contend that this stance slows the adoption of causal approaches in applications intended to generate knowledge.

A different pressure comes from computer science’s preference for algorithms requiring few assumptions, together with economic and business preferences for automation and scalability. The authors see these priorities as another obstacle to causal work. Their argument connects the difficulty of adoption to how different communities judge methods, rather than locating the issue solely in the methods themselves.

They propose a human-centered philosophy called scientific pragmatism to replace these system-centered biases. The call is for the machine learning community to find a balance that gives causal approaches room to contribute. As a position statement, the paper offers a framing for research priorities and adoption: progress depends partly on reconsidering the standards through which useful causal modeling is evaluated.
summary.tldr: The authors advocate human-centered scientific pragmatism to help causal methods advance amid conflicting expectations about correctness and automation.

title: Position: The Causal Revolution Needs Scientific Pragmatism

abstract: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) in high-dimensional spaces is a pivotal challenge in the field of machine learning. In recent years graph-based methods have emerged as the superior approach to ANNS, establishing a new state of the art. Although various optimizations for graph-based ANNS have been introduced, they predominantly rely on heuristic methods that lack formal theoretical backing. This paper aims to enhance routing within graph-based ANNS by introducing a method that offers a probabilistic guarantee when exploring a node’s neighbors in the graph. We formulate the problem as probabilistic routing and develop two baseline strategies by incorporating locality-sensitive techniques. Subsequently, we introduce PEOs, a novel approach that efficiently identifies which neighbors in the graph should be considered for exact distance computation, thus significantly improving efficiency in practice. Our experiments demonstrate that equipping PEOs can increase throughput on a commonly utilized graph index (HNSW) by a factor of 1.6 to 2.5, and its efficiency consistently outperforms the leading-edge routing technique by 1.1 to 1.4 times. The code and datasets used for our evaluations are publicly accessible at https//github.com/ICML2024-code/PEOs .

paragraphs: Graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor search finds nearby items in high-dimensional spaces by navigating connections between stored items. The paper focuses on routing decisions made when examining a node’s neighbors. Existing optimizations often rely on heuristics, so the authors formulate routing probabilistically to provide a guarantee for how neighbors are explored.

They first develop two baseline strategies using locality-sensitive techniques, then introduce PEOs. PEOs efficiently identifies which neighboring nodes should receive an exact distance calculation. The approach targets the work performed during navigation: selecting promising candidates before spending computation on precise distance evaluations can make an existing graph index more efficient.

Experiments report that adding PEOs to HNSW increases throughput by a factor of 1.6 to 2.5. The method also outperforms the leading routing technique in efficiency by 1.1 to 1.4 times in the reported evaluations. The contribution combines a probabilistic formulation with practical routing improvements, showing that decisions within graph traversal can deliver substantial speed gains without replacing the underlying index.
summary.tldr: PEOs improves graph-based nearest-neighbor search by probabilistically selecting neighbors for exact distance computation, increasing HNSW throughput in experiments.

title: Probabilistic Routing for Graph-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search

abstract: There is increasing interest in using LLMs as decision-making "agents". Doing so includes many degrees of freedom: which model should be used; how should it be prompted; should it be asked to introspect, conduct chain-of-thought reasoning, etc? Settling these questions—and more broadly, determining whether an LLM agent is reliable enough to be trusted—requires a methodology for assessing such an agent’s economic rationality. In this paper, we provide one. We begin by surveying the economic literature on rational decision making, taxonomizing a large set of fine-grained "elements" that an agent should exhibit, along with dependencies between them. We then propose a benchmark distribution that quantitatively scores an LLMs performance on these elements and, combined with a user-provided rubric, produces a "rationality report card". Finally, we describe the results of a large-scale empirical experiment with 14 different LLMs, characterizing the both current state of the art and the impact of different model sizes on models’ ability to exhibit rational behavior.

paragraphs: Using a language model as a decision-making agent requires choices about the model, its prompts, and whether it should reason explicitly or introspect. STEER proposes a methodology for assessing the economic rationality of such agents. The aim is to make evaluation of their decision behavior systematic enough to inform questions about reliability.

The authors begin with economic research on rational decision making and organize it into fine-grained behavioral elements. They also identify dependencies among those elements. A proposed benchmark distribution quantitatively scores model performance on them, and a user-supplied rubric turns those scores into a rationality report card. The rubric connects the measured behaviors to the user's evaluation priorities.

The paper reports a large empirical study involving 14 language models. It characterizes their rational behavior and examines the influence of model size. The contribution is an assessment framework that separates rationality into explicit components, together with evidence about existing models. This gives model and agent-design comparisons a structured basis grounded in the surveyed economic concepts.
summary.tldr: STEER evaluates language-model agents through fine-grained economic rationality criteria and user-weighted report cards, with a study of 14 models.

title: STEER: Assessing the Economic Rationality of Large Language Models

abstract: We consider the resolution of learning problems involving $\ell_0$-regularization via Branch-and- Bound (BnB) algorithms. These methods explore regions of the feasible space of the problem and check whether they do not contain solutions through “pruning tests”. In standard implementations, evaluating a pruning test requires to solve a convex optimization problem, which may result in computational bottlenecks. In this paper, we present an alternative to implement pruning tests for some generic family of $\ell_0$-regularized problems. Our proposed procedure allows the simultaneous assessment of several regions and can be embedded in standard BnB implementations with a negligible computational overhead. We show through numerical simulations that our pruning strategy can improve the solving time of BnB procedures by several orders of magnitude for typical problems encountered in machine-learning applications.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to solve learning problems with ℓ0 regularization using branch-and-bound algorithms. These algorithms search different regions of the feasible space and use pruning tests to rule out regions that do not contain solutions worth pursuing. The practical difficulty is that standard pruning tests require solving convex optimization problems. Repeating that work throughout a search can become a computational bottleneck.

The authors propose an alternative pruning procedure for a generic family of these regularized problems. Its distinguishing feature is that it can assess several regions simultaneously. It can also be inserted into standard branch-and-bound implementations with negligible computational overhead, making the contribution a change to how the search eliminates regions rather than a replacement for the whole solver.

Numerical simulations show that this strategy can reduce solving time by several orders of magnitude on typical machine-learning problems. The result supports more efficient pruning as a powerful way to accelerate these searches, with the stated gains applying to the tested problems and the framework’s supported family.
summary.tldr: A pruning procedure that assesses multiple search regions together can substantially accelerate branch-and-bound for a family of ℓ0-regularized learning problems.

title: A New Branch-and-Bound Pruning Framework for $\ell_0$-Regularized Problems

abstract: Anomaly detection is vital in many domains, such as finance, healthcare, and cybersecurity. In this paper, we propose a novel deep anomaly detection method for tabular data that leverages Non-Parametric Transformers (NPTs), a model initially proposed for supervised tasks, to capture both feature-feature and sample-sample dependencies. In a reconstruction-based framework, we train an NPT to reconstruct masked features of normal samples. In a non-parametric fashion, we leverage the whole training set during inference and use the model’s ability to reconstruct the masked features to generate an anomaly score. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to successfully combine feature-feature and sample-sample dependencies for anomaly detection on tabular datasets. Through extensive experiments on 31 benchmark tabular datasets, we demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing methods by 2.4% and 1.2% in terms of F1-score and AUROC, respectively. Our ablation study further proves that modeling both types of dependencies is crucial for anomaly detection on tabular data.

paragraphs: This paper studies anomaly detection in tables by considering relationships between columns and relationships between rows together. It adapts Non-Parametric Transformers, a model originally proposed for supervised tasks, to this setting. The central idea is that identifying an unusual record can benefit from how its features relate to one another and how the record relates to other examples.

Training uses normal samples with some features hidden. The model learns to reconstruct those missing values. When assessing a sample, it uses the whole training set as context, and its ability to reconstruct masked features supplies an anomaly score. This gives the detector access to other records during scoring, making relationships across samples part of its assessment.

Across 31 benchmark tabular datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art performance, with improvements over existing methods of 2.4% in F1-score and 1.2% in AUROC. Their ablation study supports the importance of modeling both kinds of relationships in the evaluated setting. These findings provide empirical support for using information across records alongside relationships within each record.
summary.tldr: The paper adapts Non-Parametric Transformers to detect tabular anomalies through masked-feature reconstruction using relationships both within and across records, reporting leading benchmark performance.

title: Beyond Individual Input for Deep Anomaly Detection on Tabular Data

abstract: Rendering novel view images in dynamic scenes is a crucial yet challenging task. Current methods mainly utilize NeRF-based methods to represent the static scene and an additional time-variant MLP to model scene deformations, resulting in relatively low rendering quality as well as slow inference speed. To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel framework named Superpoint Gaussian Splatting (SP-GS). Specifically, our framework first employs explicit 3D Gaussians to reconstruct the scene and then clusters Gaussians with similar properties (e.g., rotation, translation, and location) into superpoints. Empowered by these superpoints, our method manages to extend 3D Gaussian splatting to dynamic scenes with only a slight increase in computational expense. Apart from achieving state-of-the-art visual quality and real-time rendering under high resolutions, the superpoint representation provides a stronger manipulation capability. Extensive experiments demonstrate the practicality and effectiveness of our approach on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Please see our project page at https://dnvtmf.github.io/SP_GS.github.io.

paragraphs: Rendering a moving scene from a new viewpoint requires representing both appearance and change over time. The paper identifies quality and speed problems in approaches that combine a NeRF scene representation with a time-dependent deformation network. Superpoint Gaussian Splatting instead starts with explicit three-dimensional Gaussians to reconstruct the scene.

The method groups Gaussians with similar properties, such as rotation, translation, and location, into superpoints. These groups provide a representation for extending Gaussian splatting to dynamic scenes with only a small additional computational cost. The grouping also gives the method stronger scene-manipulation capability, connecting its representation choice to more than image generation alone.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the approach's practicality and effectiveness. The authors report state-of-the-art visual quality together with real-time rendering at high resolutions. These findings support superpoints as a way to preserve the rendering advantages of explicit Gaussians while accommodating motion. The reported combination of speed, quality, and manipulation capability is the main practical outcome of the framework.
summary.tldr: Grouping similar 3D Gaussians into superpoints enables high-quality dynamic-scene reconstruction with real-time high-resolution rendering.

title: Superpoint Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time High-Fidelity Dynamic Scene Reconstruction

abstract: We present the first learning-augmented data structure for implementing dictionaries with optimal consistency and robustness. Our data structure, named RobustSL, is a Skip list augmented by predictions of access frequencies of elements in a data sequence. With proper predictions, RobustSL has optimal consistency (achieves static optimality). At the same time, it maintains a logarithmic running time for each operation, ensuring optimal robustness, even if predictions are generated adversarially. Therefore, RobustSL has all the advantages of the recent learning-augmented data structures of Lin, Luo, and Woodruff (ICML 2022) and Cao et al. (arXiv 2023), while providing robustness guarantees that are absent in the previous work. Numerical experiments show that RobustSL outperforms alternative data structures using both synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: Predictions about how often elements will be accessed can help a dictionary data structure organize its work more efficiently. The challenge is retaining dependable performance when those predictions are inaccurate. This paper introduces RobustSL, a skip-list-based dictionary augmented with predicted access frequencies, and studies both its benefits and its safeguards.

With suitable predictions, RobustSL achieves static optimality, which the paper identifies as optimal consistency. At the same time, each operation retains a logarithmic running-time guarantee even when predictions are generated adversarially. The two guarantees address different cases: useful predictions improve performance, while misleading predictions do not remove the stated worst-case protection.

The authors present RobustSL as the first learning-augmented dictionary to combine optimal consistency and robustness. Its robustness guarantees extend beyond those available in the cited earlier structures. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets also show better performance than alternative data structures. Together, the theory and experiments support using access predictions while maintaining an explicit bound on the cost of individual operations.
summary.tldr: RobustSL exploits accurate access-frequency predictions while guaranteeing logarithmic operation time even under adversarial predictions.

title: Robust Learning-Augmented Dictionaries

abstract: This work studies sparse adversarial perturbations bounded by $l_0$ norm. We propose a white-box PGD-like attack method named sparse-PGD to effectively and efficiently generate such perturbations. Furthermore, we combine sparse-PGD with a black-box attack to comprehensively and more reliably evaluate the models’ robustness against $l_0$ bounded adversarial perturbations. Moreover, the efficiency of sparse-PGD enables us to conduct adversarial training to build robust models against sparse perturbations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed attack algorithm exhibits strong performance in different scenarios. More importantly, compared with other robust models, our adversarially trained model demonstrates state-of-the-art robustness against various sparse attacks. Codes are available at https://github.com/CityU-MLO/sPGD.

paragraphs: This paper studies adversarial perturbations constrained by the l0 norm, which limits how many input components can be changed. Such attacks are sparse: their defining restriction concerns the number of modifications. The authors develop sparse-PGD, a white-box attack inspired by projected gradient descent, to generate these perturbations effectively and efficiently.

They use sparse-PGD in two related ways. For robustness evaluation, they combine it with a black-box attack to make the assessment more comprehensive and reliable. For model training, its efficiency makes it practical to generate adversarial examples as part of adversarial training. The attack therefore serves both as a test of vulnerability and as a tool for improving resistance.

Experiments report strong attack performance across different scenarios. The resulting adversarially trained model also achieves leading robustness against various sparse attacks compared with the robust models evaluated. These findings support the method’s practical value for training and assessment together. The robustness claim concerns the tested sparse attacks; the paper’s contribution is an efficient attack procedure and its demonstrated use in building more resistant models.
summary.tldr: Sparse-PGD enables efficient sparse adversarial attacks, stronger robustness evaluation, and adversarial training against limited-component perturbations.

title: Towards Efficient Training and Evaluation of Robust Models against $l_0$ Bounded Adversarial Perturbations

abstract: Evaluation of large language models (LLMs) has raised great concerns in the community due to the issue of data contamination. Existing work designed evaluation protocols using well-defined algorithms for specific tasks, which cannot be easily extended to diverse scenarios. Moreover, current evaluation benchmarks can only provide the overall benchmark results and cannot support a fine-grained and multifaceted analysis of LLMs’ abilities. In this paper, we propose meta probing agents (MPA), a general dynamic evaluation protocol inspired by psychometrics to evaluate LLMs. MPA designs the probing and judging agents to automatically transform an original evaluation problem into a new one following psychometric theory on three basic cognitive abilities: language understanding, problem solving, and domain knowledge. These basic abilities are also dynamically configurable, allowing multifaceted analysis. We conducted extensive evaluations using MPA and found that most LLMs achieve poorer performance, indicating room for improvement. Our multifaceted analysis demonstrated the strong correlation between the basic abilities and an implicit Mattew effect on model size, i.e., larger models possess stronger correlations of the abilities. MPA can also be used as a data augmentation approach to enhance LLMs. Code is available at: https://github.com/microsoft/promptbench.

paragraphs: Fixed language-model benchmarks face concerns about data contamination and often compress many different abilities into one overall score. Meta Probing Agents, or MPA, proposes a dynamic evaluation protocol that transforms existing problems into new ones. Its goal is to support evaluation across diverse scenarios while giving a more detailed picture of model abilities.

The protocol uses probing and judging agents guided by psychometric ideas. They organize transformations around language understanding, problem solving, and domain knowledge. These dimensions can also be configured dynamically, allowing evaluations to examine different combinations of abilities. The approach therefore treats a benchmark problem as a starting point for further assessment rather than as a single fixed question.

In extensive evaluations, most tested models perform worse under MPA, indicating room for improvement on the transformed problems. The analysis also finds strong correlations among the basic abilities, with stronger correlations in larger models. The authors describe this size-related pattern as an implicit Matthew effect. MPA additionally serves as a data-augmentation approach for enhancing language models.
summary.tldr: Meta Probing Agents dynamically transform evaluation questions to reveal language models’ performance across configurable cognitive abilities.

title: Dynamic Evaluation of Large Language Models by Meta Probing Agents

abstract: As the complexity of AI systems and their interactions with the world increases, generating explanations for their behaviour is important for safely deploying AI. For agents, the most natural abstractions for predicting behaviour attribute beliefs, intentions and goals to the system. If an agent behaves as if it has a certain goal or belief, then we can make reasonable predictions about how it will behave in novel situations, including those where comprehensive safety evaluations are untenable. How well can we infer an agent’s beliefs from their behaviour, and how reliably can these inferred beliefs predict the agent’s behaviour in novel situations? We provide a precise answer to this question under the assumption that the agent’s behaviour is guided by a world model. Our contribution is the derivation of novel bounds on the agent’s behaviour in new (unseen) deployment environments, which represent a theoretical limit for predicting intentional agents from behavioural data alone. We discuss the implications of these results for several research areas including fairness and safety.

paragraphs: People often predict an agent’s actions by attributing beliefs, intentions, and goals to it. For AI systems, such explanations could help anticipate behavior in situations that are difficult to evaluate comprehensively. This paper asks how reliably beliefs inferred from observed behavior can support predictions in new environments.

The analysis assumes that the agent’s behavior is guided by a world model. Under that assumption, the authors derive bounds on behavior in previously unseen deployment environments. These bounds provide a theoretical account of the limits of predicting intentional agents using behavioral data alone, connecting observations in one setting to what can be inferred about another.

The significance lies in giving a precise mathematical treatment to a common explanatory practice. An inferred belief or goal is useful for prediction only to the extent that the available behavioral evidence supports its implications in a new setting. The paper’s bounds characterize that issue within its world-model assumption. The authors discuss consequences for safety and fairness, where predictions about unfamiliar deployment conditions can be especially consequential.
summary.tldr: Assuming an agent acts through a world model, the paper bounds how well behavioral observations can predict its actions in unseen environments.

title: The Limits of Predicting Agents from Behaviour

abstract: LLaMA-Adapter has recently emerged as an efficient fine-tuning technique for LLaMA models, leveraging zero-initialized attention to stabilize training and enhance performance. However, despite its empirical success, the theoretical foundations of zero-initialized attention remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we provide a rigorous theoretical analysis, establishing a connection between zero-initialized attention and mixture-of-expert models. We prove that both linear and non-linear prompts, along with gating functions, can be optimally estimated, with non-linear prompts offering greater flexibility for future applications. Empirically, we validate our findings on the open LLM benchmarks, demonstrating that non-linear prompts outperform linear ones. Notably, even with limited training data, both prompt types consistently surpass vanilla attention, highlighting the robustness and adaptability of zero-initialized attention.

paragraphs: LLaMA-Adapter uses zero-initialized attention as an efficient fine-tuning mechanism intended to stabilize training and improve performance. Although the technique has empirical support, the paper identifies a gap in its theoretical explanation. The authors study how its prompts and gating functions can be estimated.

Their analysis connects zero-initialized attention to mixture-of-experts models, giving a framework for examining the prompt components and the gates that control their contribution. They prove optimal estimation results for both linear and nonlinear prompts, along with gating functions. Nonlinear prompts provide greater flexibility within this analysis, motivating their use beyond the linear form.

Experiments on open language-model benchmarks support the theoretical investigation: nonlinear prompts outperform linear prompts in the reported evaluations. Both forms consistently outperform vanilla attention even with limited training data. These findings give the work two complementary contributions: a mathematical account of estimating the adaptation components, and empirical evidence that the more flexible prompt form improves performance. The limited-data results also support the authors’ claims about the method’s robustness and adaptability.
summary.tldr: A mixture-of-experts analysis establishes optimal prompt and gate estimation for zero-initialized attention, with experiments favoring nonlinear prompts.

title: On Zero-Initialized Attention: Optimal Prompt and Gating Factor Estimation

abstract: Diversity has been one of the most crucial factors on the design of adversarial ensemble methods. This work focuses on the fundamental problems: How to define the diversity for the adversarial ensemble, and how to correlate with algorithmic performance. We first show that it is an NP-Hard problem to precisely calculate the diversity of two networks in adversarial ensemble learning, which makes it different from prior diversity analysis. We present the first diversity decomposition under the first-order approximation for the adversarial ensemble learning. Specifically, the adversarial ensemble loss can be decomposed into average of individual adversarial losses, gradient diversity, prediction diversity and cross diversity. Hence, it is not sufficient to merely consider the gradient diversity on the characterization of diversity as in previous adversarial ensemble methods. We present diversity decomposition for classification with cross-entropy loss similarly. Based on the theoretical analysis, we develop new ensemble method via orthogonal adversarial predictions to simultaneously improve gradient diversity and cross diversity. We finally conduct experiments to validate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Combining networks can help defend against adversarial inputs, but the usefulness of an ensemble depends partly on how its members differ. This paper asks how to define that diversity and connect it to performance. It first shows that exactly calculating diversity for two networks in this setting is an NP-hard problem.

Under a first-order approximation, the authors decompose adversarial ensemble loss into four components: average individual adversarial loss, gradient diversity, prediction diversity, and cross diversity. They also derive a corresponding decomposition for classification with cross-entropy loss. The analysis shows why gradient diversity alone is insufficient to characterize ensemble diversity within this account: other terms also contribute to the ensemble’s loss.

The theoretical analysis motivates an ensemble method based on orthogonal adversarial predictions, designed to improve gradient diversity and cross diversity together. Experiments validate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution links a more complete, approximation-based description of diversity to a concrete training strategy, while distinguishing that tractable analysis from the hard problem of calculating diversity exactly.
summary.tldr: An approximate loss decomposition shows why adversarial ensembles need more than gradient diversity and motivates a new ensemble method.

title: On the Diversity of Adversarial Ensemble Learning

abstract: We introduce Lexico, a novel KV cache compression method that leverages sparse coding with a universal dictionary. Our key finding is that key-value cache in modern LLMs can be accurately approximated using sparse linear combination from a small, input-agnostic dictionary of 4k atoms, enabling efficient compression across different input prompts, tasks and models. Using orthogonal matching pursuit for sparse approximation, Lexico achieves flexible compression ratios through direct sparsity control. On GSM8K, across multiple model families (Mistral, Llama 3, Qwen2.5), Lexico maintains 90-95% of the original performance while using only 15-25% of the full KV-cache memory, outperforming both quantization and token eviction methods. Notably, Lexico remains effective in low memory regimes where 2-bit quantization fails, achieving up to 1.7x better compression on LongBench and GSM8K while maintaining high accuracy.

paragraphs: Lexico compresses the key-value cache used by language models through sparse coding. Its central finding is that cache contents can be accurately approximated using combinations of only a few elements from a small dictionary. The dictionary contains 4k atoms and is input-agnostic, supporting compression across different prompts, tasks, and models.

The method uses orthogonal matching pursuit to construct these sparse approximations. Controlling how many dictionary elements participate gives direct control over sparsity and therefore flexible compression ratios. This makes the size of the representation an explicit adjustable quantity within the compression method.

On GSM8K, evaluations across Mistral, Llama 3, and Qwen2.5 retain 90–95% of original performance while using 15–25% of the full cache memory. The paper reports better results than quantization and token eviction methods. Lexico also remains effective in low-memory settings where 2-bit quantization fails, with up to 1.7 times better compression on LongBench and GSM8K while retaining high accuracy. These findings support sparse dictionary representations as a useful option for severe cache-memory constraints.
summary.tldr: Lexico compresses language-model KV caches with sparse dictionary representations, retaining much of the original performance at substantially lower memory use.

title: Lexico: Extreme KV Cache Compression via Sparse Coding over Universal Dictionaries

abstract: Reinforcement learning with offline data suffers from Q-value extrapolation errors. To address this issue, we first demonstrate that linear extrapolation of the Q-function beyond the data range is particularly problematic. To mitigate this, we propose guiding the gradual decrease of Q-values outside the data range, which is achieved through reward scaling with layer normalization (RS-LN) and a penalization mechanism for infeasible actions (PA). By combining RS-LN and PA, we develop a new algorithm called PARS. We evaluate PARS across a range of tasks, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art algorithms in both offline training and online fine-tuning on the D4RL benchmark, with notable success in the challenging AntMaze Ultra task.

To address this issue, we first demonstrate that linear extrapolation of the Q-function beyond the data range is particularly problematic. To mitigate this, we propose guiding the gradual decrease of Q-values outside the data range, which is achieved through reward scaling with layer normalization (RS-LN) and a penalization mechanism for infeasible actions (PA). By combining RS-LN and PA, we develop a new algorithm called PARS. We evaluate PARS across a range of tasks, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art algorithms in both offline training and online fine-tuning on the D4RL benchmark, with notable success in the challenging AntMaze Ultra task.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from offline data must estimate action values using a limited record of experience. Predictions outside that data range can be inaccurate, producing Q-value extrapolation errors. This paper first shows that linear extrapolation of the Q-function beyond the available data is particularly problematic, motivating a different shape for those out-of-range predictions.

The proposed approach guides Q-values to decrease gradually outside the data range. It combines reward scaling with layer normalization, called RS-LN, and a mechanism that penalizes infeasible actions, called PA. Together these components form PARS. Their shared purpose is to influence value estimates where extrapolation would otherwise make unsupported actions appear attractive.

The authors evaluate PARS during both offline training and subsequent online fine-tuning. On the D4RL benchmark, they report better performance than state-of-the-art algorithms across the evaluated tasks, including notable success on AntMaze Ultra. The findings connect a specific diagnosis of extrapolation behavior with practical value-estimation changes, showing benefits in learning from fixed data and in continuing to learn through interaction.
summary.tldr: PARS combines reward scaling, layer normalization, and infeasible-action penalties to reduce harmful Q-value extrapolation in offline reinforcement learning.

title: Penalizing Infeasible Actions and Reward Scaling in Reinforcement Learning with Offline Data

abstract: Despite the success of Instruction Tuning (IT) in training large language models (LLMs), such models often leverage spurious or biased features learnt from their training data and can become misaligned, leading to undesired behaviours. While existing techniques can steer model behaviour at inference-time, they are often post-hoc and do not embed steering as an intrinsic model feature. In this work, we introduce Focus Instruction Tuning (FIT), which trains LLMs to condition their responses by focusing on specific features whilst ignoring others, leading to different behaviours based on what features are specified. Across diverse benchmarks, we demonstrate that FIT: (i) successfully steers behaviour at inference time; (ii) increases robustness by amplifying core task signals and down-weighting spurious cues; (iii) mitigates social bias by suppressing demographic attributes; and (iv) generalises under distribution shifts and to previously unseen focus features. FIT therefore offers a lightweight, intrinsic mechanism for building more robust, fair, and easily controllable LLMs.

paragraphs: Instruction-tuned language models can still rely on biased or misleading features learned from their training data. This paper introduces Focus Instruction Tuning, or FIT, to make selective attention to features part of the model's trained behavior. The model learns to shape its response according to instructions about which features to use and which to ignore.

This creates a control mechanism that is learned during training and used at inference time. Different feature specifications can produce different behavior from the same model. The intended benefit is to strengthen signals relevant to the task while reducing reliance on spurious cues, giving feature-level instructions a direct role in how responses are produced.

Across diverse benchmarks, the authors report successful steering, improved robustness, and reduced social bias through suppression of demographic attributes. They also observe generalization under distribution shifts and to focus features not encountered previously. These findings support FIT as a lightweight way to build controllability into language models, with empirical benefits extending beyond the exact feature specifications used during training.
summary.tldr: Focus Instruction Tuning teaches language models to follow feature-level guidance, improving steering, robustness, and bias mitigation across benchmarks.

title: Focus On This, Not That! Steering LLMs with Adaptive Feature Specification

abstract: Face Recognition (FR) tasks have made significant progress with the advent of Deep Neural Networks, particularly through margin-based triplet losses that embed facial images into high-dimensional feature spaces. During training, these contrastive losses focus exclusively on identity information as labels. However, we observe a multiscale geometric structure emerging in the embedding space, influenced by interpretable facial (e.g., hair color) and image attributes (e.g., contrast). We propose a geometric approach to describe the dependence or invariance of FR models to these attributes and introduce a physics-inspired alignment metric. We evaluate the proposed metric on controlled, simplified models and widely used FR models fine-tuned with synthetic data for targeted attribute augmentation. Our findings reveal that the models exhibit varying degrees of invariance across different attributes, providing insight into their strengths and weaknesses and enabling deeper interpretability. Code available here: https://github.com/mantonios107/attrs-fr-embs.
originalAbstract: Face Recognition (FR) tasks have made significant progress with the advent of Deep Neural Networks, particularly through margin-based triplet losses that embed facial images into high-dimensional feature spaces. During training, these contrastive losses focus exclusively on identity information as labels. However, we observe a multiscale geometric structure emerging in the embedding space, influenced by interpretable facial (e.g., hair color) and image attributes (e.g., contrast). We propose a geometric approach to describe the dependence or invariance of FR models to these attributes and introduce a physics-inspired alignment metric. We evaluate the proposed metric on controlled, simplified models and widely used FR models fine-tuned with synthetic data for targeted attribute augmentation. Our findings reveal that the models exhibit varying degrees of invariance across different attributes, providing insight into their strengths and weaknesses and enabling deeper interpretability. Code available here: https://github.com/mantonios107/attrs-fr-embs.

paragraphs: Face recognition models learn numerical representations of faces using training objectives centered on identity. Nevertheless, the resulting representation space can also organize itself around other properties. This paper observes geometric patterns at multiple scales associated with interpretable facial attributes, such as hair color, and image attributes, such as contrast.

The authors develop a geometric approach for describing how strongly a model’s representations depend on particular attributes or remain unchanged when those attributes vary. They introduce an alignment metric inspired by physics to make this relationship measurable. This shifts attention from whether identities can be distinguished to how additional properties shape the representations used for that distinction.

The metric is evaluated on controlled, simplified models and commonly used face recognition models fine-tuned with synthetic data targeting specific attributes. The findings show that invariance varies across attributes: a model may be relatively insensitive to some properties while responding more strongly to others. These differences provide a more interpretable account of model strengths and weaknesses, even when identity is the only information explicitly emphasized by the training labels.
summary.tldr: A geometric metric reveals how facial and image attributes shape face recognition embeddings despite identity-focused training.

title: Attributes Shape the Embedding Space of Face Recognition Models

abstract: Satisfiability Modulo Counting (SMC) is a recently proposed general language to reason about problems integrating statistical and symbolic Artificial Intelligence. An SMC problem is an extended SAT problem in which the truth values of a few Boolean variables are determined by probabilistic inference. Approximate solvers may return solutions that violate constraints. Directly integrating available SAT solvers and probabilistic inference solvers gives exact solutions but results in slow performance because of many back-and-forth invocations of both solvers. We propose KOCO-SMC, an integrated exact SMC solver that efficiently tracks lower and upper bounds in the probabilistic inference process. It enhances computational efficiency by enabling early estimation of probabilistic inference using only partial variable assignments, whereas existing methods require full variable assignments. In the experiment, we compare KOCO-SMC with currently available approximate and exact SMC solvers on large-scale datasets and real-world applications. The proposed KOCO-SMC finds exact solutions with much less time.

paragraphs: Satisfiability Modulo Counting combines logical constraints with probabilistic inference: some Boolean truth values depend on probabilistic calculations. Approximate solvers can produce answers that violate constraints. Combining separate exact logical and probabilistic solvers avoids that problem, but repeated calls back and forth between them can make solving slow.

KOCO-SMC integrates the processes in an exact solver using probabilistic circuits. It tracks lower and upper bounds during probabilistic inference, enabling useful estimation before every variable has been assigned. This allows the solver to work with partial assignments, whereas the existing methods described in the paper require complete assignments for their probabilistic evaluations.

The authors compare KOCO-SMC with available approximate and exact solvers on large-scale datasets and real-world applications. They report that it finds exact solutions in much less time. The contribution is a way to preserve exactness while making probabilistic information available earlier in the logical search, reducing the cost associated with repeatedly coordinating separate solving processes.
summary.tldr: KOCO-SMC speeds up exact reasoning with logical and probabilistic constraints by tracking inference bounds under partial variable assignments.

title: Solving Satisfiability Modulo Counting Exactly with Probabilistic Circuits

abstract: Weak-to-Strong Generalization (Burns et al.,2024) is the phenomenon whereby a strong student, say GPT-4, learns a task from a weak teacher, say GPT-2, and ends up significantly outperforming the teacher. We show that this phenomenon does not require a complex and pretrained learner like GPT-4, can arise even in simple non-pretrained models, simply due to the size advantage of the student. But, we also show that there are inherint limits to the extent of such weak to strong generalization. We consider students and teachers that are random feature models, described by two-layer networks with a random and fixed bottom layer and trained top layer. A weak’ teacher, with a small number of units (i.e. random features), is trained on the population, and a strong’ student, with a much larger number of units (i.e. random features), is trained only on labels generated by the weak teacher. We demonstrate, prove, and understand how the student can outperform the teacher, even though trained only on data labeled by the teacher. We also explain how such weak-to-strong generalization is enabled by early stopping. We then show the quantitative limits of weak-to-strong generalization in this model, and in fact in a much broader class of models, for arbitrary teacher and student feature spaces and a broad class of learning rules, including when the student features are pre-trained or otherwise more informative. In particular, we show that in such models the student’s error can only approach zero if the teacher’s error approaches zero, and a strong student cannot “boost” a slightly-better-then-chance teacher to obtain a small error.

The paper proves that this can happen in simple, non-pretrained random-feature networks. In these two-layer models, the bottom layer remains randomly fixed while the top layer is trained.

The teacher has relatively few features and is trained on the population. A much larger student then learns only from teacher-generated labels. The authors demonstrate and explain how the student's size advantage can produce better performance despite that restricted supervision. They also identify early stopping as a mechanism enabling the improvement.

The paper establishes quantitative limits that extend beyond the specific random-feature setup to arbitrary teacher and student feature spaces and a broad class of learning rules. These limits also cover pretrained or otherwise more informative student features. Within the covered models, student error can approach zero only if teacher error does, and a teacher that is only slightly better than chance cannot be boosted into a low-error student. The results establish both a simple mechanism for improvement and a boundary on its extent.
summary.tldr: Larger random-feature students can outperform their teachers through early stopping, but provable limits prevent arbitrarily strong improvement from weak supervision.

title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization Even in Random Feature Networks, Provably

abstract: Evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) often requires costly human annotations. To address this, LLM-based judges have been proposed, which compare the outputs of two LLMs enabling the ranking of models without human intervention. While several approaches have been proposed, many confounding factors are present between different papers. For instance the model, the prompt and other hyperparameters are typically changed at the same time making apple-to-apple comparisons challenging. In this paper, we propose to systematically analyze and tune the hyperparameters of LLM judges. To alleviate the high cost of evaluating a judge, we propose to leverage multi-objective multi-fidelity which allows to find judges that trades accuracy for cost and also reduce significantly the cost of the search. Our method identifies judges that not only outperform existing benchmarks in accuracy and cost-efficiency but also utilize open-weight models, ensuring greater accessibility and reproducibility.

paragraphs: Language-model judges compare responses from two models, offering a way to rank systems without repeatedly collecting human judgments. Comparing judge designs is difficult, however, when studies change the underlying model, prompt, and other settings simultaneously. This paper proposes systematically analyzing and tuning those choices so their combined effects can be evaluated.

Searching for a good judge is itself expensive because candidate judges must be assessed. The authors use multi-objective, multi-fidelity optimization to reduce that search cost while considering both accuracy and expense. The approach seeks judges offering useful tradeoffs between these objectives, making operating cost part of the selection process.

The method identifies judges that outperform existing benchmarks in accuracy and cost-efficiency. Those judges use open-weight models, supporting accessibility and reproducibility. The contribution concerns both the resulting judge designs and the efficiency of finding them. It shows that systematic tuning can improve automated evaluation while accounting for the resources needed to search for and use a judge.
summary.tldr: Multi-objective, multi-fidelity tuning finds accurate, cost-efficient open-weight LLM judges while substantially reducing the cost of the search.

title: Tuning LLM Judge Design Decisions for 1/1000 of the Cost

abstract: Fine-tuning large pretrained Transformer models can focus on either introducing a small number of new learnable parameters (parameter efficiency) or editing representations of a small number of tokens using lightweight modules (representation efficiency). While the pioneering method LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) inherently balances parameter, compute, and memory efficiency, many subsequent variants trade off compute and memory efficiency and/or performance to further reduce fine-tuning parameters. To address this limitation and unify parameter-efficient and representation-efficient fine-tuning, we propose Weight-Generative Fine-Tuning (WeGeFT, pronounced wee-gift), a novel approach that learns to generate fine-tuning weights directly from the pretrained weights. WeGeFT employs a simple low-rank formulation consisting of two linear layers, either shared across multiple layers of the pretrained model or individually learned for different layers. This design achieves multi-faceted efficiency in parameters, representations, compute, and memory, while maintaining or exceeding the performance of LoRA and its variants. Extensive experiments on commonsense reasoning, arithmetic reasoning, instruction following, code generation, and visual recognition verify the effectiveness of our proposed WeGeFT.

paragraphs: Efficient fine-tuning can reduce the number of learned parameters or limit how many token representations are edited. However, reducing parameter count alone can come with higher computation, memory use, or lower performance. This paper introduces WeGeFT to bring these efficiency goals together by learning to generate fine-tuning weights directly from pretrained weights.

The generator uses a low-rank construction containing two linear layers. These layers can be shared across multiple pretrained layers or learned separately for different layers. This simple formulation provides the mechanism for adapting the model while pursuing efficiency in parameters, representations, computation, and memory at the same time.

The authors report that WeGeFT maintains or exceeds the performance of LoRA and its variants while achieving these multiple forms of efficiency. Experiments cover commonsense reasoning, arithmetic reasoning, instruction following, code generation, and visual recognition. The findings support weight generation as a broadly useful adaptation strategy across the evaluated tasks, with efficiency assessed beyond parameter count alone.
summary.tldr: WeGeFT generates adaptation weights from pretrained weights, combining several forms of efficiency while matching or exceeding LoRA-family performance.

title: WeGeFT: Weight-Generative Fine-Tuning for Multi-Faceted Efficient Adaptation of Large Models

abstract: 3D multiple object tracking (MOT) plays a crucial role in autonomous driving perception. Recent end-to-end query-based trackers simultaneously detect and track objects, which have shown promising potential for the 3D MOT task. However, existing methods are still in the early stages of development and lack systematic improvements, failing to track objects in certain complex scenarios, like occlusions and the small size of target object’s situations. In this paper, we first summarize the current end-to-end 3D MOT framework by decomposing it into three constituent parts: query initialization, query propagation, and query matching. Then we propose corresponding improvements, which lead to a strong yet simple tracker: S2-Track. Specifically, for query initialization, we present 2D-Prompted Query Initialization, which leverages predicted 2D object and depth information to prompt an initial estimate of the object’s 3D location. For query propagation, we introduce an Uncertainty-aware Probabilistic Decoder to capture the uncertainty of complex environment in object prediction with probabilistic attention. For query matching, we propose a Hierarchical Query Denoising strategy to enhance training robustness and convergence. As a result, our S2-Track achieves state-of-the-art performance on nuScenes benchmark, i.e., 66.3% AMOTA on test split, surpassing the previous best end-to-end solution by a significant margin of 8.9% AMOTA. We achieve 1st place on the nuScenes tracking task leaderboard.

summary.tldr: S2-Track improves query initialization, uncertainty-aware propagation, and matching to achieve leading reported nuScenes 3D tracking performance.

title: S2-Track: A Simple yet Strong Approach for End-to-End 3D Multi-Object Tracking

abstract: In overparameterized logistic regression, gradient descent (GD) iterates diverge in norm while converging in direction to the maximum $\ell_2$-margin solution—a phenomenon known as the implicit bias of GD. This work investigates additional regularization effects induced by early stopping in well-specified high-dimensional logistic regression. We first demonstrate that the excess logistic risk vanishes for early stopped GD but diverges to infinity for GD iterates at convergence. This suggests that early stopped GD is well-calibrated, whereas asymptotic GD is statistically inconsistent. Second, we show that to attain a small excess zero-one risk, polynomially many samples are sufficient for early stopped GD, while exponentially many samples are necessary for any interpolating estimator, including asymptotic GD. This separation underscores the statistical benefits of early stopping in the overparameterized regime. Finally, we establish nonasymptotic bounds on the norm and angular differences between early stopped GD and $\ell_2$-regularized empirical risk minimizer, thereby connecting the implicit regularization of GD with explicit $\ell_2$-regularization.

paragraphs: In overparameterized logistic regression, gradient descent can keep increasing the size of its parameter vector while its direction approaches the maximum ℓ2-margin solution. This paper asks whether stopping earlier provides statistical benefits beyond that limiting directional behavior. Its analysis concerns a well-specified, high-dimensional logistic-regression setting, making the modeling assumptions central to the conclusions.

The authors show that excess logistic risk vanishes for early-stopped gradient descent but grows without bound for the iterates as training approaches its limit. They interpret this as suggesting good calibration for early stopping and statistical inconsistency for asymptotic gradient descent. Thus, the eventual direction of the parameters does not by itself establish good probability predictions.

For classification error, they establish another separation: polynomially many samples suffice for early stopping to achieve small excess zero-one risk, whereas any interpolating estimator requires exponentially many in the analyzed setting. Finally, finite-sample bounds compare the norm and angle of early-stopped solutions with explicitly ℓ2-regularized solutions, connecting stopping time to regularization.
summary.tldr: Under well-specified high-dimensional logistic regression, early stopping yields strong risk and sample-efficiency benefits over training toward an interpolating limit.

title: Benefits of Early Stopping in Gradient Descent for Overparameterized Logistic Regression

abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), which aligns a diffusion model with input prompt, has become a crucial step in building reliable generative AI models. Most works in this area uses a discrete-time formulation, which is prone to induced errors, and often not applicable to models with higher-order/black-box solvers. The objective of this study is to develop a disciplined approach to fine-tuning diffusion models using continuous-time RL, formulated as a stochastic control problem with a reward function that aligns the end result (terminal state) with input prompt. The key idea is to treat score matching as controls or actions, and thereby connecting to policy optimization and regularization in continuous-time RL. To carry out this idea, we lay out a new policy optimization framework for continuous-time RL, and illustrate its potential in enhancing the value networks design space via leveraging the structural property of diffusion models. We validate the advantages of our method by experiments in downstream tasks of fine-tuning large-scale Text2Image models, Stable Diffusion v1.5.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning diffusion models with reward feedback aims to make their generated outputs better match prompts. Many approaches formulate this process in discrete time, which can introduce errors and often does not accommodate higher-order or black-box solvers. This paper develops a continuous-time reinforcement learning formulation for the fine-tuning problem.

The authors express generation as stochastic control, with a reward assessing how well the final output aligns with the prompt. The key move is to treat score matching as the control or action, connecting the diffusion model’s learned behavior to policy optimization and regularization. This creates a framework for optimizing the generative process in continuous time.

The work also explores how diffusion structure can inform the design of value networks within this policy optimization framework. Experiments on downstream fine-tuning tasks using Stable Diffusion v1.5 validate advantages of the method. Its contribution combines a disciplined mathematical formulation with an empirical application, showing how the continuous-time view can guide both optimization and the supporting networks used to evaluate future reward.
summary.tldr: Treating diffusion scores as control actions enables a continuous-time reinforcement learning framework for reward-guided fine-tuning of text-to-image models.

title: Score as Action: Fine Tuning Diffusion Generative Models by Continuous-time Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Sampling from unnormalized multimodal distributions with limited density evaluations remains a fundamental challenge in machine learning and natural sciences. Successful approaches construct a bridge between a tractable reference and the target distribution. Parallel Tempering (PT) serves as the gold standard, while recent diffusion-based approaches offer a continuous alternative at the cost of neural training. In this work, we introduce Conditional Diffusion Sampling (CDS), a framework that combines these two paradigms. To this end, we derive Conditional Interpolants, a class of stochastic processes whose transport dynamics are governed by an exact, closed-form stochastic differential equation (SDE), requiring no neural approximation. Although these dynamics require sampling from a non-trivial initialization distribution, we show both theoretically and empirically that the cost of this initialization diminishes for sufficiently short diffusion times. CDS leverages this by a two-stage procedure: (1) PT is used to efficiently sample the initial distribution, and then (2) samples are transported via the transport SDE. This combination couples the robust global exploration of PT with efficient local transport. Experiments suggest that CDS has the potential to achieve a superior trade-off between sample quality and density evaluation cost compared to state-of-the-art samplers.

paragraphs: Sampling becomes difficult when a target distribution has several separated regions of high probability and evaluating its density is expensive. Conditional Diffusion Sampling combines two ways of approaching this problem: Parallel Tempering for exploration and diffusion-based transport for moving samples toward the target. The aim is to use density evaluations more effectively without training a neural transport model.

The mathematical ingredient is a family of Conditional Interpolants whose transport follows an exact, closed-form stochastic differential equation. These processes require samples from a challenging initialization distribution. The authors show theoretically and empirically that obtaining this initialization becomes less costly when diffusion times are sufficiently short, giving a concrete condition under which the construction becomes attractive.

The algorithm therefore first uses Parallel Tempering to sample the initialization and then transports those samples through the derived dynamics. This assigns global exploration and local movement to complementary procedures. Experiments suggest the combination could offer a better trade-off between sample quality and density-evaluation cost than leading samplers; the abstract presents this as potential supported by experiments.
summary.tldr: Conditional Diffusion Sampling combines Parallel Tempering with exact diffusion transport to potentially improve sampling efficiency without neural training.

title: Conditional Diffusion Sampling

abstract: Deep neural networks currently provide the leading quantitative models of neural responses in sensory systems. However, these networks remain implausible as models of sensory development, largely because they rely on supervised training with label efficiency far exceeding that of biological learning. Furthermore, these models are typically trained on manually curated datasets that lack the statistical properties of the natural environments to which the brain is exposed. Here, we demonstrate that models trained with unsupervised objectives on real-world data significantly outperform supervised models in predicting brain responses across both human auditory and visual cortex. We show that this performance advantage is not driven by network architecture or dataset size, but rather by the data distribution. Crucially, we find that unsupervised models trained on real-world data exhibit remarkable out-of-distribution generalization: a model trained exclusively on Mandarin speech accurately predicts English-driven brain responses, and a model trained on infant head-cam footage predicts adult visual responses to curated object images. Together, our results illustrate how deep neural networks can be used to reveal the real-world statistics that shape neural representations in the brain.
