paragraphs: Reward scores can become unreliable guides during online language-model reinforcement learning. This paper identifies directional inconsistency: a few highly rewarded responses imply changes in representation space that strongly disagree with the rest of the batch. Such disagreement can create high-variance updates and unstable training, particularly when rewards are noisy or misspecified.

GeoAlign curates generated responses using this geometric information. It builds preference pairs for the same prompt and learns an online projection of response hidden states that concentrates directions associated with reward ordering. It then measures angular disagreement with a batch consensus direction and rectifies inconsistent responses using stable alternatives for the same prompt.

The authors describe the curation mechanism as forward-pass only, with negligible overhead. In dialogue alignment using a learned reward model and mathematics using binary verified rewards, GeoAlign improves final performance and reduces training oscillation, outperforming the named comparison methods. The results suggest that agreement within learned representations can complement reward scores as a reliability signal when choosing which generated responses should shape policy updates.
summary.tldr: GeoAlign stabilizes online reinforcement learning by correcting high-reward responses whose representation-space directions disagree with the batch.

title: GeoAlign: Geometric Rollout Curation for Robust LLM Reinforcement Learning

abstract: According to the reformulated Learned Helplessness theory, repeated exposure to uncontrollable negative events can foster a depressogenic attributional style—increasing susceptibility to depression yet remaining a tractable target for cognitive therapy. Computational research on attributional cognition, however, is hampered by the lack of large-scale datasets and robust evaluation protocols. In this work, we introduce the Attributional Style Transfer Dataset (ASTD) along with dedicated evaluation metrics, the first benchmark designed to model, assess, and reframe attributional explanations at scale. Constructed via a Prevent–Filter–Validate pipeline that integrates LLM-based generation with specialist validation, ASTD contains 42,000 real-world events paired with psychologically grounded attributions spanning seven styles. Using this dataset, we address two key challenges: (1) scalable assessment of attributional style via both supervised classifiers and zero/few-shot LLMs; and (2) attributional reframing and evaluation, where we propose automatic evaluation metrics to quantify psychological validity. Furthermore, we leverage our proposed metrics to construct a preference dataset, fine-tuning LLMs with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and achieving substantial gains in reframing quality. Together, our dataset, metrics, and methodology offer a new paradigm for understanding and modeling attributional style, with direct implications for scalable and adaptive mental health interventions.

paragraphs: Attributional style concerns how people explain events. The paper draws on a theory connecting repeated uncontrollable negative experiences with explanatory styles that can increase susceptibility to depression and remain targets for cognitive therapy. Its computational focus is the shortage of large datasets and evaluation protocols for assessing and reframing these explanations.

The Attributional Style Transfer Dataset contains 42,000 real-world events paired with psychologically grounded attributions across seven styles. It is constructed through a Prevent–Filter–Validate pipeline combining language-model generation with specialist validation. The authors use it to study style assessment through supervised classifiers and zero- or few-shot language models, alongside the task of rewriting attributions into different explanatory styles.

The paper also introduces automatic metrics for psychological validity and uses them to build preference data for Direct Preference Optimization. Fine-tuning with that data produces substantial reported gains in reframing quality. The contribution joins a dataset, assessment methods, and a training signal for reframing, providing computational tools with potential implications for scalable mental health interventions.
summary.tldr: ASTD supplies specialist-validated attribution data and evaluation methods that support improved language-model assessment and reframing of explanatory styles.

title: Modeling Attributional Style at Scale: A Dataset and Analysis for Psychological Attribution Assessment and Reframing

abstract: Graph anomaly detection (GAD) is a fundamental task in graph learning. However, most existing methods rely on the homophily assumption, which posits that connected nodes tend to share the same labels. This assumption often fails in the presence of edge heterophily, leading to degraded performance. We first observe that down-weighting heterophilic edges, relative to the original or randomly weighted graphs, results in a more concentrated spectral energy distribution, thereby facilitating the learning of discriminative spectral representations. Moreover, existing methods typically embed graphs in Euclidean spaces, neglecting the importance of heterophily in manifold spaces. Motivated by these observations, we propose HSMAD, a novel framework for GAD. It consists of two key components: the Heterophily-Weighted Spectral Filtering module, which reconstructs the Laplacian using heterophily-based edge weighting for spectral filtering, and the Heterophily-Routed Manifold Update module, which routes neighborhood messages to the appropriate manifold for node feature updates, enabling curvature-adaptive representation learning. These spectral and geometric representations are jointly leveraged for anomaly detection. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets show that HSMAD achieves state-of-the-art performance across the average F1-Macro, AUROC, AUPRC, and G-Mean. Specifically, the average F1-Macro score improves by 2.66% over the best-performing method.

paragraphs: HSMAD detects anomalies in graphs where connected nodes may have different labels. Many graph methods assume the opposite: that neighbors are similar. The paper observes that reducing the weight of edges connecting dissimilar nodes concentrates spectral energy compared with original or randomly weighted graphs, making discriminative spectral representations easier to learn.

The framework uses this observation in two complementary components. Heterophily-Weighted Spectral Filtering rebuilds the graph Laplacian using edge weights based on heterophily, changing how the graph is filtered. Heterophily-Routed Manifold Update sends neighborhood messages to appropriate manifold spaces for node updates. This allows the geometry of the representation to adapt through curvature, rather than restricting every representation to Euclidean space.

HSMAD combines these spectral and geometric representations for anomaly detection. Across six real-world datasets, it reports leading average F1-Macro, AUROC, AUPRC, and G-Mean results. Average F1-Macro improves by 2.66% over the best-performing comparison method. These findings support using neighbor dissimilarity to guide both graph filtering and representation geometry.
summary.tldr: HSMAD uses differences between connected nodes to guide spectral filtering and geometric representations for graph anomaly detection.

title: HSMAD: Heterophily-Driven Spectral and Manifold Learning for Graph Anomaly Detection

abstract: Peer review, the bedrock of scientific advancement in machine learning (ML), is strained by a crisis of scale. Exponential growth in manuscript submissions to premier ML venues such as NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR is outpacing the finite capacity of qualified reviewers, leading to concerns about review quality, consistency, and reviewer fatigue. This position paper argues that AI-assisted peer review must become an urgent research and infrastructure priority. We advocate for a comprehensive AI-augmented ecosystem, leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) not as replacements for human judgment, but as sophisticated collaborators for authors, reviewers, and Area Chairs (ACs). We propose specific roles for AI in enhancing factual verification, guiding reviewer performance, assisting authors in quality improvement, and supporting ACs in decision-making. Crucially, we contend that the development of such systems hinges on access to more granular, structured, and ethically-sourced peer review process data. We outline a research agenda, including illustrative experiments, to develop and validate these AI assistants, and discuss significant technical and ethical challenges. We call upon the ML community to proactively build this AI-assisted future, ensuring the continued integrity and scalability of scientific validation, while maintaining high standards of peer review.

paragraphs: This position paper treats the growing volume of machine-learning submissions as a research infrastructure problem. Submission growth is outstripping the supply of qualified reviewers, placing pressure on review quality, consistency, and reviewer workload. The authors argue that developing AI assistance for the entire review process should become an urgent community priority.

Their proposed ecosystem assigns language models supporting roles for several participants. Assistants could help verify factual claims, guide reviewer performance, improve manuscripts, and support area chairs making decisions. Human judgment remains central. The proposal therefore concerns a network of complementary forms of assistance across the publication process, rather than a single system responsible for evaluating papers.

The authors identify access to detailed, structured, ethically obtained review-process data as a condition for developing these systems. They outline a research agenda with illustrative experiments for building and validating assistants, while discussing technical and ethical challenges. The intended outcome is a review process that can handle greater scale while preserving the integrity and standards of scientific assessment.
summary.tldr: The authors call for an AI-assisted peer-review ecosystem that supports human judgment and is developed using detailed, ethically sourced process data.

abstract: LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) is a useful tool toachieve the shrinkage and variable selection simultaneously. Since LASSO uses the $L_1$ penalty, the optimization should rely on the quadratic program (QP) or generalnon-linear program which is known to be computational intensive. In this paper, we propose agradient descent algorithm for LASSO. Even though the final result is slightly less accurate, the proposed algorithmis computationally simpler than QP or non-linear program, and so can be applied to large size problems. We provide the convergence rate of the algorithm, and illustrate it withsimulated models as well as real data sets.

Since LASSO uses the $L_1$ penalty, the optimization should rely on the quadratic program (QP) or generalnon-linear program which is known to be computational intensive. In this paper, we propose agradient descent algorithm for LASSO. Even though the final result is slightly less accurate, the proposed algorithmis computationally simpler than QP or non-linear program, and so can be applied to large size problems. We provide the convergence rate of the algorithm, and illustrate it withsimulated models as well as real data sets.

paragraphs: LASSO combines coefficient shrinkage with variable selection, making it useful when a model should reduce the influence of some inputs and exclude others. This paper addresses the computational burden of fitting such a model. The authors identify quadratic programming and general nonlinear programming approaches to the L1-penalized problem as computationally intensive.

They propose a gradient descent algorithm for LASSO that is computationally simpler than those optimization approaches. The intended benefit is applicability to large problems. This comes with an explicit tradeoff: the authors describe the final result as slightly less accurate, so the computational simplification is accompanied by a modest loss in accuracy.

The paper provides a convergence rate for the algorithm and illustrates its behavior using simulated models and real datasets. Its contribution is a simpler optimization route to LASSO's combined shrinkage and selection objective. The convergence analysis and examples support examining that route when the computational demands of the alternative formulations become a central concern.
summary.tldr: Gradient LASSO trades slightly lower accuracy for a computationally simpler optimization method suited to large problems.

title: Gradient LASSO for feature selection
Data association for topic intensity tracking

abstract: This paper introduces a new problem for which machine-learning tools may make an impact. The problem considered is termed “compressive sensing”, in which a real signal of dimension N is measured accurately based on K ≪ N real measurements. This is achieved under the assumption that the underlying signal has a sparse representation in some basis (e.g., wavelets). In this paper we demonstrate how techniques developed in machine learning, speciﬁcally sparse Bayesian regression and active learning, may be leveraged to this new problem. We also point out future research directions in compressive sensing of interest to the machinelearning community.

paragraphs: Compressive sensing asks how a signal with many coordinates can be measured accurately using far fewer measurements. The paper presents this as a problem where machine-learning methods may contribute. The essential assumption is that the signal has a sparse representation in some basis, such as wavelets: relatively few coefficients are needed to express it.

The authors demonstrate how sparse Bayesian regression and active learning can be applied to this setting. Sparse regression connects the reconstruction problem to learning a compact coefficient representation. Active learning brings the question of choosing measurements into the same discussion, linking signal estimation with decisions about what information to collect.

The significance is the connection between a measurement problem and tools developed for learning from data. The ability to use fewer measurements rests on the stated sparse-representation assumption, rather than applying to arbitrary signals without structure. Alongside demonstrating these connections, the paper identifies further compressive-sensing research directions for the machine-learning community.
summary.tldr: The paper connects compressive sensing with sparse Bayesian regression and active learning under the assumption that signals have sparse representations.

title: Bayesian compressive sensing and projection optimization

abstract: Policy gradient approaches are a powerful instrument for learning how to interact with the environment.Existing approaches have focused on propositional and continuous domains only. Without extensive feature engineering, it is difficult -- if not impossible -- to apply them within structured domains, in which e.g. there is a varying number of objects and relations among them. In this paper, we describe a non-parametric policy gradient approach -- called NPPG -- that overcomes this limitation. The key idea is to apply Friedmann's gradient boosting: policies are represented as a weighted sum of regression models grown in an stage-wise optimization. Employing off-the-shelf regression learners, NPPG can deal with propositional, continuous, and relational domains in a unified way. Our experimental results show that it can even improve on established results.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods learn how to act through interaction with an environment. Applying them to structured domains can require extensive feature engineering, especially when the number of objects and their relationships varies. This paper introduces non-parametric policy gradients, or NPPG, to handle such domains within the same approach used for propositional and continuous settings.

The key construction uses gradient boosting. A policy is represented as a weighted sum of regression models, and the collection grows through stage-wise optimization. Off-the-shelf regression learners supply the individual models. This lets the framework draw on regression methods suited to different data representations while retaining a common policy-learning procedure.

The authors report that NPPG can improve on established experimental results. The significance is both representational and practical: the method brings relational domains into a unified policy-gradient treatment and demonstrates that the resulting approach can perform competitively. The stated improvement is a possibility demonstrated experimentally, not a guarantee that boosted policy representations will outperform existing methods in every environment.
summary.tldr: NPPG builds policies through boosted regression models, providing a unified policy-gradient approach for propositional, continuous, and relational domains.

title: Non-parametric policy gradients: a unified treatment of propositional and relational domains

abstract: We propose a novel attentional model for simultaneous object tracking and recognition that is driven by gaze data. Motivated by theories of the human perceptual system, the model consists of two interacting pathways: ventral and dorsal. The ventral pathway models object appearance and classification using deep (factored)-restricted Boltzmann machines. At each point in time, the observations consist of retinal images, with decaying resolution toward the periphery of the gaze. The dorsal pathway models the location, orientation, scale and speed of the attended object. The posterior distribution of these states is estimated with particle filtering. Deeper in the dorsal pathway, we encounter an attentional mechanism that learns to control gazes so as to minimize tracking uncertainty. The approach is modular (with each module easily replaceable with more sophisticated algorithms), straightforward to implement, practically efficient, and works well in simple video sequences.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a gaze-driven model that tracks objects and recognizes them simultaneously. Its observations resemble retinal images: resolution decreases away from the gaze location. This makes attention relevant to the information available for both tasks, since different gaze choices change which parts of the scene are represented most clearly.

Two interacting pathways divide the work. A ventral pathway models object appearance and classification with deep factored restricted Boltzmann machines. A dorsal pathway models location, orientation, scale, and speed, using particle filtering to estimate uncertainty over these states. An attentional mechanism within the dorsal pathway learns to control gaze with the aim of reducing tracking uncertainty.

The architecture connects recognition, motion-state estimation, and the choice of where to look within one modular approach. The authors describe its components as replaceable, its implementation as straightforward, and its computation as practically efficient. They report that it works well on simple video sequences, which is the stated scope of the practical success described in the abstract.
summary.tldr: A modular two-pathway model combines recognition and tracking with learned gaze control that aims to reduce tracking uncertainty.

title: Learning attentional policies for tracking and recognition in video with deep networks

abstract: This paper considers the problem of matrix completion, when some number of the columns are arbitrarily corrupted. It is well-known that standard algorithms for matrix completion can return arbitrarily poor results, if even a single column is corrupted. What can be done if a large number, or even a constant fraction of columns are corrupted? In this paper, we study this very problem, and develop an robust and efficient algorithm for its solution. One direct application comes from robust collaborative filtering. Here, some number of users are so-called manipulators, and try to skew the predictions of the algorithm. Significantly, our results hold {\it without any assumptions on the observed entries of the manipulated columns}.

paragraphs: Matrix completion attempts to infer missing entries from an incompletely observed matrix. This paper studies the added difficulty of columns containing arbitrary corruption. The motivation is severe: standard completion algorithms can produce arbitrarily poor results even when only one column has been corrupted, making column-level contamination a consequential source of failure.

The authors investigate the case of many corrupted columns, including a constant fraction of the matrix’s columns, and develop a robust, efficient algorithm for the problem. A central feature of their results is that they impose no assumptions on the observed entries of the manipulated columns. The corrupt observations are therefore not required to follow a specified benign pattern.

Robust collaborative filtering provides a direct application. In that setting, some users act as manipulators who try to skew the system’s predictions. The paper connects this adversarial behavior to corrupted columns in matrix completion. Its contribution addresses the recovery problem while explicitly allowing unrestricted observed entries within those manipulated columns.
summary.tldr: The paper develops robust matrix completion for corrupted columns without assumptions on the observed entries within the manipulated columns.

title: Robust Matrix Completion and Corrupted Columns

abstract: Latent force models (LFMs) are flexible models that combine mechanistic modelling principles (i.e., physical models) with non-parametric data-driven components. Several key applications of LFMs need non-linearities, which results in analytically intractable inference. In this work we show how non-linear LFMs can be represented as non-linear white noise driven state-space models and present an efficient non-linear Kalman filtering and smoothing based method for approximate state and parameter inference. We illustrate the performance of the proposed methodology via two simulated examples, and apply it to a real-world problem of long-term prediction of GPS satellite orbits.

Several key applications of LFMs need non-linearities, which results in analytically intractable inference. In this work we show how non-linear LFMs can be represented as non-linear white noise driven state-space models and present an efficient non-linear Kalman filtering and smoothing based method for approximate state and parameter inference. We illustrate the performance of the proposed methodology via two simulated examples, and apply it to a real-world problem of long-term prediction of GPS satellite orbits.

paragraphs: Latent force models combine mechanistic descriptions, such as physical models, with flexible components learned from data. This combination is useful when a system has known governing structure alongside influences that need to be inferred. The paper addresses nonlinear versions of these models, for which the required inference becomes analytically intractable.

The authors show how nonlinear latent force models can be represented as nonlinear state-space models driven by white noise. That representation enables an efficient approach based on nonlinear Kalman filtering and smoothing. The method estimates both states and parameters approximately, making the approximation an explicit part of the proposed solution to the inference difficulty.

The methodology is illustrated through two simulated examples and applied to long-term prediction of real GPS satellite orbits. These applications connect the inference framework to dynamical prediction where physical structure matters. The central contribution is the state-space reformulation and its accompanying inference procedure, which make nonlinear latent force modeling accessible to filtering and smoothing techniques.
summary.tldr: A state-space representation enables efficient approximate filtering and smoothing for nonlinear latent force models, including satellite-orbit prediction.

title: State-Space Inference for Non-Linear Latent Force Models with Application to Satellite Orbit Prediction
